text:
President Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.

Trump’s Office of Management and Budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending.”

Most of the cuts are focused on Health and Human Services programs that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.

Also targeted for cuts were a Department of Education program for migrant students, a Department of Justice office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, housing counseling services from the Housing and Urban Development Department and a series of grants from the Health and Human Services Department that the administration called “outright harmful and blatantly ideological.”

A White House news release announcing the funding rescission notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the Obama administration.

Trump’s move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican in a tough reelection campaign and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.

Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions.”

“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”

Under federal law, Congress has 45 days to review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through the November election. The Government Accountability Office, which is an arm of Congress, says the maneuver known as a “pocket rescission” is illegal.

Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse.”

A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in nearly 50 years by blocking $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to block that rescission, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.

The use of a pocket rescission fits into a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exert greater control over the U.S. government, eroding Congress’ power.

What was essentially the last pocket rescission occurred in 1977 when President Carter rescinded it, and the Trump administration argues it’s a legally permissible tool, despite some murkiness, since Carter had initially proposed the claw-back well ahead of the 45-day deadline.

The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the lead Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, described the White House action as “theft from the American people, plain and simple.”

“These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people — not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families,” Murray said.

Murray said that in recent spending negotiations, Democrats fought to include language to prevent the administration from usurping Congress’ power on spending decisions, but Republicans have declined to go along.

“While Trump spends tax dollars on ads promoting himself” — a reference to a taxpayer-paid TV spot that has drawn bipartisan rebuke — “Congress needs to reassert its powers to help people, and it’s past time Republicans join us in that fight,” she said.

In addition to immigrant services, the White House said it was rescinding $70 million for what it called “woke” international education programs, $28 million in grant funding for Health and Human Services research programs, and $9 million in debt relief for foreign countries that fund climate change policies. An additional $10 million was being withheld from a minority business development program.

title: ICE Actions Hit Kansas Meatpacking Operations, Ranchers Say - Bloomberg
description:
Increased actions by US immigration enforcement are creating significant disruption to beefpacking operations in Kansas, an area where nearly all of the country’s major processors have operations.
Thousands of cattle set to be shipped to beef processors have been affected by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity, according to a joint statement from rancher industry groups.
Disruptions have also been reported at “numerous supply chain chokepoints” from beef processors to feed and grain companies, according to the statement.

text:
Client Alert | September 25, 2026

Sept. 18 E.O. and recent actions by the Departments of Labor and Justice and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission reflect Administration’s escalating campaign against alleged discrimination targeting U.S. workers.

On September 18, 2026, the Trump Administration issued an executive order[1] directing greater scrutiny of applications submitted by U.S. companies seeking to sponsor foreign workers in highly skilled positions (commonly referred to as “H-1B visas”). The introduction of the order contains findings of alleged abuse of the H-1B program to disadvantage American employees. Although there are many points that are left undefined in the new order, its issuance, a contemporaneous announcement by the Department of Labor (DOL) Inspector General touting recent actions suspending visa applications from two technology companies, a video from the Chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), and a spate of recent Department of Justice (DOJ) resolutions under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) paint a sobering picture for U.S. employers. In this alert, we survey these developments and include considerations for companies confronting this challenging landscape.

Executive Order

On September 18, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order, accompanied by a proclamation, directing federal agencies to more closely scrutinize H-1B petitions where there is a heightened risk that American workers will be displaced.[2] The order directs the Secretaries of State, Labor, and Homeland Security (DHS) to consider an employer’s recent or planned layoffs of similarly situated U.S. workers when adjudicating H-1B labor condition applications, petitions, and visas, and it calls for greater coordination among the Departments of State, Labor, Homeland Security, Commerce, and Education. Within 30 days, the Department of Labor is directed to review data from previously filed labor condition applications to identify sponsoring employers who may warrant further action under existing law.[3] The order characterizes abuse of the H-1B program as a national security threat, pointing to employers that have laid off U.S. workers while continuing to hire H-1B workers and to outsourcing-based business models.[4] Notably, the order does not itself prohibit an employer from laying off U.S. workers and later sponsoring H-1B workers; rather, it signals that this sequence will invite heightened government scrutiny.[5]

The Trump Administration has also proposed, through a DHS rule, a $103,265 fee for new cap-subject H-1B petitions, an amount close to the $100,000 H-1B fee that a September 2025 presidential proclamation imposed and that a federal court struck down in June 2026.[6]

Department of Labor

DOL has launched “Project Firewall,” an enforcement initiative under which the Secretary of Labor may personally direct investigations of employers suspected of misusing the H-1B program, and has touted the intra-agency collaboration as a “whole-of-government effort” to “proactively combat unlawful discrimination against American workers and properly enforce the law.”[7]

On July 8, 2026, the DOL Office of Inspector General (OIG) announced a major investigation into fraud in the H-1B and PERM systems, conducted with DHS, DOJ, and the White House Fraud Task Force, and reported issuing dozens of subpoenas.[8] On September 8, 2026, the Inspector General announced the first concrete enforcement actions under that investigation – suspension of processing of two technology companies’ PERM applications and H-1B applications.[9]

EEOC

EEOC Acting Chair Andrea Lucas stated in a press release last year that one of her priorities is “protecting American workers from anti-American national origin discrimination,”[10] and in November 2025, the EEOC issued a technical assistance document titled “Discrimination Against American Workers Is Against the Law,” which flags, among other practices, certain job advertisements keyed to visa status and the potentially discriminatory termination of U.S. workers “at a much higher rate” than visa holders.[11] On September 14, 2026, EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas posted a video on LinkedIn and X soliciting charges from workers who believe they experienced anti-American discrimination, asking, among other things, whether they had been “laid off and told to train an H-1B or other guest worker visa holder who replaced” them.[12] The agency has also initiated litigation. In May 2026, for example, it sued an Oregon-based services company alleging that American workers were subjected to anti-American harassment and that one was terminated after complaining.[13]

DOJ and the Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative

DOJ is responsible for enforcing the anti-discrimination provision of the INA, which prohibits employment discrimination in recruitment, hiring, or termination, on the basis of citizenship or immigration status.[14] DOJ primarily investigates complaints filed by individuals, but also has the authority to initiate independent investigations, typically into corporate policies and practices related to recruitment, hiring, or termination.[15] While DOJ has historically focused its enforcement efforts on bias against immigrants, during the first Trump Administration, the division launched a “Protecting U.S. Workers Initiative” specifically aimed at companies alleged to have discriminated against U.S. workers in favor of foreign visa workers. This initiative was relaunched in January 2025.[16]

Since the initiative’s relaunch, DOJ has entered into thirteen settlements.[17] It has also filed at least one administrative complaint against a software company alleging that the company intentionally created a separate, less favorable hiring process that deterred U.S. workers from applying to PERM-related positions.[18]

On August 4, 2026, the Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a $3.2 million settlement with a leading technology company and its subsidiary resolving allegations that the companies violated the anti-discrimination provision of the INA, 8 U.S.C. § 1324b.[19] The August 4, 2026 settlement is the latest in a string of more than a dozen publicly announced matters in which DOJ alleges that the companies engaged in a “pattern or practice of citizenship status discrimination” by preferring workers holding temporary employment visas over U.S. workers when recruiting through the permanent labor certification (PERM) process.[20]

As with other resolutions of this type, DOJ alleged that the technology companies did not allow U.S. workers to submit applications to PERM-related positions in the same manner that the companies accepted applications for non-PERM roles, such as electronically through their external job website.[21] Notwithstanding the amount of the financial penalty, the conduct alleged by DOJ was narrow, involving fewer than 10 PERM-related positions. DOJ alleged that the companies required U.S. workers to submit their applications to PERM roles by mail. DOJ alleged that this additional burden was not required under the PERM process and did not occur during non-PERM recruitment. DOJ also alleged that the companies advertised for the positions on the radio late at night, which DOJ alleged “discourage[d] U.S. workers from applying.”[22]

Under the terms of the settlement, the companies will pay $1.2 million in civil penalties and establish a $2 million back pay fund to compensate alleged victims.[23] In addition, the companies agreed to multiple non-monetary terms: they must adopt a written PERM recruitment policy subject to government pre-approval, post all PERM-related positions on their internal and external career sites, accept electronic applications through the same channels used for ordinary hiring, configure their applicant tracking system so that PERM applications are captured and searchable in the same manner as all other applications, train every employee and agent with a role in PERM recruitment using DOJ-approved materials, and submit semiannual reports detailing each PERM filing, the number of applicants, and the number found qualified.

DOJ’s recent settlements are not its first actions under this theory. In 2021, DOJ resolved a landmark PERM-recruitment matter with a major social media company for a $4.75 million civil penalty and up to $9.5 million in back pay—at the time the largest recovery in the anti-discrimination provision’s history.[24] In 2023, it reached a similar resolution with a major technology company for a $6.75 million civil penalty and an $18.25 million back-pay fund. [25] In each resolution, DOJ alleged that the company reserved positions for visa holders and ran PERM recruitment through less effective channels, such as requiring applications via mail and failing to post roles on its external careers site, in order to deter U.S. applicants.

DOJ has expanded its enforcement reach beyond major companies. Apart from the matter described above, the settlements announced since June 2025 have overwhelmingly involved IT staffing and consulting companies that allegedly posted job advertisements restricting positions to H-1B or other visa holders. The penalties assessed in these matters generally track the number of positions at issue: from approximately $5,000 to $255,000 in the matters involving smaller companies.[26] The forward-looking obligations in these matters are consistent: each company agreed to train its staff, revise its policies, cease placing advertisements that exclude U.S. workers, and submit to a period of DOJ monitoring, consistent with the broader remedial framework described above.[27]

Where companies have not settled, DOJ has shown it will litigate. In its pending administrative complaint against a software company, DOJ alleges that the company created a “separate hiring process that treated U.S. workers less favorably” for seven PERM positions paying between $180,000 and $294,000 per year.[28] U.S. workers were allegedly invited to apply through a dedicated email address that, for ten months, did not accept messages from external accounts, which the company allegedly never investigated, even as applicants for non-PERM positions allegedly applied through its standard careers site.[29] DOJ filed the complaint on April 28, 2026, and the matter remains pending before DOJ’s Office of the Chief Administrative Hearing Officer (OCAHO). Separately, DOL suspended the processing of all of the company’s pending PERM applications.[30]

The administrative forum in which DOJ litigates these matters, OCAHO, has drawn a constitutional challenge. In 2023, DOJ filed an OCAHO complaint alleging that an employer had discriminated against asylees and refugees in hiring, in violation of Section 1324b.[31] Rather than litigate before the agency, the employer sued DOJ in federal district court, arguing that OCAHO’s structure is unconstitutional because its administrative law judges issue final decisions that are not subject to review by the Attorney General, in violation of the Appointments Clause. In November 2023, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Texas found that the employer was likely to succeed on that claim and preliminarily enjoined the OCAHO proceeding.[32] The case never reached the merits. In February 2025, DOJ moved to dismiss its own complaint, and OCAHO dismissed it with prejudice.[33] The constitutional questions remain unresolved, leaving respondents with a potential structural defense to DOJ’s chosen forum.

Key Takeaways for Employers

The recent announcements and enforcement actions confirm that H-1B petitions and PERM recruitment are now key parts of the Trump Administration’s focus on anti-U.S. worker employment discrimination. A few themes emerge from related settlements and Administration actions.

DOJ does not view PERM compliance as a complete defense to a discrimination claim. Even companies technically complying with the DOL’s PERM recruitment regulations are not immune to scrutiny. DOJ’s theory in its resolved matters appears to have been that employers ran PERM recruitment through channels less effective than their ordinary hiring: mail-only applications, late-night radio advertising, positions not posted on the careers site, applicants not integrated in the applicant tracking system. Companies should consider whether aligning PERM recruitment with their standard hiring processes better inoculates them from DOJ’s scrutiny, even when that alignment goes beyond DOL’s regulatory requirements.

Specific steps to consider if and as appropriate. Across its resolved matters, DOJ has required a consistent set of PERM-recruitment reforms, which together offer a checklist of sorts for companies to consider as appropriate: post all PERM positions on the internal and external career sites used for ordinary roles, accept electronic applications through those same channels rather than requiring mailed applications, capture PERM applicants in the applicant-tracking system so they remain searchable and can be considered for other openings, adopt a written PERM recruitment policy prohibiting citizenship-status discrimination, train recruiters and hiring managers on their anti-discrimination obligations, and reject U.S. applicants only for documented, lawful, job-related reasons. Aligning PERM recruitment with ordinary hiring along these lines both reduces enforcement risk and mirrors what DOJ has required of settling companies.

Workforce reductions invite government scrutiny. The EEOC’s recent public guidance identifies, as potential evidence of unlawful discrimination, “a company terminating American workers who are on the ‘bench’ between job assignments at a much higher rate than employees who are visa guest workers” and “subjecting U.S. workers to more laborious application methods than H-1B visa holders during the PERM labor certification process.”[34] DOL states that it is “prioritizing investigations where there are signs of displacements,” and “inadequate recruitment of U.S. workers.”[35] The DOJ and DOL also appear to be scrutinizing companies in similar circumstances. Companies should be aware that conducting a reduction in force, and then continuing to sponsor PERMs or file H-1B applications, may generate government interest. Employers planning a reduction in force should involve counsel early, assess the risk of citizenship-status discrimination claims, and consider whether it is appropriate to proceed with pending and contemplated PERM or visa filings.

text:
DALLAS — ICE Dallas arrested 121 individuals during a summer-long enforcement initiative focused on improving public safety and supporting local law enforcement during peak boating season around Lake Lewisville. Two of those arrested are members of the Tren de Aragua transnational gang, which has been designated as a foreign terrorist organization and a specially designated global terrorist group by the U.S. State Department.

The initiative began June 27 and ended on Labor Day weekend. ICE Dallas led the operation with support from various state and federal agencies. The mission focused on identifying unlawfully present foreign nationals, assisting in lake-related investigations, and allowing local law enforcement to spend more time on the water enforcing boating and safety laws and protecting the public.

“This operation highlights the success we can achieve when federal, state and local law enforcement partners work together toward a common public safety mission,” said ICE Dallas Field Office Director Miguel Vergara. “ICE is committed to upholding the law, enforcing our nation’s immigration laws, and removing individuals who pose a threat to our communities. These arrests reflect our continued focus on public safety and the rule of law.”

The individuals arrested during the operation had criminal histories that included assault, family violence, assault causing bodily injury, theft, burglary, sexual assault of a child, indecency with a child by sexual contact, evading arrest or detention with a vehicle, driving while intoxicated, boating while intoxicated, criminal mischief, criminal negligence, and various traffic-related offenses.

Among those arrested were:

Both individuals were under investigation by the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department for allegedly operating an illegal livery operation on Lake Lewisville. Illegal livery operations can create significant public safety risks because they may bypass safety, inspection, and insurance and operator requirements. A similar illegal livery operation was connected to the death of an Air Force cadet over the 2025 Memorial Day weekend on Grapevine Lake.

The operation also resulted four more arrests, including those whose criminal histories or immigration histories presented additional public safety and immigration enforcement concerns.

ICE’s arrest of the 121 illegal aliens in the Lake Lewisville area this summer is in keeping with President Trump and Secretary Mullin’s promise to make America safe again, and in furtherance of the mandate of the American people to arrest and remove illegal aliens from American communities.

The summer water safety initiative highlights the value of interagency cooperation during high-traffic recreational periods, when law enforcement agencies must balance public safety demands on the water with criminal and immigration enforcement priorities on land. By assisting with identification and investigative support, ICE Dallas helped partner agencies focus resources where they were most needed while ensuring individuals who posed public safety concerns were taken into custody.

“This operation allowed our agency to use limited resources more effectively,” said Vergara. “The results speak for themselves: 121 arrests, public safety threats off the streets, and stronger coordination among federal, state, and local law enforcement partners.”

text:
The Trump administration scrambled Thursday to halt a number of imminent deportations after an appeals court blocked authorities from expelling people to third countries without a chance to contest their cases, according to documents obtained by The New York Times.

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled late Wednesday that starting immediately, migrants need "a meaningful opportunity" to present evidence that they fear deportation to a third country.

Previously, the government had concluded that it could deport the people without such an opportunity by gaining assurances from the nation taking in the migrants that they would not be persecuted or tortured there. This legal interpretation has allowed the administration to sidestep certain processes, such as the fear screening, and rapidly expel people.

The third-country deportation program has been used by the Trump administration to get around rules barring certain people from being deported to their home countries. James Percival, the top lawyer at the Department of Homeland Security, said this week that more than 25,000 people had been deported to third countries.

The program has drawn criticism because many immigrants have been sent to countries with records of human rights violations.

The court decision adds a new burden for the government as it attempts to rapidly remove people from the United States without allowing their lawyers to try to block their deportation.

On Thursday, as news of the ruling spread inside the U.S. government, officials quickly moved to take deportees off flights to third countries such as Costa Rica, Honduras and the Central African Republic, according to documents obtained by the Times.

The U.S. government has concluded that it cannot move forward -- for the time being -- with rapid deportations by simply relying on the diplomatic assurances, according to the documents.

Trump administration officials said they would immediately appeal the order.

"Without even allowing the government a chance to respond, and in the dark of night, a federal appeals court blocked us from conducting all third-country removals of illegal aliens, an entirely legal and invaluable tool to stem the tide of illegal immigration," Attorney General Todd Blanche said. "We will immediately seek relief from the Supreme Court, which previously granted a stay in this very same case."

name: Policy
title: Welcome to the Trump Administration's Board of Immigration Appeals. The Immigrant Always Loses.
description:
Part III argues that federal courts should read Volume 29 as the published minutes of a verdict reached in advance.
Across Volume 29 decisions, the Board defines “sufficient” evidence depending on whether it helps or hurts the noncitizen’s claim.
The Board has applied similar reasoning across other Volume 29 decisions to find IJs erred in granting release.
The detention precedents in Volume 29 collectively aim to eliminate the individualized inquiry that the immigrant bond system was designed to provide.
On February 6, 2026, the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) published an interim final rule that attempted to go further still.
text:
abstract.The first 100 opinions in Volume 29 of the Board of Immigration Appeals’ precedential decisions—issued at more than three times the historical pace—constitute a project. The Trump Administration has used the Attorney General’s self-referral power and a reconstituted, ideologically aligned Board to engineer a body of precedents that reliably produces one result: removal. This Essay organizes these decisions, cataloged in a full Appendix, into five main categories: (1) narrowing relief for noncitizens alleging persecution; (2) expanding mandatory detention while narrowing discretionary release; (3) maximizing the immigration consequences of criminal history while foreclosing relief; (4) tightening the exceptional and extremely unusual hardship standard; and (5) tightening the procedural rules governing immigration-court proceedings. A parallel set of agency rule changes, partially vacated by a federal court but now being reissued through notice-and-comment rulemaking, seeks to insulate most deportation orders from meaningful appellate review. This Essay identifies three implications for federal courts. First, Loper Bright’s elimination of Chevron deference, combined with the Board’s institutional redesign and the uniformity of its outcomes, undermines any claim to persuasive weight. Many decisions should not survive de novo review. Second, the exhaustion doctrine’s justifications collapse when the administrative body to be exhausted has been rebuilt to foreordain a result. Third, the Board’s selective deployment of the civil/criminal distinction, invoked to deny protections when it benefits the government and to exclude favorable criminal-law developments when it benefits the noncitizen, is a doctrinal choice that post-Loper Bright courts should examine without deference.

Introduction

In the fall of 2024, an immigration judge (IJ) considered the removal case of a Haitian man with diagnosed schizophrenia and major depressive disorder, among other mental-health conditions. The IJ found him incompetent to proceed on his own and appointed counsel. After considering voluminous evidence, including country-condition reports from the U.S. Department of State (DOS) and the testimony of an expert witness, the IJ found that the man would likely face torture if returned to Haiti’s notoriously brutal prisons and granted him deferral of removal pursuant to the Convention Against Torture (CAT). The Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) reversed. Even if the man were to be held indefinitely in “inhumane detention conditions,” the Board explained, this would not justify CAT relief because he did not “show that Haitian officials are intentionally and deliberately creating and maintaining the harsh detention conditions that he fears for the specific purpose of inflicting severe pain or suffering.”

That case, Matter of S-S-, is one of 100 precedential appellate decisions published by the BIA and Attorney General (AG) Bondi between January 31, 2025 and April 29, 2026. Read together, these precedents, which function as a rulebook for every American immigration court, reveal an unmistakable pattern. No matter what an immigrant suffered, no matter what Congress intended, no matter what the hearing-level judge found, the answer is removal. Notably, in roughly one in five of these cases, the noncitizen appeared pro se before the Board. This includes foundational cases and ones involving complex statutory-interpretation questions about the immigration consequences of criminal history. The two precedential decisions in which the immigrant technically prevailed were on the narrowest procedural grounds, and the Board has since rendered one of those wins largely theoretical.

This body of appellate precedents does not represent the case-by-case doctrinal evolution that administrative adjudication is supposed to produce. As Section III.A documents, its compressed pace, accelerated AG-designation, uniform outcomes, and overturning of multiple longstanding protective precedents mark Volume 29 as something different. It is a crucial component of the Trump Administration’s systematic dismantling of the protections built into immigration law.

To understand why Volume 29 reads the way it does, it helps to know who is adjudicating these claims. When the Trump Administration took office in January 2025, the BIA had twenty-eight members. Within months, all nine judges appointed during the Biden Administration were removed. Further, via federal regulation, the Board was reduced to fifteen members, with the Administration making no secret of its preference for adjudicators aligned with its enforcement priorities. The interim federal rule explained that “the continued expansion of the Board has had significant institutional costs, including effects on the cohesiveness of the Board’s decision-making process . . . , a loss of uniformity in its non-precedent decisions, [and] increased difficulty providing effective leadership.” More judges, the rule explained, resulted in less ‘‘coherent direction’’ and more challenges in voting to hear a case en banc or designate a decision as precedential. The appellate body that produces binding precedent for every immigration court in the country has been rebuilt to further the new Administration’s aggressive enforcement approach. A similar ideological ouster has also occurred at the IJ level. This is not the first time a presidential administration has used its control over the BIA’s composition to reshape immigration adjudication, but the current Administration has gone further and faster and has been met with less institutional resistance.

Part I of this Essay sorts the first 100 precedential decisions handed down by the AG and the Board into five categories, cataloged in full in the Appendix. The largest group (thirty-six decisions) drastically narrows relief for noncitizens alleging fear of persecution in their countries of removal, including decisions like Matter of S-S-. A second category (fifteen decisions) expands the criteria under which detention is mandatory while simultaneously narrowing any possibility for discretionary release. The third (nineteen decisions) concerns the consequences of criminal convictions and related grounds, seeking to maximize penalties and minimize available relief. A fourth group (three decisions) tightens the exceptional-and-extremely-unusual-hardship standard governing nonlawful-permanent-resident cancellation of removal, including a decision that converted the Board’s own institutional delay into a basis for denying relief already granted. The final group (twenty-seven decisions) concerns the procedural mechanisms of immigration court, eliminating the pathways through which noncitizens in removal proceedings can use congressionally authorized routes to status and tightening the rules that govern notice, motions practice, and related matters.

And then there are the rules that govern the rules. As Part II explains, the Trump Administration has also moved aggressively to restructure the appellate process itself. An interim final rule slated to take effect on March 9, 2026, would have remade BIA review to essentially close off any agency appellate review in the vast majority of deportations. While a federal court halted its most sweeping provisions, some components have already gone into effect, and the government is now reissuing the vacated provisions through notice-and-comment rulemaking.

Part III argues that federal courts should read Volume 29 as the published minutes of a verdict reached in advance. Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo’s elimination of Chevron deference means that the Board’s statutory interpretations are now subject to de novo judicial review. That promise, however, depends on courts applying Loper Bright with the force it warrants in the immigration-adjudication context rather than retreating into relabeled deference or diluted arbitrariness review. This Essay argues that searching review is more warranted than ever. A body whose output has tripled, whose membership was purged and rebuilt for ideological alignment, and whose precedential decisions resolve over ninety-eight percent of questions in the same direction is entitled to very little persuasive weight. The exhaustion doctrine’s justifications also collapse when the administrative body to be exhausted has been engineered to foreordain a result. Additionally, the Board’s selective deployment of the civil/criminal distinction, which invariably cuts against the noncitizen, is itself a doctrinal choice that post-Loper Bright courts should examine without deference.

I. the anatomy of a project

A. Noncitizens Alleging Persecution

Thirty-six of the first 100 precedential decisions in Volume 29 address asylum, withholding, and CAT claims. Asylum requires a well-founded fear of persecution on account of one of five protected grounds—race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion—while withholding of removal turns on the same protected grounds but requires showing a clear probability of persecution. An additional avenue for relief from removal, CAT, turns on whether a person would more likely than not face torture, regardless of any protected ground. Although these are formally distinct forms of protection with different requirements, Volume 29 narrows all three: the Board and AG foreclose asylum and withholding through the substantive and procedural rules described below, and deny CAT protection—which no bar or protected-ground requirement constrains—by reweighing the factual record to defeat the likelihood-of-torture and government-acquiescence elements. These cases demonstrate the Administration’s focus on limiting U.S. obligations to offer protection to persons alleging torture or other persecution in their countries of removal.

1. Foreclosing Protection at the Threshold

Under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), a refugee is defined as a person outside their country of nationality who seeks protection because of persecution or a well-founded fear of persecution on account of one of the five protected grounds. The Board’s case law has clarified that the particular social group (PSG) ground must be composed of members who share a common immutable characteristic that is defined with particularity and is socially distinct within the society in question. The Administration’s project of foreclosing protection includes new categorical rules that work to eliminate entire classes of asylum at the threshold—often reaching withholding and CAT claims as well—before any individualized review of whether a particular applicant faces persecution.

AG Bondi, using her self-referral authority, aggressively overturned three major Biden-era precedents in a matter of months. In Matter of S-S-F-M-, Bondi reinstated a 2018 Trump-era rule that gutted asylum claims based on domestic violence and gang persecution. The Biden Administration had reversed that rule in 2021. Bondi reversed the reversal. Asylum requires not only that an applicant belong to a cognizable protected group, but also that the persecution be inflicted “on account of” that protected characteristic—the statutory “nexus” requirement. S-S-F-M- operates on this second element; it treats harm inflicted by private actors—persons acting without direct governmental authority, such as an abusive partner or gang member—as personal conduct lacking the required nexus to a protected ground. Individuals fleeing domestic abuse or gang violence are once again presumptively ineligible for asylum. More generally, the decision establishes that private conduct will almost never qualify an applicant for protection in the United States, even where the country-of-origin government is unwilling or unable to control that conduct.

Bondi also reinstated an equally restrictive rule aimed at families. A 2021 precedent held that “nuclear family” could constitute a cognizable PSG, meaning a person persecuted specifically because of their family ties might qualify for asylum. In Matter of R-E-R-M- & J-D-R-M-, a woman from El Salvador and her minor son sought protection from gang members who “demanded an extortion fee from her and threatened to kill her brother if she failed to pay.” Bondi rejected their claims and used the case to reinstate the 2019 Trump-era rule rejecting family or kinship ties as a PSG. Individuals targeted by cartels because of who they are related to are now, again, largely unable to seek protection in the United States.

In Matter of Negusie, Bondi reinstated another rule from the first Trump Administration that eliminated the “duress exception” to the persecutor bar. That bar disqualifies people who “ordered, incited, assisted, or otherwise participated in” persecution from receiving asylum or withholding of removal. The question presented in Matter of Negusie was whether someone forced at gunpoint to assist in an atrocity—a child soldier in this case—can still seek asylum. The answer, under this Administration, is no. Moreover, there has been a de facto shift in burden. Whereas an applicant who acted under coercion previously had duress available as a defense to the persecutor bar, the AG has now held that “if evidence in the record indicates the persecutor bar may apply, the applicant bears the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that it does not,” with no coercion-based route to carrying that burden.

The BIA moved in lockstep with AG Bondi, issuing a cascade of precedents that work to close off every possible avenue of relief for noncitizens seeking protection from torture or other persecution. Matter of D-G-B-L- hits on several of the themes presaged by Bondi’s decisions. The case involved a Mexican woman forced by an abusive partner to launder money for the Sinaloa cartel. After being subjected to fourteen years of “severe harm,” threats at gunpoint, and threats against her daughter and other family members, she fled Mexico and sought asylum in the United States. The IJ found that she acted under duress and granted asylum and CAT protection.

Although the Board accepted the IJ’s findings, it held the serious nonpolitical crime bar precluded asylum and withholding. As with the AG’s decision in Negusie, the Board held that duress facts are legally irrelevant; there are no exceptions to the nonpolitical crime bar. Because that bar does not reach CAT, the Board addressed the torture claim separately and denied it on de novo review by reweighing the acquiescence evidence, in the manner discussed in Section I.A.2.

The Board has also aggressively foreclosed gender-based asylum claims at the threshold, before any individualized merits review. In Matter of K-E-S-G-, a Salvadoran woman proposed two PSGs: “Salvadoran women” and “Salvadoran women viewed as property.” The Board held that a PSG defined by sex, or sex and nationality, standing alone, is too broad to be cognizable under the INA. The Board acknowledged sex as an immutable characteristic, but reasoned that immutability alone is insufficient, and that groups defined solely by sex encompass too large and diffuse a cross section of society to satisfy the particularity requirement. The decision made an exception for female genital mutilation (FGM) claims and seemed to leave open the possibility that sex combined with additional narrowing characteristics might suffice.

K-E-S-G- offered two rationales, and neither holds. First, the Board reasoned that recognizing sex alone as a PSG characteristic would effectively add sex as a sixth protected ground Congress did not enumerate. But the PSG category exists to capture characteristics Congress did not separately enumerate, and the Board’s seminal PSG decision in Matter of Acosta offered sex as its first example of one. Second, K-E-S-G- held that a group defined by sex is “overbroad and insufficiently particular.” That rationale has surface appeal, because the enumerated grounds need no particularization while a social group must be “particular.” But the Board’s particularity requirement, built from that single statutory word more than two decades after Acosta, essentially asks whether a group’s defining characteristic provides “a clear benchmark for determining who falls within the group.” Sex supplies as clear a PSG boundary as any; what the Board actually objects to is size. Size, however, is not a concern reflected in the statute, which protects race and nationality without limit, and a claim does not fail because the persecutor targets all members of a given race. The statute can afford that breadth because its other elements—persecution, nexus, and state action or acquiescence—do the limiting work.

What remains is a rule that forecloses “Salvadoran women” as a PSG, so that a woman persecuted because she is a woman in El Salvador has no protected ground unless she can identify a narrowing characteristic. However, the subsequent decision in Matter of D-G-E-A- & N-G-G-E- seems to have functionally closed even that opening, rejecting formulations like “Salvadoran women in a domestic relationship with a ‘machista’ male” as failing particularity and “Salvadoran women unable to leave a relationship due to society and social pressures” as impermissibly defined by the persecution itself. The statute compels none of this.

Read together with the AG’s reinstatement in S-S-F-M- of Matter of A-B- (2018) (A-B- I), which barred domestic-violence-based asylum claims as private conduct, and the subsequent foreclosure of narrowing-characteristic formulations in D-G-E-A-, K-E-S-G- completes a pincer movement on gender-based asylum claims. K-E-S-G- and D-G-E-A- close off the PSG route, precluding the most natural formulations of gender-based groups (sex alone, sex with nationality, sex with relational or circumstantial-narrowing characteristics) as incognizable. S-S-F-M- closes off the nexus element, establishing that even if a woman’s group were cognizable, domestic violence doesn’t establish persecution on account of it. It appears that no realistic gender-based PSG formulation survives outside FGM contexts, and the Board has given IJs categorical authority to dismiss these formulations without engaging with each claim’s specific facts.

D-G-E-A- also foreclosed political-opinion-based asylum claims through two analytically distinct moves. First, the Board held that political opinion requires “expression of a belief or conviction regarding a discrete cause which is related to a government,” including a “de facto government.” But political opposition to nonstate actors has long been understood to establish a protected ground, warranting asylum, so long as the state fails to control persecution on account of that ground. Second, the Board constructed its de facto government test in a way that gangs cannot satisfy, even where the evidence demonstrates neighborhood control, taxation, regulation of worship, and lethal violence. Together, these two moves work to close off all political-opinion claims arising from nonstate persecution.

Many other decisions from Volume 29 limit relief from torture or persecution. Matter of L-A-L-T- held that if the underlying PSG is not cognizable, then being perceived to be a member of that group is also not cognizable. The respondent had never been a gang member, but he was beaten by Salvadoran police who wrongly believed he belonged to MS-13. Because actual gang members are not a cognizable social group—a judgment resting on the principle that asylum should not extend protected status to criminal gang membership—the Board held that “perceived gang members” cannot be cognizable either. The result is that a man persecuted precisely because he was wrongly believed to be something he was not has no protected ground at all. The normative judgment that gangs do not deserve protected status, generally defensible as applied to actual members, is transmuted into a bar against a nonmember who was a victim.

Beyond these substantive PSG and nexus foreclosures, the Board has constructed a parallel architecture of procedural and jurisdictional bars that foreclose asylum at the threshold without merits review. Matter of H-A-A-V- overruled longstanding Matter of Fefe authority that asylum applicants must be placed under oath and given an opportunity to testify. Instead, it authorized IJs to pretermit asylum, withholding, and CAT applications at the master-calendar stage if the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) makes an oral motion and counsel does not adequately rebut. Matter of C-I-G-M- & L-V-S-G- aggressively implemented the safe-third-country bar under recently expanded asylum cooperative agreements (ACA), which authorize the removal of asylum seekers to countries with which they have no connection for consideration of their claims there. The decision makes foreclosure of asylum consideration routine whenever the government can invoke an ACA by (1) placing the burden on the respondent to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that she is more likely than not to be persecuted or tortured in a country she may never have seen, (2) authorizing IJ resolution in abbreviated master-calendar hearings without full evidentiary development, and (3) expressly stripping IJs of authority to assess whether the third country offers a “full and fair procedure” for asylum adjudication, reserving that determination to the AG or Secretary of Homeland Security (and thus insulating it from judicial review). These changes are particularly impactful in light of the large number of noncitizens appearing pro se.

Together these appellate decisions establish categorical barriers—substantive, procedural, and jurisdictional—that foreclose protection before any adjudicator reaches the individual facts of a claim.

2. Impermissible Factfinding and the Evidentiary Hierarchy

When noncitizens do obtain merits review of asylum or CAT, a pattern of evidentiary manipulation and impermissible factfinding under cover of de novo review still leads to the Board’s predetermined outcome: removal.

Matter of J-H-M-H- illustrates the reach of this pattern. In this case, a transgender woman feared torture if returned to Honduras. Despite U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement stipulating that she was eligible for CAT protection, the IJ rejected the stipulation, refused to grant relief, and found her not credible. The Board affirmed. Its holding—that IJs are not bound by party stipulations and must exercise independent judgment—is framed as a procedural principle. But the practical consequence is that the IJ’s independent judgment, and the Board’s deference to it, can override a government concession that a noncitizen faces torture. That matters especially since the IJs in this Administration were selected to reach a particular result, and their efforts are now insulated from correction even by the government’s own enforcement arm. Further, J-H-M-H- has already functioned as building-block precedent for additional discretionary rulings that limit process rights.

Several Volume 29 decisions, including Matter of S-S-, discussed above, concern prison-condition claims. Matter of A-A-R- reinforces the Board’s emerging CAT jurisprudence, establishing that conditions in El Salvador’s notorious state-of-exception prisons do not constitute torture—even when the record documents deaths, severe physical violence, and public official statements celebrating those conditions—because the applicant could not prove that officials specifically created the harsh conditions in order to inflict severe pain and suffering rather than to deter crime. A-A-R- is consistent with S-S- and other Volume 29 cases in that it sets the specific-intent element so high that documented widespread suffering in state custody is considered ordinary penal administration, not warranting protection, rather than torture, which does warrant protection. The intentionality requirement for CAT protection is set so high that documented mass atrocities in state facilities such as El Salvador’s Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo (CECOT) would not clear it. Indeed, the effect is to reclassify acts the Convention recognized as torture as lawful and ordinary deterrence, sanctions, or criminal-law operations.

Two additional aspects of the A-A-R- decision warrant discussion because of their likely influence on future cases. First, the Board explicitly characterized DOS country reports as “highly probative evidence” and “usually the best source of information on conditions in foreign nations,” and faulted an IJ for relying on nongovernmental organization (NGO) reports from Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch and expert-witness testimony. The Board characterized the NGO and expert evidence as “anecdotal.” This is a recurring maneuver in Volume 29. NGO reports and expert witnesses, which are often the only independent sources of country conditions information, are discounted as biased, anecdotal, or insufficiently individualized, while DOS reports, whose content and emphasis are more directly susceptible to executive-branch influence, are elevated as the preferred evidentiary baseline when they support denial of relief.

This evidentiary hierarchy is not merely a legal preference but a mechanism of executive control over asylum, withholding, and CAT adjudication. An internal 2025 DOS memo directed country-report editors to remove roughly two-thirds of the content from the 2024 annual report, eliminating whole categories of violations, including gender- and sexual orientation-based violence, and limiting documentation to a single “illustrative incident” regardless of how widespread the abuses were. The report on El Salvador, for example, stated that “[t]here were no credible reports of significant human rights abuses.” An IJ who follows A-A-R-’s instruction to treat DOS reports as the preferred evidentiary baseline is now relying on a document the Administration has shaped to reach the conclusions it wants.

Second, the Board’s reasoning in A-A-R- reflects a pattern of impermissible factfinding under the guise of de novo legal review. The Board nominally applied clear-error review to the IJ’s predictive findings—what will happen to the applicant if removed—while characterizing the ultimate torture determination as a legal question subject to de novo review. But the dispositive question in this case was not a pure legal one; rather, it was whether the record supported an inference that Salvadoran officials intended the prison conditions to cause suffering rather than merely to deter crime. That is a factual inference predicated on record evidence, which the IJ drew based on her evaluation of expert-witness testimony, NGO reports, and public statements of Salvadoran officials. But the Board substituted its own reading of that evidence by dismissing the public officials’ statements as “political” and “serving to garner public support,” and faulting the IJ for not giving sufficient weight to the DOS country report’s more favorable (and outdated) account of El Salvador’s reform efforts. The Board did not acknowledge that it reweighed facts that the hearing-level adjudicator credited, which is supposed to be prohibited unless the Board finds clear error.

The same sleight of hand between review of factual questions and review of legal questions appears elsewhere in Volume 29. For instance, in Matter of D-G-B-L-, the Board characterized the applicant’s testimony about her abuser’s ability to locate her as “vague[],” a characterization that functions as a reweighing of evidence the IJ had expressly accepted as credible. Across these decisions, the Board is not simply applying established legal standards to settled facts. It is finding different facts, under cover of legal review, to reach the result it desires, a maneuver analyzed further in Section III.A.

Across Volume 29 decisions, the Board defines “sufficient” evidence depending on whether it helps or hurts the noncitizen’s claim. Matter of R-B-E- illustrates this in the changed-country-conditions context. The respondent had been granted asylum in 2004 based on her family’s political persecution during the Lavalas period in Haiti. The Board held that the fall of the Lavalas government rebutted the presumption of future persecution generated by her past persecution, dismissing her argument that current gang violence is politically continuous with the Lavalas era based partly on her own testimony that the gangs target people indiscriminately. The Board treated that lay account, from a woman who had been outside Haiti since 2001, as dispositive evidence that no political continuity exists. This stands in stark contrast with the Board’s unwillingness to credit NGO reports.

The evidentiary manipulation documented in these decisions operates not just at the level of individual cases but as a rulebook for IJs, establishing which sources of evidence count, which do not, and how to characterize the record when the noncitizen’s evidence is inconvenient to efforts to remove them. Every IJ who follows A-A-R-’s hierarchy will elevate DOS reports and discount both NGO evidence and expert testimony regardless of what those sources actually document; every IJ who follows the standard applied in D-G-B-L- will have authority to recharacterize credited testimony as “vague” to reach a preferred result.

3. Country Conditions and the Jurisprudence of Survival

A final cluster of cases addresses asylum and CAT claims of noncitizens who have survived persecution and attempt to establish that the danger persists. These cases reveal a Board that systematically converts the circumstances of a noncitizen’s survival into evidence against their claim of enduring risk.

The Board’s logic surfaces across several doctrinal settings. The first is internal relocation. Where applicants fear private actors rather than the government itself, they bear the burden of showing that relocation to somewhere else in their country of origin is unreasonable. The Board has used this burden aggressively, reversing IJ findings that relocation was unavailable.

Matter of F-B-A- presents a sharp example. After a woman converted from Islam to Russian Orthodox Christianity, she faced threats of beheading for apostasy from her brother, among other evidence of danger. The IJ found she could not safely relocate within Russia or obtain police protection. Although the Board did not challenge the IJ’s finding that she faced a real risk of persecution or death, it reversed anyway. Because Russia is a large country, because the respondent is now a member of the majority religion, and because her family had not threatened her in the two years since she fled, the Board found the IJ’s relocation finding “clearly erroneous.” It further held that the protective barriers the BIA previously recognized for child abuse survivors, who may be conditioned not to report harm to authorities, do not extend to adults even for those adults whose victimization began in childhood and whose psychological formation was shaped by that abuse. The respondent was ordered removed to Russia.

A second manifestation appears in the Board’s treatment of threats. In Volume 29, even death threats almost never suffice to show ongoing danger, no matter how credible. In Matter of E-M-F-S-, the Board held that threats to one’s life “rarely rise to the level of persecution” unless the person making them has the “immediate ability” to carry them out. Under this standard, a cartel member who sends word across the border that he will kill a respondent if she returns may lack “immediate” capability precisely because he is not where she is now—so the threat is discounted, and she may be ordered back to the place where he is. The same logic extends to harm that has already befallen others as a basis for believing harm will befall oneself: even substantial, documented evidence of harm to similarly situated people, or to the respondent’s own family members, will not establish the individualized risk required for relief. In each instance, the Board treats the fact that the applicant has not yet been killed—because a threat went unexecuted or because it was relatives, not the applicant, who were harmed—as a reason to doubt the danger.

In a third manifestation, the Board converts a respondent’s ability to evade persecution temporarily—and even their ability to depart the country at all—into dispositive evidence against their claim. Together, these cases establish an emerging jurisprudence of survival: a respondent who managed to survive for a period of time in their home country after being threatened and who was able to depart has, by those very facts, undermined the legitimacy of their fear. Asylum, withholding, and CAT ask whether a person would be in danger if returned; Volume 29 asks instead whether she was already in imminent, unavoidable danger before she left. That substitution systematically disadvantages those who flee before the worst persecution happens.

* * *

Volume 29’s precedential decisions in this area do not operate independently. Together, they constitute a systematic dismantling of the statutory framework Congress built to ensure people are not removed to countries where they face persecution, torture, or death. The Trump Administration’s immigration appellate body seeks to foreclose protection at every stage, from the threshold cognizability of a PSG through the evidentiary standards for establishing fear to the discretionary safety valves that historically have allowed adjudicators to account for the full human context of a claim. This effectively predetermines the outcome of the vast majority of asylum, withholding, and CAT claims. A body of precedent that resolves every ambiguity in the same direction, across every doctrinal mechanism available, is not engaged in neutral statutory interpretation. As Part III discusses, that pattern has direct implications for how much weight federal courts should give these decisions under Loper Bright.

B. Detention and Bond

Fifteen of the first 100 decisions in Volume 29 expand the government’s power to detain noncitizens while sharply curtailing any avenue for release.

1. Mandatory Detention and the Elimination of Bond Hearings

The Board’s most sweeping detention rulings eliminate bond hearings entirely for virtually everyone present in the United States without having been formally admitted—a population in the millions—as well as many others who were formally admitted. The statutory framework distinguishes between two categories of detained noncitizens. Section 236(a) of the INA governs the detention of deportable aliens and provides for discretionary release on bond, with IJs authorized to conduct bond hearings. Section 235(b)(2) governs applicants for admission—defined to include not just those presenting at ports of entry but anyone “present in the United States who has not been admitted”—and mandates detention for the duration of removal proceedings with no bond hearing available. The question these cases address is which provision governs noncitizens who entered without inspection (EWIs) and have been living in the United States for years.

The Board’s answer is that section 235(b) governs those who entered without inspection, requiring mandatory detention with no bond hearing. An early Volume 29 decision, Matter of Q. Li, established the rule that those arrested at or near the border without a warrant are subject to section 235(b) mandatory detention. Matter of Yajure Hurtado, one of the most impactful cases in Volume 29, then extended that rule to the entire population of noncitizens present without formal admission, regardless of how long they have resided in the United States, whether DHS issued an arrest warrant, and, most strikingly, whether the government itself has subsequently recognized their protected status. The Venezuelan respondent in Yajure Hurtado entered without inspection in November 2022 and was granted Temporary Protected Status (TPS) by U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) in 2024. After his TPS expired in April 2025, he was apprehended and put into removal proceedings. He sought release from detention during his removal proceedings, but the Board held that IJs lack jurisdiction to consider bond for EWIs based on a so-called “catch-all provision” of section 235(b) that includes all individuals inside the United States who have not been inspected and admitted.

The Board acknowledged in a footnote that this holding overturned decades of consistent practice, during which time IJs conducted bond hearings for EWI respondents. Moreover, the Immigration and Naturalization Service explicitly took the position in 1997, in the wake of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 (IIRIRA), that noncitizens present without inspection “will be eligible for bond and bond redetermination.” Yajure Hurtado also acknowledged and attempted to account for recent conflicting precedent, including Q. Li and Matter of Akhmedov, both decided just months earlier in the same volume, which treated an EWI respondent’s custody as governed by section 236(a) and did not raise the section 235(b) issue. The Board thus reversed not just decades of agency practice but its own very recent precedent.

The Board’s position that the statute is unambiguous is hard to sustain when the administering agency read it the opposite way for nearly thirty years, including in its own published guidance. Moreover, recent scholarship has called into question the historical premise that civil immigration detention has ever operated without a corresponding right to seek release, further undermining the exceptionalist framework on which Yajure Hurtado rests. As of this writing, federal courts have split on the validity of Hurtado, with the vast majority of district courts and the Second, Sixth, and Eleventh Circuits rejecting the statutory reading that makes EWI respondents ineligible for bond, while the Fifth and Eighth Circuits have sided with the Board.

2. Raising the Bar for Release

The Board has lowered the bar for mandatory detention and, for those who do have access to a bond hearing, simultaneously raised the bar for release. Matter of Ghanbari held that an IJ erred in finding that a respondent did not provide “material support” to a terrorist organization—an appellate decision that triggers mandatory detention—where the support consisted of distributing leaflets as a fifteen-year-old in 1980s Iran. Matter of Rodriguez Pena reversed an IJ who found a respondent was not a danger to the community, basing reversal on a single uncharged verbal threat, a negative reaction to police intervention, and the past use of an alias. The message across the Board’s precedential bond decisions in Volume 29 is that IJs who find a respondent safe for release should not expect deference on administrative appeal.

To obtain release during removal proceedings, noncitizens must establish that they are neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk. Although IJs have discretion to set bond where those showings are made, in Volume 29, the Board uses de novo review of that discretion as a one-way ratchet. Matter of Akhmedov found that discrepancies about which state a respondent lived in, plus a history of late change-of-address filings, were sufficient to establish flight risk. Matter of Salas Pena held that even a recent arrest—without a conviction—for cocaine trafficking established danger to the community warranting detention. The Board has applied similar reasoning across other Volume 29 decisions to find IJs erred in granting release.

The bond decisions also reflect a deeper tension in how the removal system both uses and discounts state-court judgments. Matter of Choc-Tut held that state-court custody orders should not receive deference in immigration bond proceedings, reversing the IJ’s reliance, in part, on the fact that the state court had already determined that $500 bail was appropriate and that the person was not a flight risk. The practical effect is that a noncitizen released on bail by a criminal court may still be held without bond, on the basis of arrests alone, as the result of an IJ applying a less favorable standard. The decision exemplifies a recurring pattern: state-court determinations can cut both ways, but the Board treats them as authoritative only when they work against the noncitizen.

The detention precedents in Volume 29 collectively aim to eliminate the individualized inquiry that the immigrant bond system was designed to provide. Mandatory detention has been extended to a population numbering in the millions while the Board seeks to insulate that extension from scrutiny by declaring the statute unambiguous. For those who retain access to a bond hearing, IJ discretion to find a respondent safe for release has been systematically overridden on de novo review.

C. The Removal Consequences of Criminal History and Related Grounds

Nineteen Volume 29 decisions in this study concern the immigration consequences of criminal history and related grounds. The through line of these decisions is that wherever prior law offered any ambiguity or room for mercy in how criminal convictions should be treated by the immigration system, the Board has resolved that ambiguity against the noncitizen.

1. Discretionary Relief and the One-Way Ratchet

The Board has moved aggressively to narrow discretionary relief for noncitizens with criminal histories, repeatedly reversing IJ grants of relief without identifying clear factual or legal error. Matter of Kim, a cancellation-of-removal case, presents a striking example. The lawful permanent resident (LPR) respondent had been in the United States for forty-six years since he arrived at age ten from South Korea. He developed a gambling problem, and he resorted to fraud and theft to fuel it. The IJ found that his most recent incarceration had rehabilitated him, crediting his sincere remorse and completion of prison rehabilitation programs, and took into account his close relationships with his three adult U.S.-citizen children among other positive factors. The Board reversed, holding that expressed remorse and rehabilitative efforts, standing alone, cannot outweigh prior periods of wrongdoing where previous incarcerations apparently produced no lasting change in behavior. The Board also noted that respondent’s relationships with his children “currently occur primarily over the telephone, and that can continue from South Korea.” Other Volume 29 cancellation of removal denials follow a similar pattern, in which the IJ weighs the full record, credits positive equities, and grants relief; the Board reweighs on de novo review and finds the equities insufficient.

In Matter of Garcia-Flores, the Board reversed an IJ decision that had granted LPR cancellation of removal to a respondent convicted of child indecency, on the ground that the IJ exceeded his authority by effectively finding the respondent factually innocent of the offense. The Board’s critique has validity in principle—IJs cannot re-adjudicate guilt—but it misreads what the IJ in Garcia-Flores actually did. The IJ did not ignore or nullify the conviction; rather, he treated the respondent’s credible claim of innocence as a mitigating factor in the holistic discretionary weighing that cancellation expressly requires. Discretionary relief determinations encompass the circumstances surrounding a conviction, including a respondent’s own account of events. Collapsing that inquiry into a rule that a convicted person “must be considered guilty” for all purposes, including mitigation, forecloses exactly the kind of individualized assessment that distinguishes discretionary relief from categorical bars. In Volume 29, discretion is a one-way ratchet.

2. Ambiguity Always Resolved Against the Noncitizen

Throughout Volume 29, the Board frequently selects cases to announce rules with broader reach than required by the facts. The cases in this Section are more technically complex than the discretionary relief decisions, and, because they involve persons with criminal histories, may evoke less sympathy for some readers. The Board’s analytic through line, however, is consistent. Wherever there is ambiguity about whether the conviction or process in question necessarily triggers a federal immigration consequence, the Board always resolves it against the noncitizen, and where prior precedent had constrained the immigration consequence based on encounters with the criminal legal system, Volume 29 overrules it.

The Board’s treatment of the particularly-serious-crime bar illustrates how it selects cases to announce rules with far broader reach than the facts require, a trend throughout Volume 29. In Matter of E-A-S-O-, the Board overruled Matter of Juarez, a 1988 precedent that established a general presumption against treating single misdemeanor convictions as particularly serious crimes. Every misdemeanor, whatever its nature, is now subject to a searching inquiry established in Matter of N-A-M-, and the burden rests on the respondent to establish the offense is not particularly serious. A concurring opinion in E-A-S-O-—the only nonmajority opinion thus far in Volume 29—noted that the majority eliminated a rule under which “most misdemeanor offenses would not constitute a particularly serious crime” without identifying a single case in which that rule had produced a wrong result.

Matter of Felix-Figueroa illustrates a different analytical move. The respondent was convicted in Arizona of possessing methamphetamine for sale. Arizona’s definition of methamphetamine includes positional isomers not included in the federal definition, a textual mismatch that suggests the state statute is categorically overbroad and the conviction cannot serve as a removal ground. The Board had previously remanded to the IJ for factual findings on whether Arizona actually prosecutes conduct that falls outside the federal definition; that is, the “realistic probability” test. On remand, the IJ invited DHS to present expert evidence on the isomer question. DHS declined. The IJ found DHS had not established removability and terminated proceedings. The Board reversed, holding that the burden was on the respondent rather than DHS to demonstrate a realistic probability that Arizona prosecutes the overbroad conduct.

The burden allocation is the decision’s central problem, and the Board does not adequately justify it. The INA places the burden of establishing removability on DHS by clear and convincing evidence. That is the statutory baseline in removal proceedings. The Board’s burden-shift analysis rests primarily on Pereida v. Wilkinson, where the Supreme Court required the applicant to show his conviction did not constitute a disqualifying offense. But as the Board acknowledged, Pereida arose in the cancellation of removal context, where the burden flows from the applicant’s affirmative obligation to demonstrate eligibility for a benefit. That rationale does not carry over into initial removability, where it is the government that seeks to establish that an immigration consequence follows from a criminal conviction.

In essence, Felix-Figueroa is laundering a Pereida-style discretionary relief burden into an initial removability context, essentially overriding section 240(c)(3)(A). As discussed in greater depth in Section III.A, post-Loper Bright, a reviewing court owes no deference to the Board’s reading and should start with the text of section 240(c)(3)(A).

Matter of Baeza-Galindo illustrates the Board’s consistent practice of resolving legal ambiguity against the noncitizen. The matter concerned a noncitizen who immediately fled a drunk-driving homicide; the legal question was whether that conduct involved two separate criminal acts that did not arise from the same scheme. Prior precedent established that a substantial interruption between two related criminal acts conclusively demonstrates separate schemes, but left open whether the absence of such interruption established a single scheme. The Board has now resolved that ambiguity in the government’s favor, holding that proximity in time is necessary but not sufficient to find a single scheme. This makes it easier to establish the two crimes involving moral turpitude needed to trigger the multiple-conviction ground for removal.

The Board’s selective treatment of state-court outputs is also visible in cases like Matter of De Jesus-Platon, where successful postconviction relief in state court failed to undo immigration consequences. The respondent had his California conviction vacated under section 1473.7 of the California Penal Code, a statute that provides exactly three grounds for vacatur, all of which read as substantive or procedural: (1) legal invalidity due to failure to understand immigration consequences, (2) newly discovered evidence of actual innocence, or (3) a conviction obtained on the basis of race, ethnicity, or national origin. On its face, the statute does not permit vacatur for reasons of rehabilitation or immigration hardship alone. Yet because the respondent’s court order cited section 1473.7 generally, rather than specifying which subsection applied, the BIA held that the respondent had failed to demonstrate the vacatur was for a procedural or substantive defect and denied remand. According to this Board, a noncitizen whose conviction was vacated under a statute that only authorizes vacatur on legitimate legal grounds nonetheless bears the burden of proving which legitimate legal ground the state court applied, and loses if the order does not specify. The pattern is by now familiar. State court processes provide the predicate for the removal system, but their outputs are credited selectively, deferred to when they condemn and discounted when they exonerate or mitigate.

3. The Misrepresentation Ratchet

The decisions in the prior Sections concern noncitizens with criminal histories. This Section turns to misrepresentation decisions—cases turning on false statements or concealment of material facts in dealings with immigration authorities that can lead to fraud-based removability. These cases do not involve criminal charges or convictions, yet the Board’s approach is the same. In Volume 29, the conduct that triggers fraud-based removability is defined more broadly than before, the statutory mechanism for forgiveness has been foreclosed for a large class of LPRs, and the discretionary residual—for those who retain access to it—is structured so that the very conduct creating the liability defeats the only available cure.

Matter of Forjoe restructured the fraud waiver through statutory reinterpretation. The respondent, a Ghanaian national who had been a LPR for nearly two decades, had concealed a fraudulent marriage when he adjusted status in 2007, disclosing it only upon applying for naturalization five years later. Invoking Loper Bright as justification for reexamining its own precedent, the Board overruled Matter of Agour and held that the phrase “at the time of admission” in section 237(a)(1)(H), which provides a fraud waiver, refers only to an alien’s original lawful entry after inspection, not to adjustment of status from within the country. The practical reach of this decision is substantial because the majority of LPRs obtained their status through interior adjustment rather than consular admission. Forjoe eliminated the fraud waiver for all of them, regardless of equities, when the misrepresentation occurred at the adjustment stage.

Matter of M-K- presents a stark expression of the Board’s Volume 29 misrepresentation jurisprudence. The respondent, Mahmoud Khalil—a Syrian-born LPR and prominent organizer of pro-Palestinian protests at Columbia University—faced two independent charges of removability. One was a foreign policy charge under section 237(a)(4)(C)(i) based on a letter from Secretary Rubio, and the other concerned a misrepresentation charge under section 237(a)(1)(A) for failing to disclose a six-month United Nations Relief and Works Agency internship on his adjustment of status application. On the misrepresentation charge, the Board applied the “shut off a line of inquiry” materiality standard recently expounded in another Volume 29 decision. The green card form asks whether the applicant has ever been “a member of, involved in, or in any way associated with any organization . . . in the United States or in any other location.” Although DHS had charged nondisclosure of “membership” in an organization that the Board acknowledged is not membership-based, the Board held this language encompassed Khalil’s six-month internship. The Board found his omission willful because he was “well-educated on matters of international administration and policy” and material because it might have prompted an adjudicator to ask additional questions about security-related grounds of inadmissibility. This standard goes beyond Khalil’s case. The form’s question reaches any organization, association, club, or similar group anywhere in the world; any noncitizen who has worked, interned, or volunteered with any such group without disclosing it faces exposure.

The Board then turned to the fraud waiver. Applying Forjoe’s new rule prospectively, it found Khalil statutorily eligible for the waiver but denied the waiver on two independent discretionary grounds. First, Secretary Rubio’s letter alone outweighed all equities.
