Second, and more consequentially for future cases, the Board held that Khalil’s U.S.-citizen wife, infant U.S.-citizen child, completed graduate degree, and clean record did not outweigh the misrepresentation itself and absence of significant property or business ties. That holding requires no Secretary of State intervention or campus protest involvement. It is a routine discretionary framework that will govern future cases. The charge creates the liability; the same conduct then defeats the only mechanism Congress provided to forgive it. No matter how minor the omission and whatever the equities, this Board’s precedents preclude waiver-based relief.

D. Narrowing Hardship, Weaponizing Delay

Three Volume 29 decisions raise the exceptional-and-extremely-unusual-hardship standard governing non-LPR cancellation of removal. The cases do not involve negative factors like criminal history, procedural failures, misrepresentation, or contested credibility; rather, they concern U.S.-citizen children whose hardship the Board concludes is not exceptional enough to prevent the removal of their noncitizen parent. While the existence of a U.S.-citizen child alone has not historically been sufficient to meet the exceptional-and-extremely-unusual-hardship standard, through these cases the Board has systematically narrowed what facts meet the noncitizen’s burden even further, both by reweighing IJ findings on appeal and by tightening documentation requirements.

The respondent in Matter of Buri Mora had a U.S.-citizen daughter with autism and anxiety, along with two U.S.-citizen sons with developmental delays, all of whom were receiving individualized interventions. His U.S.-citizen wife had taken on additional hours at her job to compensate for the loss of his income after his detention. The Board reversed the IJ’s grant of relief on de novo review, holding that the economic detriment the family was experiencing was “a common feature of a parent departing the United States” and that emotional hardship from family separation does not meet the standard for requisite hardship. Because the children could remain with their mother and continue to receive specialized educational services, their disabilities did not establish the requisite hardship.

Matter of Pelagio Mendoza raised the hardship bar even higher. The respondent had three U.S.-citizen children, ages eight, eleven, and sixteen, the oldest of whom testified that he had wanted to commit suicide “at some point in [his] life” and had been seeing a psychologist for anger issues. The IJ had granted cancellation, finding that the son’s credible testimony tipped the evidentiary balance to exceptional hardship. The Board reversed, holding that a qualifying relative’s testimony about his mental-health conditions—including suicidal ideation—is generally insufficient to establish exceptional hardship where expert evidence regarding those mental-health conditions “could reasonably have been produced.” The Board’s elevated documentation burden will fall heavily on pro se respondents like Pelagio Mendoza, functioning to foreclose meritorious claims that indigent or uneducated families lack the resources or knowledge to document.

Matter of Arevalo-Vargas completes the cluster, applying the Board’s stringent hardship analysis on a six-year-old record while adding a novel doctrinal move. In this case, the agency’s appellate delay, rather than any substantive legal ruling, supplied the principal ground for the deportation order. An IJ granted the respondent cancellation of removal in 2019, finding that his U.S.-citizen children would suffer exceptional and extremely unusual hardship if he were removed. The Board took six years and seven months to decide the government’s appeal. By that time, the respondent’s children were over twenty-one years old. The Board held that the children had aged out of qualifying-relative status in the interim, so the IJ’s grant could not stand; it added that it would have reversed the hardship finding on de novo review in any event.

The Board grounded its age-out reasoning in the “continuing application” doctrine, under which eligibility for cancellation of removal must be satisfied not just at the time of filing but through the date of the final administrative decision. The Board cited Matter of Isidro and Matter of Ortega-Cabrera for this proposition, but neither case supports its novel use in Arevalo-Vargas. That the Board reached for these cases suggests the cupboard of actual authority was bare. This is not a close legal question dressed up in difficult doctrine. The extension of precedent here goes beyond the stated terms of the cases cited, ignores their limiting language, and borrows a pro-noncitizen doctrine for an anti-noncitizen end. Ultimately, it rewards six years of institutional failure by the Board and punishes the person that the failure harmed.

Bureaucratic delay has long served as a structural mechanism of state control over immigrant populations. What Elizabeth F. Cohen has called the “political value of time”—the deployment of temporal requirements as instruments of state power rather than neutral administrative necessity—finds salient illumination in a case where an adjudicative body’s six-year delay is transformed by that same body into an affirmative legal basis for denial. When institutional delay systematically produces adverse outcomes, the delay is not incidental to the system but constitutive of it.

The Board did not simply make a legal error in Arevalo-Vargas. It converted its own failure to act into a legally operative fact, and one that extinguished relief already granted by a factfinder who had evaluated the claim on its merits. The asymmetry is rhetorical as well as doctrinal: when the government benefits from time, delay is treated as routine administrative function; when noncitizens benefit from time—aging into eligibility, accumulating equities, or developing rehabilitative records—that benefit is often recharacterized as exploitation or as obstruction. As the next Section shows, the Board has systematically eliminated every procedural mechanism that allows time to work in the noncitizen’s favor.

E. Procedural Foreclosure

Twenty-seven Volume 29 precedents concern the procedural mechanisms of immigration court. They fall into two related clusters. The first forecloses procedural avenues that Congress created, or that longstanding practice developed, to allow vulnerable noncitizens on statutory pathways to legal status to defer removal while their claims are resolved by USCIS. The second governs the mechanics of how immigration cases proceed, including notice, in absentia orders, motions practice, and access to fee waivers for appellate review. Taken together, the two clusters of precedents ensure that no procedural tool allows time, discretion, or administrative-error correction to work in the noncitizen’s favor.

1. Statutory Pathways to Status

Thirteen of these precedents address what happens when a noncitizen qualifies for a congressionally created immigration benefit but cannot yet access it because of visa-queue backlogs or agency delay. The Board’s answer is consistent: no procedural tool should let them remain in removal proceedings while they wait.

A few involve the U visa, which Congress created in 2000 to protect noncitizens who are victims of crimes and to encourage their cooperation with law enforcement. U visa applicants who qualify and have assisted law enforcement face a massive backlog—decades-long waits for a visa to become available—resulting from both a statutory cap and USCIS’s delayed implementation of the program. Further, while Congress authorized protective interim benefits, the agency has failed to implement these in a reasonable manner. In response, immigration courts have often used “administrative closure”—a procedural pause in removal proceedings—to let U visa applicants wait out the queue. The premise behind this procedure is that a person Congress meant to protect should not be deported while waiting for the protection to become available.

Matter of Ibarra-Vega effectively ends the practice of administrative closure, holding that administrative closure over the government’s objection is improper where a U visa is not available “in the reasonably near future.” The Board’s rhetoric was extreme, declaring that administrative closures amount to a “de facto extra-statutory form of relief that effectively grants amnesty to thousands of removable aliens because they may be eligible for a visa sometime in the future.” Even where respondents meet the statutory criteria to receive lawful status, the BIA wants them deported before the line moves. Matter of J-A-N-M- extended this logic to withholding-only proceedings, in which noncitizens with reinstated removal orders are seeking protection from persecution or torture, holding that IJs have no authority to terminate such proceedings as a discretionary matter, including for U visa-eligible noncitizens.

The Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS) program is even more unambiguous in its legislative intent. Created in 1990, SIJS exists to protect abused, neglected, or abandoned children who cannot safely return to their home country. An approved SIJS petition represents an affirmative determination by USCIS that the child has been abused, neglected, or abandoned; cannot be reunified with one or both parents; and cannot serve their best interest by returning to their home country. SIJS youth are statutorily exempt from most inadmissibility bars, including unauthorized entry and unlawful presence, and generally should be granted LPR status once there is a visa available as long as there are no significant negative discretionary factors. In other words, in most cases, once the child has cleared Congress’s substantive hurdles, what remains is queue management: waiting for a visa number to become current.

But the Board has now closed off all procedural tools available to SIJS youth awaiting visa availability. Matter of Cahuec Tzalam held administrative closure inappropriate where visa availability is indeterminate and extended, even where the respondent has demonstrated prima facie SIJS eligibility. Matter of Pinzon Rozo went further, holding that an approved SIJS petition—meaning USCIS has already made the on-the-merits determination that the child deserves protection—does not warrant even a continuance of an individual hearing where a visa number will not be current for an uncertain period. Together, these holdings leave approved SIJS petitioners without mechanisms to avoid removal while waiting for the visa Congress created for them. The harshness of that rule is sharpened by the fact that the Trump Administration has also eliminated routine deferred action for approved SIJS beneficiaries, removing the informal protection that previously provided a measure of interim security.

Matter of Medina Madrid extends this logic. In that case, the pro se respondent had been in removal proceedings since 2004. In 2013, on DHS’s own motion as an exercise of prosecutorial discretion, the respondent’s case was administratively closed. She then married a lawful permanent resident, her spouse filed a family petition on her behalf, and USCIS approved it in November 2024. In June 2025, DHS moved to recalendar her removal proceedings. The IJ denied the motion because she was diligently pursuing a viable pathway to status. The Board reversed, characterizing thirteen years of administrative closure—closure that DHS itself had initiated—as having “operated, in effect, as amnesty.” At the precise moment when Ms. Medina Madrid had neared the front of the visa line and was close to resolving her case “the right way,” the Board handed DHS the keys to restart her removal proceedings.

The Board has applied similar reasoning to motions to reopen and related post-order mechanisms. In Matter of D-E-B- and Matter of B-S-H-, the Board narrowed the availability of Violence Against Women Act (VAWA)-based reopening; in Matter of Roque-Izada and Matter of Yadav, the Board held that neither pending collateral relief (Cuban Adjustment Act) nor post-order equities (a valid marriage to a U.S. citizen) warrant sua sponte reopening.

Together, these cases establish a comprehensive roadmap for IJs. The BIA has decreed that no pending immigration-benefit application justifies pausing or reopening removal proceedings. The Board is not merely interpreting the statute narrowly. It is recharacterizing the humanitarian commitments made by Congress as amnesty, while the Administration simultaneously strips away the informal protections that had filled the gaps.

2. The Rules of the Courtroom

Another fourteen precedents govern the mechanics of how immigration cases proceed. These decisions are less individually dramatic than those discussed above, but their cumulative effect is consistent with the Board’s project and will have significant impact. Every procedural mechanism that could slow a removal proceeding, preserve a noncitizen’s options, or create space for error correction has been tightened or eliminated.

On notice and in absentia proceedings, the Board has expanded the circumstances under which IJs must enter removal orders against noncitizens who fail to appear. Matter of Laurent Castro held that an IJ erred in continuing proceedings rather than entering an in absentia order where DHS had established removability and the respondent had been properly served but failed to appear. Matter of Bolivar-Bolivar went further, holding that an IJ must proceed to an in absentia removal hearing where a noncitizen fails to appear, even where DHS fails to appear, so long as DHS pre-filed a Form I-213 establishing alienage. Matter of Arana Castillo takes on another permutation, holding that IJs must require respondents—whether or not represented by counsel—to admit or deny charging document allegations at the master calendar even when DHS does not appear.

The decisions aim to ensure that regardless of which combination of parties appear, the cases will proceed toward removability. The Board’s architecture thus converts proceedings that the INA structures as adversarial, and in which DHS has the initial statutory burden of proving the elements of deportability, into something approaching administrative self-disposition. The framework also structurally removes the government actor whose presence in adversarial proceedings is necessary for stipulations, prosecutorial discretion, and error-correction function.

Volume 29 completes the Trump Administration’s implementation of Campos-Chaves v. Garland, systematically closing off every avenue noncitizens had available for challenging removal orders based on defective notices to appear (NTAs). Under Campos-Chaves, noncitizens who concede removability before the defect was actionable cannot withdraw those pleadings; those who fail to appear face in absentia orders regardless of whether the original NTA was compliant; and IJs who exercise discretion to pause or continue proceedings rather than enter in absentia orders are reversed. These decisions systematically reduce the procedural space in which noncitizens, many of whom are unrepresented, can contest the threshold conditions of their proceedings.

On motions practice, the Board held in Matter of A-M-Z-F- that parties have no right to present closing arguments unless denial would itself constitute a due-process violation, building on its prior Volume 29 holding that IJs are not bound by party agreements in civil proceedings. And on fees and access to appellate review, Matter of Garcia Martinez held that a nondetained noncitizen with private counsel is presumptively able to pay the $1,030 filing fee required to appeal an adverse IJ decision, making fee waivers effectively unavailable to a large portion of represented respondents, regardless of respondents’ potential indigent status.

* * *

The Board has foreclosed the statutory pathways through which noncitizens in removal could preserve their cases while tightening the rules of notice, motions practice, and appellate access. Together with the procedural rules described in Part II, these precedents make the path from immigration court to meaningful federal review expensive, treacherous, and stacked against the noncitizen.

II. towards a procedural architecture of futility

A noncitizen who loses before an IJ cannot reach federal court without first appealing to the BIA. To submit this notice of appeal requires a $1,030 filing fee, and as discussed, a noncitizen with private counsel is presumptively ineligible for a fee waiver.

On February 6, 2026, the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) published an interim final rule that attempted to go further still. Had the rule taken full effect, noncitizens would have had ten days to file a notice of appeal with the fee, identifying all appellate issues on pain of permanent waiver. Given this tight timeline, in most cases an appeal would have had to have been filed without access to a transcript or written decision from the IJ. The default for every appeal would have been summary dismissal unless a majority of permanent Board members voted within ten days to accept it for merits review.

Nonprofit organizations challenged this rule under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), and on March 8, 2026, one day before the rule was set to take effect, District Court Judge Moss vacated its most sweeping provisions—the ten-day deadline, the waiver rule, and the presumption of summary dismissal—finding that they operated “in lockstep” to “foreclose effective opportunity to make one’s case on the merits” and required notice-and-comment rulemaking the agency had bypassed.

That victory, however, should not obscure what survived or what may come in the future. Briefing schedules are now simultaneous for all appeals, meaning that when DHS appeals a decision favorable to the noncitizen, the noncitizen has no opportunity to respond directly to the government’s arguments. Appeals are due within twenty days, and extensions are available only when the noncitizen personally can demonstrate exceptional circumstances (attorney scheduling conflicts or family emergencies are now considered irrelevant). Reply briefs are prohibited entirely. And any appeal not resolved by a BIA panel within the required time frame is automatically assigned to the Chairman, Vice Chairman, or Attorney General.

Further, the Administration’s setback on the harsher interim final rules may prove only temporary. As of April 2026, EOIR has confirmed it is engaged in rulemaking to reissue the vacated provisions, and the litigation challenging the original interim final rule has been stayed by joint stipulation to allow that process. A predecessor rule enacted through notice-and-comment in 2020 made similar, though less sweeping, procedural changes before being reversed by the Biden Administration, offering support for the Trump Administration’s apparent belief that the procedural path remains available for the more aggressive provisions as well.

If the Trump Administration is successful, the fee wall, simultaneous-briefing requirement, and summary-dismissal default will together ensure that the appellate process functions not as a check on the system Part I describes, but as its capstone—the final procedural guarantee that the immigrant loses.

III. reading the blueprint

The body of Volume 29 decisions analyzed in Part I and the revisions to the BIA’s procedural architecture described in Part II constitute a coordinated conversion of an adjudicative system nominally committed to individualized review into one engineered to produce a predetermined result.

The cases in Part I do not exist in isolation. Matter of Z-R-C-N- illustrates how they form a system, its components operating in lockstep.As an Ecuadorian mother fleeing domestic violence, the respondent’s asylum claim was precluded by the AG’s 2025 reinstatement of A-B- I. The Board’s decision in K-E-S-G-, together with the AG’s reinstatement of A-B- I, means the PSGs she would propose—women unable to leave domestic relationships, women viewed as property—are categorically foreclosed. The reinstatement of L-E-A- means her family ties provide no cognizable group. Under the standards S-S-F-M- restored, she cannot establish nexus because, says the Board, her ex-husband harmed her due to their personal relationship, not her political opinion.

But Volume 29’s impact does not end there. Her daughters have approved SIJS petitions, meaning that USCIS already credited a family court’s determination that they were abandoned, abused, or neglected by their father and cannot safely return to Ecuador. Under Cahuec Tzalam, Pinzon Rozo, and now Z-R-C-N- itself, however, that approval is too speculative to warrant administrative closure, a continuance, or reopening. The current visa backlog for SIJS adjustment of status is her problem, not the court’s.

Finally, Z-R-C-N- presented the BIA with the opportunity to address a claim not elsewhere raised in Volume 29. The respondent was defrauded by a fake lawyer who collected $8,000 from her, sabotaged her case by advising her to omit the very facts that formed the basis of her claim, disappeared before her hearing, and told her for over a year an appeal was pending that he had never perfected. Readers will intuit how the Board came down on whether this constituted ineffective assistance of counsel.

Considered together, this body of administrative work, which continues to grow every week, cannot be reasonably understood as applying statutory law with fairness and fidelity. The remainder of this Part identifies three implications of this Essay’s analysis that deserve further attention from federal courts, Congress, and commentators. First, because Loper Bright now requires courts to review the Board’s statutory interpretations de novo, and because Volume 29’s institutional condition forfeits any persuasive weight its decisions might otherwise command, courts should independently reject the statutory readings this Essay documents rather than defer to them. Second, because the exhaustion doctrine presupposes an agency capable of meaningful self-correction, courts should hesitate to enforce it rigidly against a Board whose decisions reflect prejudgment rather than adjudication. Third, the Board’s selective invocation of the “civil” character of removal—deployed to justify outcomes that would be impermissible in any criminal proceeding—warrants closer scrutiny than it has received.

A. Loper Bright and the Case for Independent Review

Prior to Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, federal courts reviewing BIA legal interpretations applied Chevron deference, accepting the agency’s reasonable construction of ambiguous statutory provisions even when the reviewing court might have read the statute differently. Post-Loper Bright, courts review questions of statutory interpretation de novo, owing the agency’s view no special deference, though they may still find it persuasive under Skidmore v. Swift & Co.

This shift has significant implications for Volume 29. Many of the Board’s most consequential rulings turn on statutory interpretation questions that were previously insulated from rigorous judicial review by deference doctrines. Further, many of these interpretations depart from longstanding prior practice and could not have been reasonably anticipated by noncitizens. Under Loper Bright, these decisions now present pure questions of law for courts to decide using the traditional tools of statutory construction and interpretation. These tools include the longstanding rule of lenity—or strict construction of removal statutes in favor of the noncitizen—whose role in resolving ambiguity is strengthened now that the competing gravitational pull of agency deference has been removed.

The traditional justification for Chevron deference was that agencies possess technical expertise and democratic accountability that courts lack, and that Congress implicitly delegates interpretive authority to agencies when it leaves gaps or ambiguities in statutory schemes. But those justifications were always weakest in the removal adjudication context where the interpretive choices directly determine individual liberty infringements on the scale of detention and banishment.

They are weaker still now. The BIA’s decisions in Volume 29 fly in the face of congressional intent in designing the modern immigration system. Congress enacted a framework for asylum that presupposes individualized adjudication of each claim, but the Board is systematically dismantling the evidentiary tools that make individualized adjudication meaningful by discrediting expert witnesses, dismissing country-conditions evidence, and treating the harm of family members as statistical coincidence. The Supreme Court held in 2009 that the Board had erred in treating the persecutor bar as foreclosing a duress defense, and in 2018 the Board recognized a narrow duress exception. AG Barr eliminated it two years later, and although AG Garland’s stay of that ruling effectively restored it, AG Bondi reaffirmed the elimination in 2025. Congress created the U visa to protect crime victims who cooperate with law enforcement and authorized interim respite to applicants with bona fide pending petitions, but the Board now seeks to keep pending applications from earning even a pause in removal proceedings while the visa queue clears. Similarly, Congress created SIJS to protect children who have been abandoned, abused, or neglected, but the Board has decreed that approved SIJS petitions are insufficient to delay deportation.

While agencies have leeway to develop doctrine through adjudication, Volume 29’s features—its pace, uniformity, outsized AG role, and simultaneous overruling of multiple longstanding protective precedents—mark a project rather than ordinary doctrinal evolution. Volume 29 already contains 100 entries issued between January 31, 2025 and April 29, 2026, a pace more than three times the recent historical average and achieved with a Board half the size of its predecessor. Further, forty-one of the ninety-seven Board-issued decisions—more than forty-two percent—were not initially published as precedent but were later designated as precedential by the AG. As documented in the Appendix, roughly one in five of these precedents was issued in a case where the respondent had no counsel, including foundational cases and complex statutory-interpretation questions. The pace, publication methodology, and reliance on pro se cases as vehicles for setting binding rules do not suggest careful or reasoned analysis.

The Administration’s signals to its immigration adjudicators reinforce this diagnosis. The Department of Justice has warned IJs that “statistically improbable outcome metrics” may warrant “potential action,” fired or transferred approximately 141 immigration judges, and—in a clear statement of institutional purpose—renamed the position “deportation judge.”

Under Skidmore, persuasive weight tracks the thoroughness, consistency, and validity of agency reasoning. Volume 29 warrants very little persuasive weight on any of those measures. First, it does not reflect thorough consideration. A Board whose published decisions resolve every question in the same direction and have produced only one separate concurrence opinion across 100 cases reveals little evidence of the deliberation, internal debate, and authentic engagement with counterarguments that thorough reasoning produces—particularly at the pace Volume 29 has been generated. Nor is it the kind of consistency Skidmore rewards. The Board manipulates precedent-management doctrine in whichever direction removes the noncitizen, citing Loper Bright’s reexamination language to justify overruling protective precedent in one case and Gamble’s “special justification” requirement to cast a protective precedent as vulnerable in another while exempting its own departures from settled practice from either form of scrutiny. And the validity factor, which turns not on the agency’s decisional process but on the merits of its interpretation, fares no better. The Board’s decisional dynamics—uniform outcomes, departure from precedent, accelerated pace, narrow record of reasoning, and expansive agency-head review—collectively forfeit any presumption of persuasive weight on the merits as well.

Still, whether Volume 29 will face meaningful federal review depends on how courts apply Skidmore. Some judges treat Skidmore as the persuasiveness inquiry it was designed to be; other post-Loper Bright decisions have converted the persuasiveness inquiry into a de facto deference regime, applying the agency’s interpretation after a superficial review rather than exercising genuinely independent judgment. The case for de novo review holds under each approach. Under genuine Skidmore, Volume 29’s institutional condition forfeits any persuasive weight; if Skidmore does not survive Loper Bright at all, the case is even stronger; and even under a Skidmore-as-Chevron approach, the institutional features documented here should disqualify Volume 29 decisions. De novo means de novo, and this is not an appellate body to which courts should be looking for guidance, regardless of which framework controls.

Volume 29’s precedents should not fare well if courts exercise independent judgment on questions of statutory meaning. For example, L-A-L-T-’s holding that perceived membership in a noncognizable group is itself noncognizable rests, as discussed above, on a moral judgment about the underlying group that has no application to someone who, by the Board’s own account, was never a member. The respondent was barred not for anything he did but for what the state, wrongly, thought he was. The Board’s broader dictum that the INA’s plain language does not include “imputed” as a modifier for any protected ground reads more as a forecast than a holding, and reviewing courts under Loper Bright have substantial basis in authority, practice, and interpretive principle to reject it.

Felix-Figueroa illustrates another statutory interpretation problem. As discussed, the Board placed the burden on the respondent based on its reading of Pereida v. Wilkinson, a cancellation case whose applicant-burden rationale has no place in initial removability proceedings. The Board’s invocation of Pereida to override the INA’s express burden allocation in the removability context is an interpretive choice, which reviewing courts should now examine without deference. The same pattern of resolving statutory ambiguity against the noncitizen extends to the Board’s notice decisions in Volume 29, which implement Campos-Chaves v. Garland in the most government-favorable direction available on questions that decision left open. De Jesus-Platon further illustrates the pattern; the Board required the respondent to demonstrate which of a state statute’s three grounds the vacating court applied, even though any vacatur necessarily rests on one of its three substantive or procedural grounds. In each instance, the Board resolved statutory ambiguity in the harshest available direction. Pursuant to Loper Bright, courts should scrutinize whether each reading is the strongest available.

Forjoe eliminated the fraud waiver for LPRs who adjusted status from within the country, and the Board’s route there is telling. Loper Bright governs how reviewing courts treat agency interpretations, not whether an agency may discard its own precedents—yet the Board cited it for the latter, treating the Court’s language about reexamining precedent as license for the Board itself to abandon its own decades-long reading. A reviewing court examining the Board’s reading de novo would find a statutory text (“at the time of admission”) that courts and the Board itself read for decades before Agour to exclude adjustment of status. The Board’s new reading is not compelled, and its downstream consequences—illustrated in M-K-’s foreclosure of relief for a respondent with a U.S. citizen spouse and infant child—are precisely the kind of high-stakes interpretive choices Loper Bright places before federal courts.

In Matter of Dor, which concerned whether time-of-conviction or time-of-removal adjudication determines whether a state drug conviction matches the federal controlled-substance schedules, the Board acknowledged that the statutory text does not resolve the issue. A de novo reviewing court applying lenity to the statutory ambiguity could reasonably conclude that where the federal- and state-controlled-substance definitions diverge, the comparison should be made at whichever point protects the noncitizen from removal.

Loper Bright’s independent-review command reaches questions of law, not the Board’s factual findings, which courts review under the deferential substantial-evidence standard. But the Board’s handling of the factual record warrants comparable skepticism on its own terms. Some of these moves involve pure and simple factual substitution; others are the same kind of interpretive overreach Loper Bright addresses, relabeled as factfinding. While the Board’s nominal posture toward IJ findings is clear-error review, Part I documents how the Board has developed a set of moves that function as factual substitution while formally preserving that posture. For example, it recharacterizes credited IJ testimony as “vague” or insufficient, elevates DOS country reports as the preferred evidentiary baseline while dismissing NGO evidence and expert witnesses as “anecdotal,” and reclassifies inferential factual questions, such as whether prison officials specifically intended to cause suffering, as legal questions subject to de novo review.

This factfinding substitution has largely been achieved through wildly expanded deployment of the Matter of J-F-F-’s “series of suppositions” framework, treating IJ predictive findings as speculative whenever they require inferential reasoning from country-conditions evidence even where the IJ’s inferences were anchored in specific record facts about the respondent and the persecutor. The Board has also begun imposing asymmetric reason-giving burdens on IJs. In these ways, the Board frequently reaches different factual conclusions than the hearing-level adjudicator without acknowledging that it is doing so.

For federal courts reviewing these decisions, the Board’s factual characterizations should not be accepted at face value. Circuit courts have long required administrative adjudicators to demonstrate meaningful engagement with record evidence and to provide adequate reasoning, what Professor Aadhithi Padmanabhan calls the “consideration and explanation requirements.” But Padmanabhan has also documented how some circuit courts following the Supreme Court’s decision in Garland v. Ming Dai have begun to dilute these requirements—relaxing the reason-giving obligation, softening the consideration requirement, and in some cases recasting both as impermissible “judge-made procedural requirements” under Vermont Yankee. Volume 29’s factfinding moves are precisely the kind that benefit from a weakened consideration-and-explanation regime, and federal courts should resist that retreat.

Loper Bright also has implications for the retroactive application of Volume 29’s new, result-driven interpretations. As other commentators have observed, “[T]here are unique harms that can flow from the immediate and retroactive application of immigration adjudication decisions” and noncitizens who structured their claims or pleas in reliance on prior law—for example, asylum applicants who formulated PSG claims under standards the Board has now categorically foreclosed—should press retroactivity arguments on appeal.

Part I does not merely document a parade of individual errors. Rather, the pattern it presents makes the affirmative case against treating immigration adjudication as a domain where courts should retreat from utilizing their full power. Immigration policymaking through adjudication raises serious separation-of-powers concerns, because Congress alone is afforded responsibility for defining the outer limits of a system imposing consequences as harsh as detention and removal. Mariano-Florentino Cuéllar has documented that concern at a structural level, describing how “a newer, less constrained, expansive domain of presidential adjudication,” enabled by personnel control, doctrinal expansion, and eroding norms against White House interference in agency decision-making, has become a potent threat to governmental legitimacy and separation-of-powers principles. But the structural consequences of that expansion are uneven. As Adam B. Cox and Emma Kaufman have argued, the Roberts Court’s administrative-law jurisprudence points toward a bifurcated system, in which regulated industries gain increased access to Article III independent review while mass adjudication of the claims of politically subordinated populations remains trapped within an empowered administrative state. Volume 29 illustrates what the second tier looks like when fully operational.

Mary Hoopes has argued that judicial scrutiny should be calibrated to evidence of a compromised adjudicative system, with deference responsive to agency quality rather than oblivious to it. Volume 29 supplies exactly the evidence that warrants that calibration. The ordinary justifications for judicial deference—institutional expertise, careful record development, accurate factfinding, insulation from political direction—all collapse in the face of the Board that Parts I and II document. If Loper Bright’s independent-review command means anything in practice, it must apply with full force here. An adjudicative system exhibiting precisely the pathologies that justify robust judicial oversight is the worst possible candidate for exceptionalist treatment in the other direction. The result-driven determinations and lack of analytic care that characterize Volume 29 must be taken into account when considering whether to afford the BIA any deference.

B. Reconsidering Exhaustion

Federal courts generally require noncitizens to exhaust their administrative remedies at the BIA before filing a petition for review in a circuit court of appeals. The exhaustion doctrine serves legitimate interests in the ordinary case. But those justifications rest on an assumption that the administrative process is capable of providing meaningful adjudication—that the agency will “have an opportunity to correct its own errors,” “afford the parties and the courts the benefit of its experience and expertise,” and “compile a record which is adequate for judicial review.”

Consider the BIA that would receive an exhausted claim today, as described above—rebuilt for ideological alignment, subject to direct AG override, and governed by procedural rules restructured to minimize meaningful briefing and review. Exhaustion is justified by the premise that the agency should have a meaningful chance to correct its own errors first. M-K- shows that chance to be illusory: even with jurisdiction to provide review, the Board exercises it to foreclose relief rather than correct error. And Arevalo-Vargas shows exhaustion inflicting the very harm it is meant to prevent—a six-year wait for the Board to decide a government appeal transformed a valid grant of relief into an adverse outcome, the delay itself becoming the dispositive legal fact.

In these circumstances, federal courts should reconsider whether strict exhaustion requirements continue to serve their intended purposes. The doctrine’s own exceptions point the way. Exhaustion may be excused where an agency has “predetermined” an issue such that resort to it would be futile. Requiring a noncitizen to exhaust all issues before a Board whose decisional culture and procedural rules foreordain the result no longer provides a meaningful opportunity for administrative correction. Volume 29 shows exhaustion in this institutional posture to be not merely futile but structurally adverse; the procedural barrier compounds rather than corrects the institutional bias the noncitizen seeks to challenge.

C. The Civil/Criminal Asymmetry

One thread running through several troubling decisions in Volume 29 is the Board’s invocation of the civil nature of removal proceedings to justify outcomes that would be unavailable in any criminal context. The civil/criminal distinction in immigration law has long been contested. To be sure, the Supreme Court has recognized that “deportation is a drastic measure and at times the equivalent of banishment or exile,” yet the notion that removal is not punishment in the constitutional sense remains bedrock doctrine, so the procedural protections of criminal law do not automatically apply.

Padilla v. Kentucky illustrates the practical stakes of this distinction. Padilla held that the Sixth Amendment requires criminal defense attorneys to advise noncitizen clients about the immigration consequences of guilty pleas, and practitioners throughout the country have built expertise on that obligation. But when the Board expands the immigration consequences of criminal convictions in ways that could not have been anticipated from prior law, for example by overruling the misdemeanor presumption in E-A-S-O-, narrowing the single-scheme doctrine in Baeza-Galindo, or eliminating the fraud waiver for adjustment-based LPRs in Forjoe, it frustrates the reliance interest Padilla created. A safe plea today may not be a safe plea tomorrow.

The civil label does real work in Volume 29. In D-G-B-L-, for instance, the Board held that the duress defense is irrelevant to the serious-nonpolitical-crime bar because “[r]emoval proceedings are civil in nature and are not considered a criminal process that may result in punishment.” The Board’s reasoning is that while criminal courts may guard against imposing punishment for what someone was forced to do, immigration courts merely assess whether the person committed the act at all.

Volume 29’s treatment of the civil/criminal distinction is notably selective. In both D-G-B-L- and Negusie, the civil nature of removal proceedings was invoked to deny duress defenses available in criminal courts because, according to the Board, immigration proceedings do not decide criminal culpability. Rather, they concern only whether a disqualifying act was committed. But in Dor, the Board invoked the same distinction in the opposite direction, holding that Congress’s removal of hemp from the federal controlled substance schedules does not carry over into immigration proceedings because such criminal law changes are “not primarily about immigration.” The same selectivity governs the Board’s treatment of state-court outputs more generally. State criminal processes serve as the government’s primary proxy for identifying noncitizens deemed dangerous or undesirable, but their judgments are credited only when they cut against the noncitizen—authoritative when they convict or deny bail, irrelevant when they exonerate, mitigate, or grant pretrial release.

The civil label thus cuts both ways, but always against the noncitizen. When it benefits the government to treat immigration proceedings as insulated from criminal law protections, they are civil. When it benefits the noncitizen to import a favorable criminal law development, they are also civil, but in a way that keeps the development out. In the rare instances when both parties agree that the noncitizen should be protected, the party control that defines civil litigation disappears. In J-H-M-H-, DHS and the respondent jointly stipulated that she was eligible for CAT protection, and DHS maintained that position on appeal; the Board nonetheless held that IJs “are not required to accept party stipulations.” The selective deployment of the distinction is itself a doctrinal move worth scrutinizing. This selectivity complements a parallel asymmetry documented at the enforcement level, where the civil classification enables system actors to disclaim criminal-court outcomes that benefit noncitizens while freely importing criminal investigative tools to accomplish deportation ends. What Volume 29 reveals is the same asymmetry operating at the adjudicative level, wielded by the Board and the Attorney General as a doctrinal instrument, and always in the direction of removal. Post-Loper Bright, courts reviewing the Board’s selective deployment of the civil/criminal distinction owe that deployment no deference and should examine it as what it is: a doctrinal choice that always tilts in the government’s favor.

Conclusion

The first 100 precedential decisions of Volume 29 reveal an appellate immigration body rebuilding the system to accomplish the removal of as many noncitizens as possible, as quickly as possible. Across the Essay’s five categories—narrowing relief for noncitizens alleging persecution; expanding mandatory detention while raising the bar for release; maximizing the immigration consequences of criminal history and misrepresentation; tightening the hardship standard for discretionary dispensations while converting the Board’s own institutional delay into a basis for denying relief; and tightening the procedural rules that govern immigration court—Volume 29 produces the same result through similar methods. Immigration judges who grant relief are reversed as a matter of course with their factual findings displaced under cover of de novo legal review. Expert witnesses who support asylum claims are discredited as anecdotal while DOS reports are elevated as authoritative even as those reports come under increasing political control. Statutory ambiguities and discretionary balances are resolved against the noncitizen. Statutory pathways to status have been recast as gamesmanship or de facto amnesty when noncitizens become eligible for them during pending proceedings, and basic procedural protections like adequate notice and the burden of proof have been narrowed.

text:
On 9/14/2026, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) released Policy Alert PA-2026-13, which will change the USCIS Policy Manual regarding referrals that can lead to denaturalization. These changes are in Volume 12 Part L of the Policy Manual. The policy went into effect as soon as it was published. USCIS allowed for public comment through 9/25/2026 but has since extended that to 10/14/2026.

The grounds for denaturalization have not changed. USCIS only changed how it will find cases, review them, and prioritize referrals.

When USCIS looks at your Citizenship

There are many ways that a naturalized citizen’s file can be audited. Typically, someone will file a form that requires citizenship, such as an I-130 to petition for your spouse or parent, or even an N-600 for your child. They will then check if you became a citizen properly. Another reason for an audit could be that they flagged your case for fraud detection, or DHS or another agency requested a review (i.e., the State Department).

Grounds for Revocation

We will discuss two main grounds for revocation. This includes situations where an individual unlawfully secures citizenship because they didn’t fulfill a necessary naturalization condition. Such as lawfully being a permanent resident. Residing/physically present for the required amount of time or having good moral character. You don’t need to have intent to commit fraud. The other ground is if you concealed a material fact or willfully misrepresented. This could be a false declaration or statement on your N-400, during your interview, or in your documentation.

There are two additional grounds. One is becoming a member of certain organizations within 5 years of naturalization. Another is becoming a U.S. citizen through military service and being dishonorably discharged before serving 5 years honorably.

Burden of Proof

USCIS cannot revoke citizenship independently; only a federal court has this authority. In civil cases, the Department of Justice must provide clear, convincing, and unambiguous evidence and is not subject to a statute of limitations. In criminal cases, the standard is beyond a reasonable doubt, and action must be taken within ten years.

Which cases get Priority

The document outlines priority categories for referral. These include national security concerns such as terrorism and espionage, serious threats to public safety, human rights violations, associations with gangs or cartels, and cases flagged by Interpol. Priority is also given to cases involving undisclosed felonies, human trafficking, sex offenses, violent crimes, certain financial fraud, government corruption, false identities, false claims of U.S. citizenship, unlawful voting before naturalization, and marriage fraud.

Most referrals will be sent to ICE. If they decline the case or it is past the statute of limitations for a crime. Then USCIS can refer them to the department of justice to file a civil action with the office of immigration litigation.

What happens after Denaturalization

When someone is denaturalized, they are considered not naturalized from the date of naturalization. They will have to give up their naturalization. And go back to their previous immigration status. Other people can be affected as well. USCIS can reopen any petition the person filed for family members to see if they qualify. There may be a case where your spouse or child can be denaturalized as well based on what your naturalization was canceled for.

What you should do Now

For most naturalized citizens, this update will not affect daily life. However, if you plan to sponsor a family member or submit an application based on your citizenship, review your naturalization record carefully. Address any prior arrests, previous marriages, gaps in residence, or inconsistencies in earlier applications before submitting new forms.

If you have questions about your history, our lawyers can review your file and help you determine your next steps.

text:
As Canadians witness the violence and overreach of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in the United States, less visible changes to immigration enforcement in Canada are making everyday life far more difficult for refugees and other migrants.

Through her research and teaching, Lincoln Alexander Law Professor Idil Atak is determined to increase our understanding of the structural barriers and systemic discrimination that migrants increasingly face, and the effects of hardening border control practices.

In July, Atak’s research project was among 14 projects at TMU to receive a Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC) Insight Grant supporting research into complex societal challenges and potential solutions.

Over the next five years, Atak will serve as the principal investigator on the project, called Bordering Canada: Examining the Impacts of Multi-Level Border Enforcement Policies At, Within, and Beyond the Canada-US Border. Atak is collaborating with Julie Young, Canada Research Chair in Critical Border Studies at the University of Lethbridge, and David Moffette, a professor in Criminology at the University of Ottawa.

The research project examines systemic inequalities embedded in Canada’s current border and immigration processes across urban, national, and transnational contexts. It seeks to promote greater accountability and advance policies that protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of refugee claimants and migrants without legal status. These groups have been the primary targets of state measures designed to prevent and punish unauthorized entry and residence.

To investigate the ways immigration enforcement is becoming more active both within Canada and beyond its borders, the team is filing access to information and freedom of information requests and will conduct structured interviews with approximately 70 people, including federal, provincial and municipal officials as well as representatives from police services, international organizations, and advocacy organizations.

Data-sharing with other countries can put refugees at risk, Atak says

Atak’s research shows that through partnerships with other governments, international organizations and, increasingly, technological tools such as shared databases, Canada is monitoring migrants’ movements abroad and making it harder for them to seek refugee protection in Canada.

“Canada has been extending migration controls beyond its territorial borders to intercept migrants deemed undesirable before they reach Canada,” Atak explains. “This is happening in collaboration with ‘like-minded’ countries, especially the U.S. the U.K. and the other Five Eyes countries. This development threatens refugees’ access to protection.”

For example, if someone makes a refugee claim in the United Kingdom and later travels to Canada to seek protection, shared databases can reveal the earlier claim and make that person ineligible to make a refugee claim in Canada, even if no decision was ever made on the U.K. claim. There are multiple reasons refugees choose to make a claim in Canada after living in a third country, Atak explains, including changes in that country that make living there too risky (such as the targeting of migrants under the Trump Administration in the U.S.).

At the same time as Canada increasingly shares information to “immobilize” refugee claimants, federal and provincial governments have invested heavily in border security. This includes expanding the use of drones, helicopters and other technology along the U.S. border as well as expanded cooperation among law enforcement agencies, Atak explains.

“Since the COVID pandemic, we’ve seen an increased collaboration between the Canada Border Service Agency, and municipal police who check immigration status during routine interactions like traffic stops, especially in large cities such as Montreal and Toronto,” she says. Repressive immigration enforcement has resulted in rights violations, injury and deaths among migrants.

A key challenge is understanding how these systems operate across local, national, and transnational scales, and how they interact with and reinforce one another. Atak explains that little public information is available about immigration enforcement collaborations between Canada and other states, and international organizations. Similarly, little is known about the deployment and effectiveness of the surveillance technologies and capabilities or about the role of private companies in enhancing the state’s capacity to detect and contain migrants deemed undesirable. Another challenge is determining the effects of changing immigration enforcement practices on a vulnerable, difficult-to-reach population that includes people without legal status. The project aims to address these challenges.

Atak’s previous research led to recommendations to improve services for refugees

Atak’s SSHRC project is a natural extension of work she has pursued for more than two decades on international human rights law, irregular migration and the growing securitization of migration. From 2019 to 2025, Atak led a project that explored the human rights impacts of Canadian and international immigration control laws, policies, and practices.

As part of that project, Atak recently partnered with Newcomer Women’s Services Toronto and conducted participant interviews and surveyed close to 1,000 migrants in the Greater Toronto Area about access to settlement programs, health care, housing, employment and other services. The research revealed the vulnerability of refugee claimants and non-status migrants, many of whom are women, children, and elderly people, and how compounding barriers to housing, health care, employment and other services affect their everyday lives. For example, Atak spoke to a nurse who explained that pregnant women don’t access prenatal care that can improve health outcomes for themselves and their children, because of fear.

Third-year law student Isabel Vilarino worked with Atak on the project, helping to organize and analyze the large survey dataset. “I learned a lot about the different intersections of vulnerability and about how to centre migrants’ perspectives,” Vilarino says, noting that the project incorporates recommendations offered by migrants themselves. “To understand where the barriers exist, you need to understand the larger structural systems. For example, to access housing you need a credit check, and for a credit check, you need immigration documentation. Idil has a very holistic understanding of how vulnerabilities interconnect with one another.”

Second-year student Todd Westcott, who took a Legal Theory course taught by Atak last year, describes her as open, inquisitive and empathetic. Many asylum seekers coming to Canada “are dealing with a complex vector of racial and gender discrimination, and having traumatic experiences and sometimes the conditions in which these people are expected to exist in Canada is frightful,” he explains. “In her academic research and her teaching, Professor Atak highlights the extreme experiences that people go through.” He also sees the impact of research and advocacy from Atak and others, including the increased use of alternatives to immigration detention in Canada over the last two decades.

Despite the challenges of advocating for human rights amid increased surveillance and the criminalization of migrants worldwide, Atak remains hopeful. “Canada is a democratic country with strong democratic institutions. Courts, tribunals, and civil society organizations have played a vital role in advancing the rights of migrants. I also have the privilege of teaching at a law school committed to access to justice. My students will go on to become legal practitioners and leaders equipped with the knowledge and tools to drive positive change,” she says.

description:
Research shows that nearly half of U.S. adults’ faces are already stored in facial recognition databases, and that Black, Brown, and Asian individuals are up to 100 times more likely to be misidentified by a facial recognition algorithm than white men.
“Facial recognition and other biometric technologies in the hands of government agencies have become tools of authoritarianism.
“Facial recognition technology threatens the privacy and security of all Americans.
They're using the very same facial recognition technologies that regularly misidentify people of color, leading to unjust arrests and detainment.
The Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act is cosponsored in the Senate by Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.
text:
Bill Text (PDF)

Washington (September 25, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), member of the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, Senator Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), and Representatives Pramila Jayapal (WA-07), Rashida Tlaib (MI-12), and Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), announced the reintroduction of the Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act, legislation to prohibit the government from using facial recognition and other biometric technologies.

The legislation responds to the federal government’s growing use of biometric recognition technology, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection’s (CBP) mobile facial recognition app, which has been used to target immigrants and intimidate communities across the country. Research shows that nearly half of U.S. adults’ faces are already stored in facial recognition databases, and that Black, Brown, and Asian individuals are up to 100 times more likely to be misidentified by a facial recognition algorithm than white men.

“Facial recognition and other biometric technologies in the hands of government agencies have become tools of authoritarianism. Agencies such as ICE and CBP are using this technology to track, target, intimidate and surveil communities across the country,”said Senator Markey. “Black and Brown communities — already subject to the most aggressive policing and immigration enforcement — are disproportionately affected and more likely to be wrongly flagged, detained, or targeted by a faulty facial recognition match. We must stop the Trump administration’s growing web of surveillance technology, and that starts with a moratorium on dangerous, discriminatory biometric recognition.”

“Every American who values their right to privacy, stands against discrimination, and believes people are innocent until proven guilty should be concerned about facial recognition technology fueling a national surveillance state,” said Senator Merkley. “Enacting a federal moratorium on this technology is critical to ensuring we can rein in inappropriate surveillance and protect our communities’ fundamental right to privacy.”

“We have to stop the constant, nonconsensual state of surveillance that we live in, and that starts with placing a moratorium on our government’s use of facial recognition technology,” said Congresswoman Jayapal. “Black and Brown people are more likely to be misidentified and wrongfully put in jail because of this unregulated technology, and our government has used it to unjustly target protestors and immigrants. Putting the brakes on this technology is necessary to protect civil rights and ensure public safety.”

“Facial recognition technology is racist, misidentifying Black, Brown, and Asian residents and pinning them as suspects in crimes they did not commit,” said Representative Tlaib. “When such flawed and biased technology is used to invade our privacy, we are all less safe. I'm proud to reintroduce this bill that will ban facial recognition technology and protect all our civil liberties.”

The Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act would:

Place a prohibition on the use of facial recognition technology by federal entities, which can only be lifted with an act of Congress;

Place a prohibition on the use of other biometric technologies, including voice recognition, gate recognition, and recognition of other immutable physical characteristics, by federal entities, which can only be lifted with an act of Congress;

Condition federal grant funding to state and local entities, including law enforcement, on those entities enacting their own moratoria on the use of facial recognition and biometric technology;

Prohibit the use of federal dollars for biometric surveillance systems;

Prohibit the use of information collected via biometric technology in violation of the Act in any judicial proceedings;

Provide a private right of action for individuals whose biometric data is used in violation of the Act and allow for enforcement by state Attorneys General; and

Allow states and localities to enact their own laws regarding the use of facial recognition and biometric technologies.

“Face surveillance is one of the most intrusive surveillance technologies. It’s past time for the federal government to end its use. Face surveillance in the hands of the government is a fundamentally harmful technology, even under strict regulations or if the technology was 100% accurate. We thank the authors of this bill for their leadership in ending the federal government’s use of this dangerous and invasive technology,” said India McKinney, Director of Federal Affairs at Electronic Frontier Foundation.

“We can no longer afford to ignore the very real harms of AI surveillance technologies, including facial recognition. We have seen how ICE and other federal agencies utilize facial recognition to abuse immigrants, Black and Brown communities, and people participating in protests and other First Amendment protected actions. There is no more excuse for inaction or justification for allowing the continued use of this surveillance technology - the time to pass this legislation is now,” said Caitlin Seeley George (she/her), Campaigns and Managing Director at Fight for the Future.

“Facial recognition poses a significant threat to our privacy and our democracy. The technology has been shown to be biased, inaccurate, and disproportionally harmful to people of color. Even 100% accurate facial recognition poses considerable threats to our privacy and civil liberties. The Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act takes the right approach on this urgent issue, effectively banning its current use and ensuring Congress will give careful consideration to if and how the technology can be used in the future. EPIC is proud to support it,” said Jeramie D. Scott, Director of Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC)’s Surveillance Oversight Program.

“The rapid adoption of powerful surveillance tech by our federal government benefits companies that amass billions in profits through contracts with law enforcement agencies, at the expense of our civil rights. This bill by Senator Markey couldn’t be more timely. Not only does this bill disrupt the money flow for surveillance profiteers; it prevents the use of one of the most invasive forms of surveillance and grants users a private right of action, urgently needed as we still lack federal data privacy protections and a prohibition on law enforcement purchases of sensitive data. We’ve seen how dangerous these tools can be and how easily bad actors can weaponize them against any person or community. Without proper guardrails or consideration for how our privacy will be protected, surveillance tech becomes a tool of oppression, not safety. We are proud to endorse this bill and appreciate Senator Markey’s continued leadership in this area,” said Amanda Beckham, Government Relations Director at Free Press.

“Right now, just walking down the street could allow you to be detected by AI-powered cameras and put into a database. Sen. Markey’s Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act is a critically needed safeguard against a surveillance apocalypse where the government and unaccountable corporations can collect and store your face and voice,” said Hajar Hammado, Senior Policy Advisor at Demand Progress. “Facial recognition technology threatens the privacy and security of all Americans. Every member of Congress who cares about invasive surveillance must support this bill.”

“We should all be free to move freely in our communities -- drive to work, walk our neighborhoods, travel to see family -- without constant monitoring. ICE officers and other federal agents are out in our neighborhoods targeting Black and Brown people because of the color of our skin and scanning our faces without consent to fuel a cruel mass deportation machine. They're using the very same facial recognition technologies that regularly misidentify people of color, leading to unjust arrests and detainment. Senator Markey’s Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act would put a stop to this racist invasion of privacy,” said Alejandra Montoya-Boyer, Vice President of The Leadership Conference’s Center for Civil Rights and Technology.

The Facial Recognition and Biometric Technology Moratorium Act is cosponsored in the Senate by Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), and in the House of Representatives by Representatives Greg Casar (TX-35), Judy Chu (CA-28), Jim McGovern (MA-02), Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-At Large), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), and Jan Schakowsky (IL-09).

This legislation is endorsed by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF), Fight for the Future, Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, Color of Change, Access Now, Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), Free Press, Demand Progress, and UnidosUS.

text:
Three organizations representing thousands of ranchers in Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas issued a joint statement Friday warning operations by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement are disrupting the agricultural community and will make beef prices spike again. Their statement is the beef’s industry latest salvo against policies and actions by the Trump administration.

The Texas Cattle Feeders Association, Kansas Livestock Association, and Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association said they are closely monitoring ICE’s activity and the impacts it’s creating. They described hearing reports of delays in shipping thousands of cattle to processors and workforce disruptions in important links of the supply chains such as dairies, feedyards, transportation hubs as well as feed and grain companies.

“These ICE operations are having a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers that put beef on the table and keep the supply chain moving,” the groups said. “Additionally, these types of disruptions will lead to higher beef prices for consumers.”

The ranchers’ statement about ICE is just the latest complaint they’ve had about the Trump administration’s impacts that they say are hurting the beef industry.

As beef prices reached record highs this year and the U.S. cattle herd shrunk to its lowest in 75 years, there has been a growing discontent among ranchers about some of the policies made by President Donald Trump. Most recently, Trump announced plans to suspend tariffs and import 300,000 metric tons of ground beef from countries such as Argentina and Brazil.

The meat would be sold at a discount for American consumers. While this was done to bring beef prices down for consumers, U.S. ranchers said it undercut their business. In response to the backlash, Trump issued a set of executive orders to see how to make it easier for ranchers to process and sell their own meat directly to consumers, as well as changes to labeling and mapping more than two million additional acres of grazing land to be managed by the Department of the Interior.

In response to a request for comment from The Tribune, the Department of Homeland Security shared a post on X by DHS Sec. Markwayne Mullin.

“ICE is not conducting worksite operations in Kansas,” Mullin said. “ICE law enforcement has conducted operations targeting heinous criminals including murderers, rapists, and drug traffickers and illegal aliens with final orders of removal.”

Mullin did not mention Texas or Oklahoma in his statement.

In their statement, the three cattle organizations called the disruptions caused by ICE operations come at a time of “enhanced focus and pressure” on the cattle and beef supply chain.

“They are a costly and unnecessary impact to cattle producers already suffering from unwelcome political interference to both the markets as well as the physical supply chain,” they said in the statement. “Frustratingly, the harm these actions cause to cattle producers last for days and weeks after such operations conclude.”

The three associations said they respect the responsibility federal agencies have to “enforce the law.” However, the groups said rural businesses depend on a stable workforce. They added the sudden workforce disruptions can create immediate animal-welfare, operational and economic consequences that go beyond a single business.

“We urge federal officials to conduct enforcement actions in a lawful, orderly, and transparent manner; respect due process; and communicate clearly with affected employers and communities,” the organizations said in their statement.

text:
The Department of Homeland Security sent 159 agents to Maine during the January immigration enforcement surge, according to records filed in a lawsuit alleging that agents violated the constitutional rights of people who were filming them.

One record includes a list of agents and the regions they were sent from, including New England, California, Utah, New York, Maryland, Illinois, Louisiana, Washington, D.C., New Jersey and Pennsylvania. The agents’ names are blacked out in a version of the federal court record publicly available online.

The government also uploaded partial depositions of three federal agents, including a Homeland Security Investigations officer who was assigned to work in Maine during the surge. According to court records, the agent’s team was involved in interactions with three observers who were told — on camera — that they were being added to a watchlist.

That agent testified that he believed the surge ended earlier than scheduled because of the cold weather.

While the agents’ names are largely redacted in the deposition documents, they appear to be included as the file names when downloaded from the federal court’s electronic records system. Wyn Hornbuckle, a Department of Justice spokesperson, confirmed on Friday that this was an error.

A spokesperson for DHS did not respond to requests for comment Friday.

The lawsuit was filed in February by two Maine residents who allege agents working for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement violated the rights of several people who observed and recorded their activity. The lawsuit was amended in April to add two more plaintiffs, who said they were detained at the border for an hour in March, two months after an ICE agent said he was placing one of them in a database.

The government has denied the allegations, including the existence of a database of observers.

On Sept. 18, the government filed a motion to dismiss the case, attaching several exhibits to support its arguments. The motion was filed on the same day that a federal judge in Minnesota dismissed a lawsuit that protesters filed earlier this year, also alleging First Amendment violations.

The plaintiffs are still working on a response to the government’s motion, but their attorney, JoAnna Suriani, said arguments supporting their allegations are included in a motion for a preliminary injunction filed on Sept. 11.

That motion — and all of the accompanying exhibits — has been sealed at the government’s request, in a motion that also was sealed as of Friday when the courthouse closed at 4:30 p.m.

Redefining First Amendment rights?

“If the government gets what it wants in its motion to dismiss, their definition of what it means for a protester to ‘interfere’ is going to completely swallow the First Amendment right that everyday Americans have,” Suriani said.

In the lawsuit, the four observers say they recorded videos of agents conducting arrests and transporting detainees. While they were recording, they allege masked agents took the observers’ biometric information and said they were adding them to a database. In one case, the lawsuit alleges, someone claiming to be from DHS called an observer’s spouse and told them that they should “not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist.”

The government’s attorneys argued in the motion to dismiss that the agents behaved appropriately in responding to what they perceived as threats from observers to interfere with immigration arrests.

The agency argued that its policy prohibits agents from recording observers, but that agents have “legitimate reasons to identify individuals or vehicles encountered during enforcement activity, assess whether they present safety or operational concerns, and to obtain address information in connection with those functions.”

One agent who was deposed testified that he feared that observers meant to “dox” him and other agents, and that he believed they were trying to stop an arrest.

The agent’s comments were included in an exhibit filed by the government titled “Coleman, Jhon, 08-13-2026.” The agent is referred to by his initials in other court records, and he is referred to as “Mr. Coleman” at one point in the portion of his deposition filed as an exhibit by the government.

In its motion to dismiss, the government said that agent “J.C.” of Homeland Security Investigations in Boston was involved in three of the four interactions with the plaintiffs in the case. The government argued that there were only a limited number of agents who were briefly in Maine from other states and mentioned a database to observers.

“While I was in Maine, from multiple different locations, I heard multiple times that people were going to find me and my family, and we’re going to pay for it,” Coleman said in the deposition. “I heard many threats, and I heard tons of profanity towards us.”

Suriani — who declined to discuss the agents’ names — said her clients “vigorously deny” allegations that they were interfering with arrests. She said the government’s exhibits offer a “very small sampling of the deposition testimony,” and that the plaintiffs look forward to their filings becoming public.

‘A nice little database’

In another deposition record that lists “Reddish, Officer Jordan 08-11-2026” in the file name, an agent testified that he normally works in Utah. The agent’s name is redacted at the top of the deposition. He is referred to at one point in the document as Officer Reddish.

According to his deposition, and the government’s motion to dismiss, that agent spoke with another officer who was filmed telling a woman in South Portland on Jan. 23 that the agency has “a nice little database.” That video was shared widely on social media during the January surge.

“I believe I was just trying to tell him to watch what he says,” the agent testified, according to the deposition. “He explained to me that he was trying to be funny. The joke didn’t land clearly. And I said just watch what you say.”

A reporter emailed all three men from the government’s deposition documents and received no response. Other attempts to reach them by phone and social media were not successful.
