title: Why is ICE making arrests so close to schools? San Diego grapples with enforcement surge
description:
The following day, ICE agents arrested the mother and father of a 2-year-old and a 5-year-old about a block away from their children’s San Diego school, just after they had dropped the children off.
And last Thursday, ICE agents detained a father outside a San Diego Head Start daycare after he dropped off his 2-year-old daughter.
The ICE surge, they say, has sown fear and panic among families, and kept some students home from school.
Immigration detentions surged in San Diego in July, according to federal data obtained by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by the San Diego Union-Tribune.
“When immigration enforcement occurs near a school, the effects do not end with the individual being detained.
text:
On Sept. 8, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detained a second-year student at San Diego City College as he drove next to campus and chased another student onto the school grounds as he fled on foot.

The following day, ICE agents arrested the mother and father of a 2-year-old and a 5-year-old about a block away from their children’s San Diego school, just after they had dropped the children off. School staff had to move their car and contact a family friend to pick the children up after both parents were taken into ICE custody.

And last Thursday, ICE agents detained a father outside a San Diego Head Start daycare after he dropped off his 2-year-old daughter. He reportedly threw his car keys and ID to school staff during the arrest.

A flurry of immigration enforcement activity in California’s second-largest city has sparked outrage among educators and local officials who have questioned the presence of federal agents several feet from school doorsteps. The ICE surge, they say, has sown fear and panic among families, and kept some students home from school.

“This level of anxiety and fear for basic safety and security, from a child’s perspective, is creating chaos,” said Allison Ohle, executive director of DEEP San Diego, an organization that partners with schools to increase literacy proficiency. “It’s an impossible environment to effectively teach children when they are afraid, rightly, that their families will be torn apart on the way to school.”

The Trump administration said over the summer that it expected to increase the number of ICE arrests, with some reports of a goal of 2,000 arrests per day. Immigration detentions surged in San Diego in July, according to federal data obtained by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed by the San Diego Union-Tribune. Some of that enforcement activity has happened near schools, according to recent reports.

A kindergarten teacher who teaches at a school in San Diego’s City Heights neighborhood said one of her 5-year-old students had been fearful of ICE since school began in August. Then one of the child’s family members was detained.

The teacher said the child gets nervous during pickup time while they wait for her parents outside the school.

“‘Are we safe here? Should we go back inside?’” she said the child asks her.

The teacher, who asked to only use her first name, Allison, to protect her student, said she does her best to reassure the child.

“I always tell my students my job is to teach them to read and write and learn to do math, but my No. 1 job is to keep them safe,” Allison said. “I’m not going to lie, though. When I say goodbye to her at the end of the day, it hits my heart, because I hope that I see her again.”

A teacher at Hamilton Elementary, also in the City Heights neighborhood, who also spoke on condition of anonymity, said immigration agents detained a neighbor no more than 100 feet from the school’s entrance about an hour before the first bell. Several students were present at the school for before-school care.

“Kids were incredibly alarmed and scared,” the teacher said. “We had very low attendance that day, and we had parents texting us, ‘Is ICE still there? Am I safe to go?’ ”

Another San Diego Unified teacher said her preschool class has about half the number of students compared to last year, which school staff suspect is due to families’ fear of immigration enforcement. Earlier this month, one family kept their child home for three days after witnessing law enforcement officers they believed to be ICE agents knock on doors of homes near the school. The teacher spoke on condition of anonymity to avoid ICE targeting families at her school.

Several of those detained were Haitian immigrants, according to local news reports. Many Haitians had permission to live and work in the U.S. under Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, a status offered to people from countries that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) determines would be unsafe to return to due to conditions such as ongoing armed conflict or the aftermath of a hurricane or earthquake. The Trump administration has ended TPS for citizens of several countries, including Haiti, a decision the Supreme Court upheld last month.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said in an email that there have been no targeted operations at or nearby elementary schools.

“ICE does not target schools. This is just another false narrative to try and demonize our brave ICE law enforcement, who are facing a 1,300% increase in assaults against them and an 8,000% increase in death threats,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson also said the couple detained on Sept. 9 near a school entered the country lawfully in 2022, but “overstayed their welcome.” DHS did not say if that meant their visa expired.

Earlier this month, San Diego Unified Superintendent Fabi Bagula, school board trustees and several elected officials asked federal immigration authorities to cease immigration enforcement activity near schools and during school arrival and dismissal times.

“When immigration enforcement occurs near a school, the effects do not end with the individual being detained. Children see it. Families hear about it,” reads the statement. “Fear travels quickly through classrooms, playgrounds, and neighborhoods. Students arrive at school carrying questions and anxiety that no child, especially our youngest learners, should have to carry.”

Bagula said in an interview Thursday that she had not received a response from DHS to the letter, but hopes the federal government changes its approach to immigration enforcement.

“We don’t have to do it in such a way that actually hurts children. That’s actually the part that is devastating to me,” Bagula said. “It’s not necessary. You could wait for another hour, do it five blocks away. We actually can mitigate this and protect children at the same time.”

Bagula said staff acted quickly to connect a family with legal aid organizations after federal agents arrested two parents after dropping off their young children at school. The parents’ first call from detention was to the school to check on their children.

“I’m really concerned about what our plan is for healing,” Bagula said. “I wouldn’t be able to concentrate if I saw my neighbor be taken. I would be worried about my own parents. And that’s literally what’s happening.”

Not all schools have seen attendance drops during the city’s ICE surge, Bagula said. A principal at a high school serving a large immigrant community told her that kids were coming to campus because they “actually feel safer here, so they actually want to come to school.”

The teachers union and the classified staff union also put out a statement, demanding “strict no-access policies” for ICE on campus, know-your-rights education and legal support for families and students and “trauma-informed” support or counseling for teachers and school staff.

Hundreds of people marched and rallied on Sept. 16 in the City Heights neighborhood, where at least three schools have experienced nearby ICE activity. Some demonstrators carried a big banner that read “ICE Out of SD” and others had signs saying “ICE Out of Our Schools” and “End Raids Now.”

Dozens of San Diego City College students also protested the detention of student Renatho Casseus. The college has raised about $11,000 for legal aid for Casseus, who entered the U.S. while in 10th grade and had no criminal record, according to San Diego City College President Ricky Shabazz.

Hundreds of students saw the arrest happen near a campus entrance during a passing period, Shabazz said.

“This has wreaked havoc and terror on our fall semester,” he said.

He said some students are still weighing whether it is safe for them to come to campus.

“There are more humane ways to address these matters than chasing college students who don’t have records onto campus in masks with guns out,” Shabazz said. “The effects of this administration’s approach to immigration is going to have lasting effects on generations because people are scarred by observing their colleagues, their friends, their fellow students being snatched out of cars and chased.”

text:
(CN) — The Department of Homeland Security turned to the U.S. Supreme Court on Thursday, seeking permission to continue its controversial deportation of immigrants to countries they are not originally from.

In an emergency application, President Donald Trump’s administration asked the high court to put a hold on a Massachusetts federal court order from February that found the removal policy violates due process rights.

That decision was upheld late Wednesday by the Boston-based First Circuit, despite the government’s pending appeal to the Supreme Court. The government argues it should have been allowed to file a response to the motion first before it was granted.

“The First Circuit has spoken clearly: The government’s third-country removal policy is unlawful, and class members have a right to meaningful notice of third countries and a meaningful opportunity to raise fear-based claims,” said attorney Trina Realmuto with the National Immigration Litigation Alliance.

“It is not at all surprising that the administration is now asking the Supreme Court to stay the First Circuit’s decision — the administration has publicly and repeatedly said it wants to continue sending people to third countries where we know that they face horrific and potentially life-threatening conditions,” Realmuto added.

Last year, the justice allowed the government to continue allowing detainees to be removed to third nations, as long as the receiving country has made blanket assurances that they will not persecute or torture the deportees.

The government has thus been conducting such removals over the last 15 months, Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote.

He said the government has been able to remove thousands of detainees to third countries in recent months and thousands more are eligible for such removal.

Sauer said the unexpected reversal has created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations, leading to a canceled flight to three separate countries carrying 70 immigrants with criminal convictions.

“To halt that chaos, an immediate administrative stay should be entered while the court considers this application,” Sauer wrote.

Because the noncitizens who are challenging the policy have already been given final removal orders, the government argues they have already had an opportunity to challenge their removals and cannot establish irreparable harm.

The lower court’s order that deportees must receive notice and a meaningful opportunity to raise torture or persecution objections has thwarted the government’s ability to remove any detainees at all and disrupted its agreements with foreign countries, Sauer wrote.

The vast majority of the deportees have been sent to Mexico, but under a series of costly agreements with other countries, the government has deported thousands of others to 35 different countries. This includes Central African Republic, a country the Department of State warns U.S. citizens not to travel to because it is too dangerous.

Earlier this month, the Associated Press reported that lawyers for two men deported to Equatorial Guinea said they were beaten and held at gunpoint in a hotel-turned-detention center as part of a $7.5 million deal with the African nation.

The policy is one of a number of mass deportation measures the administration has taken in its pursuit of Trump’s sweeping crackdown on immigration.

text:
In a new report released today, Amnesty International documented widespread human rights violations committed by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and other federal agencies during the Trump administration’s large-scale, militarized immigration enforcement operations in Chicago, Minneapolis-St. Paul, New Orleans and Washington, DC.

The report, “We Had Whistles, They Had Guns”: Human Rights Violations in U.S. Immigration Enforcement Operations and the Case to Abolish ICE, demonstrates that the Trump administration is implementing a mass detention and deportation system, fueled by racist, xenophobic and false narratives, whose objective is to detain and deport as many migrants, asylum seekers and refugees from the United States as possible and spread fear throughout immigrant communities more broadly.

Take action: Tell Canada to withdraw from the Safe Third Country Agreement with the USA

“Our report documents a chilling pattern of human rights violations across the U.S. intended to instill fear within migrant, asylum seeker and refugee communities,” said Nadia Daar, Executive Director, Amnesty International USA. “ICE’s record of violating human rights is nothing new, but our report shows many of these abuses have reached a perilous new level.”

The Trump administration has committed a host of human rights abuses, including unlawful killings, some of which may amount to extrajudicial executions; arbitrary and discriminatory incommunicado detentions, including possible enforced disappearances, in some cases in conditions of confinement that may violate the prohibition on torture; violent repression of peaceful protests, and more. Based on these findings, Amnesty International is joining the chorus of community voices calling for ICE to be abolished, immediately.

ICE must be abolished

Amnesty International’s findings demonstrate that the violations documented across the four operations were not isolated or exceptional incidents, but part of recurring patterns of abuse with devastating consequences for immigrants and entire communities.

Related: Canada illegally returning refugees to the U.S. amid widespread rights violations

“Masked and armed federal agents attacking people in the streets with impunity doesn’t make our communities safer — it puts everyone in danger,” said Daar. “ICE is fundamentally broken and cannot be fixed. For the U.S. government to have an immigration enforcement system that complies with international human rights law and standards, ICE needs to be abolished and we need to start over.”

ICE was created in the wake of the September 11, 2001 attacks, and an extremely problematic security framework was adopted in the years following. Amnesty International and other organizations have documented human rights violations committed by ICE and a troubling lack of oversight and accountability since its creation in 2003. However, the scale and horror that we have witnessed since January 2025, fueled by billions of new dollars and persistent impunity, has reached new levels.

Widespread human rights violations

The four operations resulted in human rights violations against immigrants, asylum seekers and refugees, people profiled as immigrants, Black and Brown communities, and those who came to their aid and challenged the conduct of the Trump administration. They also created a pervasive climate of fear that extended throughout entire communities.

Across all four operations, Amnesty International documented:

Racially discriminatory immigration enforcement operations and arbitrary detention

Harassment, intimidation, degrading treatment and unjustified use of force by federal agents

Use of lethal force and unlawful killings by federal agents, which should be investigated as extrajudicial executions

Repression of protests and use of less lethal weapons, including tear gas and pepper spray, by federal agents

Unlawful surveillance and facial recognition technology

Inhumane detention conditions and denial of due process, which should be investigated as torture

Unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance

As the report documents, ICE agents operated within an institutional environment – openly supported and expanded by the Trump administration – in which violent and racially discriminatory immigration enforcement practices were encouraged by senior government officials, including President Trump. Agents frequently operated with masks and without identification; safeguards intended to prevent and address misconduct were weakened or dismantled; and human rights violations were rarely followed by meaningful investigation or accountability.

The report details an account from Minnesota State Representative Liish Kozlowski, who is Obijwe-Latine, who said: “My cousin was in her car going to work with her husband. ICE rolled up, literally looking for Black and Brown people. They smashed her window at gun point. They roughed her up; she was pregnant. Her husband yelled ‘She’s Native American, here’s her Tribal ID card’. An ICE agent responded, ‘That doesn’t [expletive] matter, this is our land now’.”

This is just one example from dozens in the report where ICE agents appeared to be engaging in explicit racial profiling.

“Racially profiling and snatching people off the street, separating families and arbitrarily detaining people are not only unlawful, cruel practices, but profoundly damaging,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International. “These practices violate human rights and cause fear and psychological distress and long-lasting health concerns to children, other family members and entire communities.”

Communities coming together to resist, protect one another

The report also highlights how communities came together to resist and protect one another. These networks played an essential role in documenting human rights violations, and being there for their neighbors, through mutual aid networks, constitutional observer trainings, rapid response networks, walking school buses, and more in order to stand by and protect those most directly impacted. Protests were one important tool of resistance, but were frequently met with additional acts of lawlessness by ICE and Border Patrol agents.

For example, in Chicago, the Broadview facility became a focal point for protesting against ICE and Border Patrol’s actions in the city. Reverend David Black, who frequently went to the Broadview facility to do ministry, said, “The escalation of violence by ICE and CBP at Broadview when we were just praying and chanting was terrifying.” During one ministry service he led at the facility, Reverend Black, who was dressed as Clergy, was calling on three federal agents who were standing on the facility’s roof to repent, when the agents suddenly shot him in the face, arms and torso with exploding pellets of pepper spray. He is one of the numerous people whose experiences are documented in the report.

The report highlights numerous additional human rights violations during these cruel immigration enforcement operations. Amnesty International researchers interviewed 154 people across the four locations, allowing the organization to analyze how immigration enforcement operations affect diverse communities across different political, legal, and historical contexts, and to conclude that the human rights violations documented reflect broader national patterns rather than being isolated local incidents.

“It is heartbreaking to see the pain and suffering caused by this Administration as it criminalizes and demonizes immigrants,” said Daar. “I’m also hopeful 3 communities have rallied around those targeted and in some instances forced the Trump administration to back down. We must hold accountable those government officials responsible for this reign of terror, and we must keep fighting for an immigration system that is grounded in human rights and dignity, not cruelty.”

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials are moving forward with removal proceedings against Kentucky State University basketball player Aminata "Amina" Seck, who was taken into federal custody last month, authorities said.

The 26-year-old from Senegal was arrested by ICE agents on Aug. 7 at Louisville's Muhammad Ali International Airport, according to Sadiqa Reynolds, an attorney assisting in Seck's case.

Reynolds said Seck was taken into custody as she was about to travel to New York with her teammates to a basketball tournament involving other Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs).

"She is not a criminal," Reynolds said in a statement on Facebook.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement that Seck was in the country illegally and that an immigration judge issued a final order of removal on Sept. 8, 2025, after she failed to show up at her immigration hearing.

"She will remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings," DHS said.

Seck legally entered the country on Sept. 1, 2019, in Los Angeles, on a temporary basis, according to DHS.

"She chose to overstay her welcome in violation of our country's laws," DHS said. "To be clear: a pending application or work authorization does NOT confer legal status in the United States."

Reynolds could not immediately be reached on Thursday for comment. The attorney told the Louisville Courier Journal that Seck might have missed the deadline to renew her student visa because she was undergoing back surgery, and was nursing a knee injury.

At the time of her arrest in August, Seck was wearing a leg brace and has since been receiving medical treatment, according to DHS.

Reynolds said in a social media post on her Facebook page on Tuesday that she last spoke to Seck on Sept. 15, adding that at the time, Seck complained of being in a lot of pain.

Reynolds told Courier Journal that neither she nor Seck's family and friends have been able to see her in person since she was detained.

"I pray that her chains are removed and she is able to receive the medical treatment she deserves and then released to recover fully," Reynolds said in her Facebook post.

According to online records, Seck is being held at the Grayson County Detention Center in Leitchfield, Kentucky.

DHS said in its statement that Seck was referred on Sept. 21 to a hospital, where she is receiving treatment for knee pain. The department noted that it's "a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care" to people in its custody.

"This includes medical, dental, and mental health services as available, and access to medical appointments and 24-hour emergency care," DHS said.

Rep. Morgan McGarvey, D-Kentucky, whose district includes Louisville, said in a statement that he has been monitoring Seck's situation.

"Aminata is a student-athlete who was arrested by ICE at the airport while traveling with her teammates," McGarvey said. "The Trump administration's cruelty knows no bounds, but we will never let this become normal and we won't stop fighting for her."

Seck was named to the Southern Intercollegiate Athletic Conference All-Conference (SIAC) Third Team last season, according to the Kentucky State University Athletic Department's website. She was also named the SIAC Women's Basketball Elite 16 award winner, which is presented to student-athletes who demonstrate exemplary performance in athletics and the classroom.

The university declined to comment on Seck's case, saying, "Out of respect for the privacy of those involved, Kentucky State University does not have information to share."

text:
MANHATTAN (CN) — A federal judge lambasted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Thursday in a final order against the agency’s treatment of detainees at 26 Federal Plaza, a controversial immigrant detention center in New York City that has been subject to more than a year of litigation over its living conditions.

In the scathing 127-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan describes the treatment of those jailed in the facility as “dreadful” and “squalid.” Kaplan pointed to trial evidence that suggested detainees were jam-packed into holding rooms far beyond capacity and for far longer than they were supposed to be.

“Detainees often had to try to sleep while sitting upright given the overcrowding,” Kaplan wrote. “They simply did not have enough room to lay down. Some even resorted to sleeping next to the toilets, behind the half-wall partitions.”

The Bill Clinton appointee previously issued temporary relief to the suing detainees, requiring ICE to improve the conditions inside the scrutinized holding rooms. But in his Thursday ruling, Kaplan chastised the agency for selectively flouting parts of what he’d demanded.

“The court’s orders to some extent have worked,” the judge said, referencing crowding is down since last summer’s peak. “But, as described at length above, defendants have complied with its orders only when convenient for them and persistently have disregarded them in certain ways.”

Capacity, at times, exceeded Kaplan’s requirements after his first order came down, according to trial evidence. Detainees also routinely complained of a lack of attorney access.

In his initial injunction last year, Kaplan issued a hard space cap of one detainee for every 50 square feet. He also ordered inmates to get a clean bedding mat, hygiene supplies and private and accessible phone access to their attorneys within a day of being detained.

His new, permanent order adds to those old requirements. Kaplan ordered ICE to give detainees pillows and dim the lights in the holding rooms between 9 p.m. and 7 a.m. — detainees have reported bright, fluorescent lights were typically kept on all night as they tried to sleep.

With the Thursday order, the judge also strengthened protections for legal calls within the facility, demanding every detainee be offered the opportunity to make a call within one hour of being detained. On-site medical services are also required, as are medical screenings of each detainee before they enter a holding room.

These new requirements are backed by evidence that Kaplan saw during a one-day bench trial earlier this year, which offered an extensive look into what detainees actually face inside 26 Federal Plaza.

Text messages from ICE officials revealed infectious diseases — including monkeypox and tuberculosis — permeated throughout the facility.

“This week has been one gross contagion after another,” Nancy Zanello, an assistant field office director for ICE in New York, wrote in a 2025 email.

Others remarked about the overcrowding, revealing even ICE’s own employees thought the head count in the holding rooms was unacceptable.

“This is insane,” one ICE employee wrote to another in an email shown to the court. “We desperately need to get some detainees out of 26 Fed.”

Kaplan ruled the treatment of inmates during this time was “inhumane and unconstitutional.”

“By detaining far more persons in the hold rooms than ever was intended and for far longer than ever was intended, ICE objectively deprived detainees of sleep, sanitary living conditions, basic personal hygiene needs, sufficient food and water and adequate medical care,” he wrote. “ICE prevented detainees from accessing counsel, who might have stood in the way of what it was doing. Some of these deprivations impacted detainees immediately; others only after longer periods. ICE knew, or should have known, that how it was treating detainees was wrong, yet it continued to do it anyway.”

The judge added ICE did this “to inflict punishment on detainees and induce them to self-deport.”

Kaplan’s order also grants class certification for all immigration detainees inside 26 Federal Plaza, both currently and in the future. Doing so, he acknowledged, may allow detainees with little resources to bring actions that otherwise wouldn’t be possible, using this case’s framework.

Harold Solis of Make the Road New York, who represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement that Kaplan’s decision is “a testament to the courage of those who endured and spoke out against conditions no human being should ever be forced to bear.”

“The horrific detention conditions inside 26 Federal Plaza are emblematic of this administration’s contempt for the rule of law and hostility toward immigrants,” he said. “Thanks to the bravery of those who came forward to support this lawsuit, this ruling will help ensure that no one else is forced to endure the same inhumane treatment at 26 Federal Plaza … Today’s decision is a firm reminder that the Constitution demands better.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

The federal building in Lower Manhattan has become a centerpiece of the Trump administration’s ongoing and unprecedented detention campaign against noncitizens. In addition to 26 Federal Plaza’s holding rooms, subject to Kaplan’s ruling in this case, the building also houses immigration courtrooms, where ICE agents have been seen waiting to detain immigrants on their way in and out of routine court proceedings.

text:
In July, the Trump administration stripped temporary protected status (TPS) from more than 500,000 Haitian nationals in the United States.

Here in San Diego, the community is trying to cope with this new reality.

“Us Haitians, we are very big in finding ways to be self-reliant,” said Wister Gaetan, cofounder of the nonprofit Haitian Bridge Alliance.

The organization advocates for fair and humane immigration policies for migrants. Gaetan is among the nearly 12,000 Haitians immigrants living in San Diego County. He said a strong work ethic is a shared characteristic.

“(They’d work) a whole 12-hour shift, then find themselves in the Mid-City community college learning English, taking skills training, improving their chance of actually establishing and becoming more self-reliant,” Gaetan said.

Gaetan has seen dozens of Haitian immigrants succeed in the region, but along with the second Trump administration comes the realization that they are at risk of losing everything they’ve worked hard for.

Many now find themselves without the ability to work legally and are at risk of detention and deportation.

From inflammatory rhetoric to policy changes

President Donald Trump began vilifying Haitians before he was reelected. In his debate with former Vice President Kamala Harris on Sept. 10, 2024, he falsely claimed Haitians were eating neighborhood pets.

“In Springfield, they’re eating the dogs,” Trump said while discussing immigration. “The people that came in, they’re eating the cats. They’re eating — they’re eating the pets of the people that live there.”

Officials in Springfield, Ohio, have publicly stated the claim was false.

After becoming president, Trump eliminated humanitarian parole and temporary protected status for Haitians and Syrians. These programs allow people to live and work in the United States when conditions in their home country prevent them from returning.

Without that legal protection, Haitian immigrants can now be detained and deported.

Arrest sparking fear

That happened on Sept. 8, when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) stopped two Haitian students on their way to class at San Diego City College. Renatho Kemsley Casseus was arrested. The other student fled onto campus.

That incident is reverberating in the Haitian community. Everyone is affected — even those with legal status, Roseline said. She didn’t want to give her last name out of fear. Her children are U.S. citizens but were terrified of being detained by ICE.

“Every day they try to talk to me,” she said. “They really scared because at school they talk to them too. They explain to them the situation. Even though they’re born here, they don’t really feel safe.”

She runs a daycare center out of her East County home. Some of her Haitian clients were either too afraid to leave the house or had already lost their job. Either way, she was losing customers.

And she has no easy answer to her children’s questions about what would happen if she were detained by ICE. She doesn’t even know the answers herself.

“‘I don’t feel comfortable to live by myself. I don’t feel comfortable to live with somebody else. Who is going to pay the bills?’ These are the questions they ask me every day,” Roseline said.

Broken promises

Gaetan said he still believes in the American dream and America’s promises. It’s a country that respects the rule of law and provides opportunities that few others do, he said.

“The U.S. markets itself as an exceptional country where anybody who is seeking safety will have a safe home here,” Gaetan said.

But Trump’s policies are breaking that promise, the American exceptionalism that he and other Haitians grew up believing was what the United States stood for. Gaetan said he regularly hears from Haitian nationals struggling to find their place in Trump’s America.

“I’ve got phone calls of people calling me asking, ‘Is there a way that you could go and buy for me basic necessities for my children because I’m afraid to leave my house,’” he said. “Think about it, you have families with American-born children not able to go to a supermarket to buy milk, bread and eggs so that they can feed their kid breakfast because they are afraid that if they go out they’ll be taken by ICE.”

‘The rules kept changing’

Many of the most vulnerable people affected followed the rules and did everything they were supposed to do. That was the case of a woman who asked not to use her name because she lost her legal status. She was a doctor in Haiti who fled because of its gang violence.

She entered the U.S. legally through Processes for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans, and Venezuelans (CHNV), a Biden-era humanitarian parole program. Trump terminated that program in 2025.

After losing parole, she was covered through TPS and had a work permit, which she used to work at a hotel and take English classes while also raising a toddler.

She lost her ability to work legally when Trump eliminated TPS in July. She spoke to KPBS in Spanish.

“Para mi es una falta de respeto así a la gente (To me, that is disrespectful to people),” she said.

She said she followed the rules, but the rules kept changing.

“Viniendo, pidiendo ayuda, que necesita seguridad en un país donde el derecho humano, si se respeta, se escucha, un país democrático y uno no lo está viviendo (Coming here to ask for help, seeking the security of a country where human rights are respected and heard, a democratic country, yet that is not what anyone is experiencing),” she said. “No se siente asi (It doesn’t feel that way).”

As with many Haitians, the doctor still has hope. She was able to file an asylum claim, which comes with a work permit. She is still waiting for the permit to be processed, which could take up to six months.

text:
Charges filed against four demonstrators arrested during a July protest outside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office in Arapahoe County will be dismissed Friday, the 18th Judicial District announced Thursday.

Yoselin Corrales, Arnie Carter, El Moss and Terry Burnsed were each charged with obstructing a passageway outside the Centennial ICE facility, at 12445 E. Caley Ave., according to court records. Corrales and Moss were also charged with obstructing a peace officer.

Community rallies around 4 charged in Arapahoe County protests against ICE

The group was arrested after ignoring orders from Arapahoe County sheriff's deputies to stop blocking a driveway during the protest at the ICE field office, according to a news release from the 18th Judicial District Attorney's Office.

After further review, prosecutors decided the criminal cases should not move forward, the release stated.

"I believe strongly in the First Amendment and the right of people to peacefully assemble, speak out and protest," District Attorney Amy Padden said in a statement. "Those rights are fundamental to our democracy. The law is clear that criminal statutes cannot criminalize speech."

"However, the right to freedom of speech is not absolute and does not protect against prosecution for criminal conduct," Padden's statement continued.

Padden said dismissing the four cases is an "appropriate exercise of prosecutorial discretion" and "in the interest of justice."

The protesters were not violent, did not harm or threaten law enforcement and did not damage property or disrupt traffic, according to the release.

Andy McNulty, Carter's attorney, called the dismissal "a great move that really respects the First Amendment." He said he was happy to see Padden take the step and dismiss the charges.

"These are the sorts of charges that get weaponized by police officers against those who are lawfully protesting," McNulty said.

The group's arrest was a "tax" for having the "audacity to use their First Amendment rights," McNulty said. Although the charges will now be dismissed, the four protesters still had to hire attorneys and go to court before the legal process was cut short.

Dozens of community members showed up to support the four protesters during their arraignments at the Arapahoe County Justice Center on Sept. 9.

During a gathering outside before those hearings, McNulty said that obstructing passageways is a "classic crime" used to charge protesters. Like jaywalking, it is rarely prosecuted but often appears in cases against demonstrators, he said.

This is a developing story and may be updated.

text:
White House border czar Tom Homan stood behind U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Thursday, saying the agency is “not going anywhere” despite recent scrutiny surrounding its escalated enforcement operations.

“You can hate us all you want. We’re not going anywhere,” Homan said during an introductory speech at the Justice Department’s Victims of Violent Crime summit.

Homan’s comments come as the agency breaks detention and deportation records, and several cases involving ICE agents’ use of force draw the attention of lawmakers.

An ICE officer in Austin, Texas, on Sunday shot Venezuelan national Wilber Rafael Garces Perez while he was in his vehicle completing a food delivery for DoorDash. He was taken to the hospital before being released into ICE’s custody.

The Department of Homeland Security claimed the 28-year-old man “illegally entered” the U.S. under the Biden administration — which his lawyer has denied — and “had a final order of removal” from an immigration judge.

The shooting sparked backlash from Texas officials, including Rep. Greg Casar (D), who pushed for ICE to leave the Lone Star State’s capital. On the day of the incident, Casar called for “full transparency” from the agency as Austin officials investigate the shooting — days before The Associated Press reported the agent involved was not wearing a body camera.

In Michigan, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer (D) directed state police to investigate an ICE vehicle pursuit in Grand Rapids over the weekend, which resulted in a fatal collision. Mario David Coronado Juarez, an immigrant from Guatemala lacking permanent legal status, was killed in a car crash after allegedly attempting to flee from an immigration agent’s traffic stop.

While Homan did not mention these widely covered ICE-involved incidents during his Thursday remarks, he attributed the “hate” against the agency to members of the media after asserting, “We’re going to keep pushing. We’re not going to apologize.”

“ICE will continue doing the job every day across this country, especially in sanctuary cities, where we’ll surge resources and flood the zone. We’re going to enforce the law without apology,” the border czar said. “You got my word on that.”

Health care workers and members of 1199SEIU, along with community allies, rallied Thursday at the University of Rochester Nursing School to demand protections for immigrant workers in the field and their families.

The event was part of “Healthcare Needs Us All,” a national day of action held in cities across the country that called on Congress to protect immigrant health care workers and the patients and residents who depend on them.

During the 30-minute lunchtime walkout in Rochester, organizers spoke about the role immigrants play in health care and criticized the Trump administration’’s immigration crackdown and cuts to health care.

“No matter if you live in a big city or a small town, we’re all paying the price of these cruel policies,” said Tracey Harrison, 1199SEIU vice president for the Rochester area.

“People with disabilities and seniors will be told there are no home care workers or spots available in community-based programs,” he said. “Nurses and doctors who already feel the pressures of short staffing will scramble to try to provide care without enough staff to do so safely. (Certified nursing assistants) will be unable to respond to the immediate needs of all residents assigned to them. We will feel the literal pain of this.”

Harrison said immigrants make up about 20% of essential caregivers and workers in hospitals, nursing homes, and home care in the U.S.

Organizers called for restoring legal status for Temporary Protected Status holders and other immigrants, passing the American Dream and Promise Act to create a pathway to citizenship, ending what they called discriminatory travel bans and processing delays, and increasing funding for health care.

Workers like Sharif Hill contrasted health care cuts with a surge in money and staff for immigration enforcement. He said funds that could be used to support American health care programs and essential workers are instead being funneled into the Department of Homeland Security to conduct mass deportations.

“Just a few years ago (during COVID-19), as health care workers, we were heroes. Now, we are expendable,” he said. “I look at the cuts that we have done all over America with hospital closings, jobs being cut, just for ICE to be able to pick someone up off the street and send them to a country they’re not even from. It’s unacceptable. They are tearing families apart and we can no longer remain silent.”

In July 2025, Congress passed H.R. 1, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a sweeping tax and spending law that made major changes to Medicaid nationwide. New York stands to lose $10 billion to $13.5 billion in annual funding once the law is fully in place in 2032, according to a report by the New York State Bar Association. The report estimates about 450,000 New Yorkers will lose coverage this year, with another 1 million losing Medicaid when the law is fully implemented.

“The loss in revenue for uncompensated or lower payments from underinsured will place additional financial pressure on providers across the state,” the report states. “With better-than-expected revenue collections in the current fiscal year (2026), the state is in a position to advance short-term strategies to mitigate significant financial impacts on the health care system, but such measures are unlikely to be sustainable.”

The law also set aside about $170 billion for immigration enforcement and border security through 2029, including roughly $75 billion for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. ICE’s annual budget had been about $10 billion. Some of that money is likely to go toward a 100-bed expansion of the Buffalo Federal Detention Facility in Batavia, announced in July.

More than a dozen health care providers or services in the region have closed or been cut since the law passed, according to a live tracker kept by the advocacy group Protect Our Care. They include Rochester Regional Health’s developmental and behavioral pediatrics services at its Irondequoit practice and inpatient labor and delivery at Newark-Wayne Community Hospital. The health system cited workforce strain for the pediatric cuts, and changing community needs, declining delivery rates across the region and ongoing workforce challenges for ending labor and delivery.

Organizers closed the event by emphasizing the importance of voting in the Nov. 3 midterm elections, then workers and their allies led chants in support of immigrants.

David Wazana is a Rochester Beacon contributing writer and a member of the Oasis Project’s second cohort.

title: Republicans in tough races are suddenly concerned about ICE, too | CNN Politics
description:
And now we can add another one to the list: They’re suddenly taking issue with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
An ICE enforcement operation in Kansas drew some concerned statements from both of the state’s GOP senators on Wednesday.
“When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement,” Marshall posted on X.
And that’s especially given the prior rhetoric of some of the GOP lawmakers who are suddenly expressing concern.
But elections have a tendency to make people suddenly notice problems from which they might have previously averted their gaze.
text:
One of the surest signs that Republicans are quite concerned about the 2026 midterm elections is the sudden onslaught of them distancing themselves from President Donald Trump and his unpopular policies. They’ve called for an end to the Iran war, criticized his tariffs and removed Trump references from their website.

And now we can add another one to the list: They’re suddenly taking issue with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

And that includes some of the agency’s strongest allies.

An ICE enforcement operation in Kansas drew some concerned statements from both of the state’s GOP senators on Wednesday. And in Maine, congressional candidate Paul LePage is crying foul over what he said was the wrongful deportation of a family member.

The situation is Kansas is still fluid, but ICE appears to be targeting cities in the southwestern portion of the state with large populations working in the meatpacking industry. The enforcement actions drew statements urging care from both Sens. Jerry Moran and Roger Marshall – the latter of whom is perhaps the most surprisingly vulnerable GOP senator right now.

After local officials cried foul over the lack of coordination, and both businesses and schools struggled to deal with the upheaval, Moran and Marshall each issued statements urging ICE to coordinate better.

“When ICE operates in Kansas, it needs to coordinate with our local law enforcement,” Marshall posted on X. “Our sheriffs and police know these communities better than anyone, and working together keeps officers and residents safe.”

He added that he was “closely following what’s happening in SW Kansas” and has been in touch with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

Marshall’s comments are particularly notable given his past commentary about ICE.

While Moran raised concerns about the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents in Minneapolis in January, Marshall went in a very different direction.

A week after Good was killed, Marshall told CNN’s Jake Tapper that “sometimes there’s collateral damage” and that “we could be just as easily talking about the death of ICE agents.”

Two days later, he told Fox Business Network that “we’re grateful for all the ICE officers in there risking their lives.”

He continued praising ICE in the months that followed and, in March, authored an op-ed defending how ICE carries out apprehensions.

The story is similar with LePage in Maine.

The former governor has a long history of strident immigration views, including criticizing asylum-seekers in his state as liabilities who bring disease and drain public resources.

And after an ICE agent shot and killed a man in Biddeford, Maine, in July, LePage cautioned that law enforcement are “often in situations where they have to make split-second decisions.” He also accused the other side of trying “to politicize this incident to try and perpetuate illegal immigration.”

But this week, LePage held a press conference where he accused ICE of wrongfully moving to deport his son’s father-in-law, despite his having a work permit.

LePage said the man is “being deported because he came from a country that’s not liked by certain people in Washington.”

“That’s not right,” LePage said.

He also called for ICE to focus more on “people in the gangs and criminals.”

The comments from Marshall and LePage come after some Republicans from heavily Hispanic congressional districts recently distanced themselves from Trump’s deportation policies.

That made sense for Reps. Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida and Monica De La Cruz of Texas, given polls showing Hispanics have swung hard against Trump over the past two years.

But it’s perhaps more telling to see this dynamic stretch into Kansas, which Trump won by 16 points in 2024, and Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, which Trump won by nine points. And that’s especially given the prior rhetoric of some of the GOP lawmakers who are suddenly expressing concern.

Of course, as with the long-unpopular Iran war, the writing has been on the wall when it comes to Americans’ concerns about ICE and Trump’s deportations for a while now.

A July CNN poll showed three-quarters of Americans said ICE uses force inappropriately at least “sometimes,” including 54% who said it happens “often.” A Quinnipiac University poll at the time showed registered voters disapproved of ICE 60%-37%.

But elections have a tendency to make people suddenly notice problems from which they might have previously averted their gaze.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other agencies have wasted tens of millions of dollars pursuing ill-conceived plans to rapidly increase detention capacity, and the total will likely rise due to ongoing mismanagement, congressional investigators warned Thursday.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office documented costly problems in several initiatives ICE has pursued since President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025 and ordered the mass arrest and deportation of people who are in the country illegally.

Among the misspending was nearly $3 million to erect tents at Guantanamo Bay that were never used, $20 million to maintain purchased warehouses that are now being sold without having housed a single detainee, and excessive rates paid to hold detainees at a deficient and now-shuttered Florida lockup.

ICE has no strategic plan for spending its windfall

Congress gave ICE an unprecedented $45 billion to expand detention capacity last year as part of the Trump-backed One Big Beautiful Bill, but the agency still lacks a comprehensive strategic plan for how to spend it wisely, the report warned. The detainee population has increased from 39,000 in January 2025 to 67,000 as of July 30.

“Without taking action to manage detention investments in accordance with program and project management practices, ICE will likely continue to make uninformed decisions and risk further inefficiency and wasted resources,” warned the GAO, a nonpartisan agency that investigated at the request of congressional Democrats.

The Department of Homeland Security, ICE's parent agency, told GAO it would develop a plan to guide its detention expansion by Aug. 31, 2027, but that may be too late to prevent more waste, the report said.

ICE and DHS offered no immediate additional comment on the report.

The government scrapped a plan for mass detention at Guantánamo Bay

Shortly after Trump returned to the White House, the government began blowing money by hastily pursuing plans to detain more people who were in the U.S. illegally, the report found.

After the White House directed officials to use the military base in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, for immigration detention in January 2025, the Department of Defense assembled enough tents to hold 5,000 people there at a cost of $2.85 million, the report said. But DHS found that the tents didn't meet detention standards, and they were removed before they housed a single detainee.

The plan for mass detention at Guantánamo Bay was later found to be “infeasible” and scrapped because of the costs of building facilities that could meet federal standards. Instead, the agency housed an average of 16 detainees daily there this year, at a cost of millions of dollars, the report found.

ICE is wasting millions of dollars on empty warehouses

Earlier this year, ICE purchased 11 large warehouses across the country for $1.07 billion as part of a plan backed by former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to increase detention capacity. But that idea was scrapped amid public opposition before any detainees were housed in them because the department didn't conduct “appropriate due diligence and planning," according to the GAO report. DHS is now planning to sell seven of the facilities.

ICE has spent $20 million on costs and services related to those seven warehouses that it will not recover, including zoning assessments, title insurance, utilities and security, and will need to sell them for the total purchase price of $707 million to avoid more waste, the report said.

ICE has also “incurred significant costs” for the four warehouses that it plans to keep, including a $426 million outlay to renovate facilities in Arizona and Maryland that is on hold due to legal challenges.

Report finds waste on ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ and other plans

After the warehouse initiative faltered, ICE launched a plan to purchase facilities owned by private contractors that were already housing detainees, saying it would give more control over infrastructure and limit local governments' ability to restrict their use.

The agency spent $1.5 billion to buy two of them in July and could buy more even though ICE has “not assessed the long-term affordability of owning these facilities," the report said.

The report found fault with other initiatives. ICE never reached a contract with the state of Florida to operate the facility nicknamed “Alligator Alcatraz,” which housed detainees for a year until it was closed in June following reports of substandard and abusive conditions.

Instead, DHS agreed to reimburse the state through a special $608 million Federal Emergency Management Agency grant that authorizes a charge of $249 per detainee per day — 171% higher than ICE's normal rate of $92, the report found. DHS is also paying the state the higher rate for a second facility that's still open in Sanderson, Florida.

ICE is also facing high costs under an agreement in which the Bureau of Prisons is housing detainees at eight facilities. The agreement requires ICE to reimburse the full cost, which has ballooned because of overtime and other staffing assignments, and pay a rate of $182 per detainee per day, the report said.

Amnesty International reported on Thursday that the United States government committed human rights violations during federal immigration enforcement operations in Washington DC, Chicago, New Orleans, and Minneapolis between 2025 and 2026.

The non-governmental organization reached this conclusion following an investigation into actions taken by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, and other federal agencies. The probe included 154 interviews and an analysis of more than 30 audio-visual items.

The findings are detailed in a 130-page report released on Thursday titled,“‘We Had Whistles, They Had Guns’: Human Rights Violations in US Immigration Enforcement Operations and the Case to Abolish ICE.”

According to a summary, the human rights violations documented by the organization include racial profiling, discriminatory and arbitrary stops and arrests, harassment, intimidation, and unlawful use of force, particularly lethal force, which in some instances may constitute extrajudicial execution.

The report also cited the «repression of peaceful protests, unlawful use of less-lethal force, unlawful surveillance, cruel, inhumane and degrading detention conditions that may violate the prohibition on torture, and unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance.»

Possible ‘extrajudicial executions’

According to Amnesty International, the mass detention and deportation system of US president Donald Trump administration is driven by «racist, xenophobic and false narratives and white supremacist theories,» targeting «as many racialized migrants, asylum seekers and refugees from the United States as possible.»

In that regard, the report highlights that operations across the four cities relied on racially discriminatory actions, leading to arbitrary arrests accompanied by harassment, intimidation, degrading treatment, and unjustified force by federal agents.

Specifically, the organization lists examples of unlawful lethal force, including the shootings of Marimar Martínez and Silverio Villegas González in Chicago; Julio César Sosa-Celis, Renee Good, and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis; and Philip Brown and Justin Bryant Nelson in Washington, D.C.

“The unlawful killings of Villegas González, Good and Pretti may amount to extrajudicial executions,” the report stated.

Additionally, the report denounces the crackdown on protests and the use of less-lethal weapons, such as tear gas and pepper spray, against rapid response network members, observers, and demonstrators, as well as the use of facial recognition technologies that infringe on the right to privacy.

Calls for the dismantling of ICE

Regarding detentions, Amnesty International noted a pattern of misusing field offices, processing centers, and official facilities for prolonged holding, at times under «inhumane conditions» and involving «coercion» that it asserts could constitute «torture.»

The organization also documented instances where detainees were denied legal counsel and family contact. Lawyers were prevented from reaching clients, and ICE occasionally refused to confirm custody or reveal individuals’ locations, amounting to «incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance.»

The report adds that human rights violations are not merely attributable to individual agent misconduct, lack of training, or poor oversight, but rather stem from an institutional framework «openly supported and expanded by the Trump administration,» coupled with a lack of accountability.

Amnesty International concluded that the «scale, persistence and structural nature of these institutional failures cannot be adequately addressed through discrete reforms,» making the «fundamental institutional dismantling» of ICE necessary to bring the system into alignment with international obligations.

Finally, the report highlighted that the operations created a pervasive climate of fear across immigrant communities and beyond, causing many individuals to withdraw from public life and disrupting daily activities in schools, healthcare centers, places of worship, workplaces, and neighborhoods

text:
Telling the justices that it had been deprived of “an essential tool to remove certain aliens, including some of the worst criminal aliens,” the Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Thursday afternoon. Specifically, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asked the court to clear the way for the government to deport noncitizens to countries that are not identified in their removal orders – a procedure known as “third-country removals.”

The 42-page filing was the third time that the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to intervene in the battle over third-country removals. Sauer told the justices on Thursday that “[t]he latest order” by U.S. District Judge Brian Murphy barring the third-country removals “rests on the same fundamentally flawed legal premises as the previous rulings.” Sauer also asked the court to enter an “immediate administrative stay” – an order that would allow the government to continue deportations while the justices consider his request.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who has initial responsibility for emergency appeals from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit, from which the case hails, directed the immigrants in the case to respond to the government’s request by 4 p.m. EDT on Monday, September 28.

The dispute began last year, in the wake of a Jan. 20 executive order in which President Donald Trump instructed the Department of Homeland Security to take “all appropriate actions” to remove noncitizens who were in the United States despite having orders to deport them.

That order prompted DHS to issue internal guidance in February instructing a division of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement to determine whether undocumented immigrants who had received deportation orders but had not yet been removed because of the possibility that they would be tortured if they were returned to their home countries could instead be removed to a different country. Additional guidance issued the following month indicated that before immigrants can be removed to a country that is not specifically identified in their removal orders and that has not assured the United States that the immigrants will not face torture, DHS must follow a series of procedures: It must notify the immigrants of the planned removal, give them a chance to “affirmatively express” fear that they will face torture, and – if needed – conduct a screening to determine the likelihood that they will indeed be tortured.

In March, four immigrants with removal orders went to federal court in Massachusetts, where they argued that they feared being removed to a country that was not identified in their orders.

Murphy issued an order that barred the government from deporting the immigrants and others like them to third countries without first providing their lawyers and them with written notice of the third country to which they might be removed, as well as a “meaningful opportunity” to challenge that removal. DHS should also, Murphy instructed, decide whether the immigrants’ fears of torture were “reasonable,” rather than whether it is “more likely than not” that they will be tortured. If immigrants cannot make that showing, Murphy added, DHS must give them at least 15 days to seek to reopen their immigration proceedings.

Sauer went to the Supreme Court for the first time, asking the justices to put Murphy’s order on hold while the government’s appeal moved forward. Over a dissent by Justice Sonia Sotomayor that was joined by Jackson and Justice Elena Kagan, the court on June 23 granted that request.

Sauer returned to the court for the second time one day later, asking the justices to “clarify[]” that, in the wake of their first order, the Trump administration could move forward with the deportation of eight men being held on a U.S. military base in Djibouti after Murphy had ruled that efforts to remove them to South Sudan violated his order.

On July 3, the court issued a brief opinion in which it indicated that its June 23 order paused Murphy’s order “in full” – and also applied to his later order regarding the South Sudan deportations. Kagan wrote a brief concurring opinion, in which she indicated that although she disagreed with the court’s decision to pause Murphy’s order, she did “not see how a district court can compel compliance with an order that this Court has stayed.” Sotomayor again dissented, joined by Jackson.

When the case went back to the lower courts, Murphy issued a final judgment in the immigrants’ favor and threw out the third-country removal policy. He ruled (among other things) that before immigrants can be removed to a third country, they have the right to “meaningful notice” and a “meaningful opportunity” to contest removal to that third country on the ground that they have a reasonable fear of being persecuted or tortured there.

On Friday, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 1st Circuit largely upheld Murphy’s ruling, and on Wednesday it dissolved the March 16, 2026, order that put Murphy’s ruling on hold while the government appealed.

The Trump administration then came to the Supreme Court for the third time on Thursday afternoon, asking the justices to intervene. Sauer wrote that the reinstatement of Murphy’s order has “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations—including the cancellation of flights—and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals.”

Sauer contended that Murphy and the court of appeals had “simply relied on the same meritless grounds on which” the earlier order in the immigrants’ favor was based. “The courts,” he said, “again disregarded multiple jurisdictional bars that preclude” courts from reviewing an immigrant’s “claims of persecution or torture except in a petition for review from a removal order. And they again rejected the government’s reliance on countrywide assurances that particular nations will not torture or persecute anyone.”

If the third-country deportation process is delayed, Sauer said, “the consequence … is that the government will often need to restart the entire removal process afresh, freezing things as the government attempts to rework arrangements with foreign countries.”

The Supreme Court reviewed the policy at an earlier stage of the case last year and allowed it to continue over the dissent of the court’s three liberal justices – Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.
The administration began the policy last year as part of its broader crackdown on immigration.

text:
President Donald Trump’s administration urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to allow it to remove migrants to countries other than their homeland without giving them an opportunity to raise human rights concerns.

The Justice Department filed an emergency appeal after a decision from the Boston-based 1st US Circuit Court of Appeals late Wednesday effectively blocked the removals, which have been taking place since the Supreme Court sided with the administration on the issue more than a year ago.

That decision has “created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations – including the cancellation of flights – and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals,” US Solicitor General D. John Sauer, the administration’s top appellate attorney told the high court in the new filing.

“While certain aliens may benefit from stalling their removal, the nation does not,” Sauer wrote.

The Supreme Court reviewed the policy at an earlier stage of the case last year and allowed it to continue over the dissent of the court’s three liberal justices – Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson.

The justices then sided with the administration again in a case involving a specific group of migrants that had been held for several weeks on a military base in Djibouti.

The administration began the policy last year as part of its broader crackdown on immigration. One of the biggest hurdles previous administrations have faced is trying to deport migrants back to their home countries who would refuse to receive them for a host of reasons, including frosty relations with the United States. Trump’s answer to that problem was to deport those migrants to some other country, even if the migrant had no ties to the destination.

The policy drew considerable scrutiny last year after immigrant rights groups revealed that one group of migrants, initially bound for South Sudan, were being detained in Djibouti. The migrants, including some from Cuba, Vietnam and Laos, were held in a converted Conex shipping container. An estimated 25,000 migrants have been removed under the policy.

At issue is the Convention Against Torture, ratified by the Senate in 1994, that generally bars deportation or extradition to countries where there is a possibility that the migrant might be tortured. The law is vague about how an administration is supposed to make that determination and what process rights are due to the migrant at issue.

In its emergency appeal on Thursday, the administration asked for an immediate “administrative” stay that would allow the flights to continue.

The Justice Department told the court in its filing that it had cancelled flights and “has had to pull nearly 150 aliens from removal flights to at least four different countries.”

The high court ordered the immigrant rights groups fighting the administration to respond by Monday afternoon.

text:
(CN) — Three men who have been in the U.S. for over a decade asked the full Fifth Circuit on Thursday to rule they have a constitutional right to challenge their detention through a bond hearing while they go through deportation proceedings.

The immigrants say a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for all noncitizens in removal proceedings who were not legally admitted into the country violates due process. In July, a three-judge Fifth Circuit panel agreed, with the majority ruling that even if they entered the country illegally, immigrants who have lived in the U.S. for a substantial period of time have a constitutional right to a bond hearing within 90 days of being detained where they can challenge their detention by showing they are not a flight risk or a danger to the community.

The full appeals court then voted to rehear the case and stayed rulings by several federal judges preventing the government from detaining the three men without bond hearings.

Previously, a divided Fifth Circuit panel ruled that regardless of how long they’ve been in the country, immigrants who entered without authorization are “applicants for admission” who can be held without bond hearings under federal immigration law, a statutory interpretation that conflicts with rulings from nineothercircuits.

Deputy Assistant Attorney General Drew Ensign told the Fifth Circuit Thursday that the statutory issue decides the case, as Congress made the decision to mandate detention for all applicants for admission without regard to whether they are dangerous or a flight risk.

“A hearing on flight risk or dangerousness in this context would thus be a bootless exercise that procedural due process cannot compel,” Ensign said. “It would be the equivalent of a 14-year-old plaintiff demanding a hearing on whether or not they’re a safe driver to get a driver’s license, something that could only be accomplished by overcoming the substantive policy choice of the legislature to restrict driver’s licenses to those 16 and above.”

But Rebecca Cassler, an attorney with the American Immigration Council representing the three immigrants, argued that regardless of what the statute says, the Constitution requires the government to show it has a sufficient reason to detain someone.

“The interest here is the right to physical liberty, and the question is, when is an individual’s right to physical liberty outweighed by sufficiently compelling government interest, what is that interest, and then under what circumstances will it be sufficient to show that that interest is served by the person’s detention?” Cassler said.

But some of the judges appeared skeptical of this argument.

“How can there possibly be in the abstract an enumerated right to be free in the country that you’re seeking admission to?” Chief U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod, a George W. Bush appointee, asked.

Several of the judges wanted to know if immigrants could voluntarily leave the country to avoid detention while still continuing to challenge their removal in immigration court, but both Cassler and Ensign said they knew of no way for an immigrant to continue challenging their removal after voluntarily departing.

U.S. Circuit Judge Cory Wilson, a Donald Trump appointee, questioned how courts could determine whether an immigrant has sufficient ties to the U.S. to have a constitutional interest in being free from detention. Cassler suggested factors like the length of time a person has been in the U.S., whether they have family members who are U.S. citizens and their involvement in the community. But Wilson dismissed such factors as “cotton candy,” saying they are not a “measurable yardstick” for determining an immigrant’s constitutional interest.

“It’s utterly going to be in the eye of the beholder, whoever the district court judge is, or whoever the court is, isn’t it?” Wilson asked. “Because everything you’re saying has no measurable yardstick whatsoever, as opposed to the statutory framework, which does.”

Last year, the Trump administration announced that going forward all immigrants who entered the country without being legally admitted would be treated as “applicants for admission” and subject to mandatory detention without bond hearings. This was a major policy change, as for the past 30 years the government had treated only people detained at the border as applicants for admission, while those detained within the country were held under a separate provision of immigration law that provided for discretionary detention that allowed them to seek release through bond hearings.

text:
LOS ANGELES (CN) — A federal judge indicated Thursday she would issue a new order to block U.S. Customs and Immigration Enforcement agents from stopping people solely because of their race in LA County.

U.S. District Judge Maame Frimpong tentatively granted the request for a preliminary injunction brought by the American Civil Liberties Union of Southern California, the United Farm Workers and others.

The judge’s tentative ruling wasn’t made publicly available, and she didn’t issue a final decision at the end of the hearing in downtown LA.

Frimpong, a Joe Biden appointee, last year issued a temporary restraining order — a more short-term remedy — to stop ICE agents, frequently masked and driving in unmarked cars, from violating the constitutional rights of predominantly working-class Latinos caught up in the unprecedented immigration crackdown the Trump administration unleashed last year in Southern California.

While the Ninth Circuit rejected the government’s request to stay that temporary restraining order, the U.S. Supreme Court stepped in and paused it a year ago.

Daniel Mummolo, an attorney with the U.S. Justice Department, urged the judge at Thursday’s hearing to follow the guidance of last year’s Supreme Court decision. Justice Brett Kavanaugh observed the plaintiffs likely lacked standing to seek a broad injunction restricting immigration officers from making investigative stops because they were unlikely to face future harm from such stops.

“On this record, it’s hard to believe that any of these plaintiffs face a real threat of imminent harm,” Mummolo argued, noting there have been very few instances in which people had been stopped more than once by ICE agents.

Frimpong, however, noted the plaintiffs have accumulated more evidence since last year, including depositions of immigration agents and officials as well as body camera footage, to beef up their claims that Latinos are targeted by ICE solely because of their ethnicity rather than a reasonable suspicion they are in the country without proper authority.

“Isn’t it possible that the Supreme Court stayed the original TRO because the court didn’t have enough evidence before it,” she asked the government lawyer.

The ACLU and other plaintiffs argue that ICE agents to this day continue to roam Southern California, armed and masked, and seizing citizens and noncitizens alike based on a demographic profile the agency deems “suspicious” — people who appear Latino and low-income or working class.

“This policy has race at its core,” Anne Lai, an attorney with the UC Irvine Law Clinic, told the judge.

Sara Worth, another attorney for the plaintiffs, argued that the so-called targeted operations, in which ICE agents are looking for a particular individual, are pretextual. The agents will stop any individual who looks Latino — even though he or she may look nothing like the person they are looking for — and claim mistaken identity, she claimed.

Most of the plaintiffs’ arguments at the hearing, however, focused on fine-tuning the preliminary injunction Frimpong outlined in her tentative decision.

That designation was terminated earlier this year, and in August 2026, DHS ordered roughly 7,000 Nepali TPS holders to leave the country or face deportation.
It would allow Nepali community members in the United States to remain safe, work, and support loved ones and recovery efforts in Nepal.
