text:
Castro had come into power two decades earlier, in 1959, a year before Sánchez was born. Under Castro, Cuba rapidly shifted from a market economy heavily dependent on the US to a centralized socialist system. The US embargo imposed in 1962, along with escalating tensions between the two countries, further isolated Cuba’s economy. The Cuban government began restricting emigration to curb political opposition and prevent the loss of skilled workers.

By April 1980, social unrest had reached a breaking point. In response, Castro opened the port of Mariel to those wanting to leave, in what became known as the Mariel boatlift. Sánchez was one of roughly 125,000 Cubans who arrived in the US that year. About 85,000 would ultimately settle down in the Miami and south Florida area.

When Sánchez first arrived in Miami, Florida, he had no relatives and no plan. He remembers being warmly received by US officials, religious groups, and civil society organizations that had mobilized to welcome the “Marielitos” as they arrived. He was soon transferred to Wisconsin, where the government provided him shelter, food, and he recalled with a smile, “even cigars.”

Most “Marielitos” later became US permanent residents and citizens. In 1985, Sánchez had spent months learning English while working at a museum and school when he applied for US residency but was denied. “I don’t know why,” he said. “I hadn’t committed any crime.” He maintained a valid work permit and was required to report and sign in at monthly immigration check-ins.

In 1991, he was sentenced to 36 months in prison after a street fight with a local. He made the most of his time behind bars, earning certificates in cabinet making, blueprint reading, and technical drawing. In 1994, when he was released, he stopped attending his immigration check-ins. A couple of years later, he relocated to Florida. Several decades passed while Sánchez built a life in Florida.

Our international consortium of 72 journalists from 26 media organizations interviewed 35 people removed to countries to which they had no ties. Under international law, countries must offer people facing removal the possibility of claiming “fear of persecution,” a genuine threat to life in their country of origin or a third country.

Under US law, when a person subject to expedited removal–a fast-track immigration process that allows the deportation of a noncitizen without a hearing–tells US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) or ICE that they intend to apply for asylum and fear persecution in their country of origin, they are entitled to a “credible fear interview.” The interview, required under US law and conducted by an asylum officer with the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, is a pivotal step in the asylum process and provides people the opportunity to establish valid risks of return.

Most people we interviewed were not given credible fear interviews and were unable to claim a fear of persecution in their home or third countries. Many were not informed to which country they would be deported until they arrived.

Meredyth Yoon, Litigation Director at Asian Americans Advancing Justice, told our consortium that in many cases, people transit through a third country before they are “quickly” refouled back to their countries of origin, even when they had proven that they would more likely than not face persecution or torture there. Additionally, she explained that many of them, while still in immigration detention in the US, and sometimes upon arrival in a third country, were being “detained indefinitely in deplorable conditions without access to medical care [or] life-saving medications.”

Among the countries that have received third country nationals from the US, Mexico stands out. Despite no public agreement on US removals to Mexico, it has received some 20,000 deportees, the highest number anywhere, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a tracking site run by Refugees International and Human Rights First. Our consortium found that Mexico received more than the next top three receiving countries combined: Guatemala (at least 2,981), Costa Rica (at least 599), and Honduras (at least 543).

Unlike other countries receiving third country nationals from the US, people do not arrive in Mexico by plane, but in a more secretive way: by bus. A report by Human Rights Watch (HRW) identified four main land deportation routes: crossing via San Ysidro-Tijuana, Nogales-Sonora, El Paso-Juárez and Port Isabel-Matamoros. From these border crossings, Mexican officials take legal control and transfer people to two cities near the border with Guatemala: Villahermosa, the capital of Tabasco state and an oil and gas hub; and Tapachula, in Chiapas state, a gateway for migrants traveling north. According to interviewees, the transfers often last more than 30 hours, during which they remain shackled and are barely fed.

Cubans are the largest nationality group sent to Mexico from the US. The report by HRW identified some 4,300 Cubans deported to Mexico between January, 2025 and March, 2026. Historically, Cuba and the US had no agreement permitting the regular return of deportees. Over time, many Cubans “came to believe that deportation was no longer possible,” the report found Cubans like Sánchez, who had pending deportation orders, were often allowed to remain in the US under ICE supervision, with required check-ins.

Last Spring, when Forbidden Stories traveled to southern Mexico, our team met Vicente, a 60-year-old Cuban who crossed the Darién Gap, one of the world’s most dangerous migration routes, in 2023. Vicente, who preferred to use a pseudonym, feared US immigration agents might identify and prevent him from reuniting with his family.

In 2009, he left Cuba for Venezuela under a Cuba-Venezuela Bilateral Cooperation Agreement. There, he met his wife, had children, and built a career as a baseball coach, eventually training players who went on to the professional ranks. Disillusioned with Cuban politics, he remained in Venezuela. But after a decade there, he began receiving threats from the Technical Investigation Directorate of Cuba’s Ministry of the Interior, a specialized investigative body within the Cuban law enforcement and internal security apparatus. According to Vicente, agents from this bureau called him “stateless” and “a traitor” and threatened that his family would “pay the price.” Meanwhile, conditions in Venezuela were deteriorating, too; with millions unable to access basic healthcare and adequate nutrition, social unrest spread across the country. In 2023, Vicente decided to leave for the US, determined to build a better future for his youngest son, who was then nine.

From Venezuela, he waited for an appointment through the CBP One app, a platform created by former President Joe Biden’s administration as the designated pathway for requesting asylum at the US-Mexico border, but none opened up. A friend then told him about a group of people planning to travel across the Rio Grande, along the Texas-Mexico border, into the US, and he decided to join them. When the group of approximately 300 people arrived on US soil that August, they were intercepted by US authorities.

Vicente was among 21 people separated from the group and taken to prison in Texas, where he spent 23 days. Having crossed the border illegally, he attended a court hearing, during which the police presented no evidence, and he was released. But as he was leaving the facility, ICE officials took him into custody and returned him to Port Isabel. There, he began yet another legal process, hired an attorney, and presented evidence for an asylum claim, including the threats he said he had received in Venezuela. But his claim was denied, and he was issued a deportation order.

From Port Isabel, where the prison was “saturated” with people, Vicente was transferred to the Geauga County Safety Center, an ICE facility in Cleveland. He spent 90 days there, waiting for the Cuban government to claim him. When that did not happen, his stepson, who lived in the US, secured his release. On Christmas day, 2023, Vicente reunited with his wife and son in Ontario, California, after the two had recently made the trip via the Darién Gap and were released by border agents.

Vicente hoped to obtain a pardon for having entered the country illegally and was working with a lawyer to secure formal residency in the US. He never missed an ICE check-in. Around August, 2025, he went for a routine check-in, a process he had grown accustomed to, in which an ICE officer typically reviewed his status, verified his personal information, and updated his reporting schedule. On this occasion, though, an agent brought him to a different room for fingerprinting. “It was all a lie. A set-up. When I walked through the door, four agents were waiting for me. They handcuffed my hands, legs, and feet, and told me not to resist.

Tonatiuh Guillén López was the former commissioner of Mexico’s Instituto Nacional de Migración, the country’s immigration enforcement agency under the supervision of the Interior Ministry, during part of President Andrés Manuel López Obrador’s term. Guillén told Forbidden Stories that, with negotiations beginning as early as 2018, Mexico ultimately aligned its migration policy with that of the US, in 2019. Guillén claimed this was not the result of a formal agreement but a policy Mexico accepted under mounting US pressure, including demands to militarize migration enforcement.

Asked about the institution’s role in third country removals from the US to Mexico, Guillén described it as an act of “cruelty.” He also stressed that “the more people on the move, the more organized crime groups stand to gain.”

Guillén, who began his role in December, 2018, resigned in June, 2019, amid one of the sharpest diplomatic disputes between Mexico and the US in recent years. He departed after Mexico agreed with Washington to avert a possible trade war in exchange for measures to curb the flow of migrants toward the US border. He was replaced by Francisco Garduño, a former prison official who oversaw the militarization of Mexico’s immigration apparatus and was later prosecuted (in January, 2025, the judge overseeing the case approved suspending the criminal proceedings on the condition that Garduño carried out a series of compensatory measures) over the deaths of 40 migrants in a fire at a detention center in Ciudad Juárez.“The paradox is that, in the end, it’s the US economy that stands to lose,” Guillén said about the removal program.

Meanwhile, thousands of third country nationals remain stranded in Mexico, unable to work. Many of them, like Vicente, are simply waiting to see their loved ones again.“I only want to be reunited with them,” he said. “But there’s the uncertainty of time. I’m not 20 years old anymore. It can’t be in 10 years.” Others have accepted their fate in Mexico. Sánchez, who was eventually recognized as a refugee, is now settling into long-term shelter in Guanajuato.

title: Immigrants Fighting for Release on Their Own Face Daunting Odds - Bloomberg Law News
authors: Megan Crepeau, Seamus Hughes, Alexia Fernández Campbell
description:
Fewer than a dozen of those pro se petitions were granted.
Habeas petitions allow detainees to turn to the judicial branch for a chance at release.
The few successful pro se petitioners generally won release on the same grounds: they’d been locked up too long.
And, Doughty said, the number of law clerks assigned only to pro se cases is set to more than double.
As of this spring, public defenders are representing an Afghan man who’d been in immigration detention since January 2025.
text:
Cristian Mancillas had been detained less than a day before an immigration officer told him might as well agree to be deported.

“You’ll never win your case,” he recalled the officer saying. If he didn’t sign the form they offered him, he’d just stay in detention for a few months and be flown back to Guatemala anyway.

Mancillas had a steady job in Alabama remodeling homes, a pending visa application, and two young daughters. “I’m not signing nothing,” he said.

But after four months in custody, during which he lost 50 pounds, and with scant legal options left, Mancillas realized the officer had been right. He was flown back to Guatemala in April.

He’s one among thousands of people picked up by Trump administration immigration enforcers around the country and funneled to Louisiana, which is set up to hold massive numbers of immigration detainees with minimal legal obstacles. The US Department of Homeland Security didn’t comment in response to emailed questions.

The state has nine immigration detention facilities, plus a “staging facility” attached to Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s busiest airfield, where deportees can be flown overseas at a moment’s notice. Federal judges there must follow the directives of the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, which in February blessed Trump’s broad mass-detention policy — a policy the vast majority of other circuits have rejected. Immigration detainees, unlike criminal defendants, don’t have the right to a court-appointed lawyer. And there’s long been a dearth of legal-aid options in Louisiana, advocates say.

So without ready access to representation, detainees like Mancillas have frequently and often futilely tried to go it alone, filing habeas corpus petitions “pro se” — that is, without a lawyer — to argue that being in custody violates their rights.

Of about 400 immigrant habeas petitions filed in the US District Court for the Western District of Louisiana from January through early March, more than a third were filed without an attorney, according to a Bloomberg Law analysis of 11,000 pages of files that were accessible only by going to the court in person and obtaining them on paper. Fewer than a dozen of those pro se petitions were granted.

Some were thrown out for minor procedural errors a non-lawyer couldn’t be expected to know, or for failing to pay a $5 filing fee. Others lingered unresolved, leading to petitioners being deported before their pleas for release got a full hearing.

The court has fought for more resources and made significant procedural changes in response to the influx of unrepresented immigrants, Western District Chief Judge Terry Doughty said in an interview. He said he expects the avalanche of petitions will continue at least another couple of years.

But people like Mancillas, detained toward the beginning of the wave of Louisiana petitions, were brought in too early to reap those benefits.

“No one gives you a chance to continue in USA, never,” Mancillas said via phone from Guatemala. “What Immigration wants all the time is deport, deport.”

‘Oh, I Filed a Habeas’

At Winn Correctional Center in rural Louisiana, the tap water was yellowish and smelly, Mancillas said. The food was like cardboard, and if you didn’t finish it quickly enough officers would throw it in the trash. The rooms were frigid; the blankets were itchy and irritating. People were constantly ill.

Immigration custody is civil detention — that is, it’s not supposed to be punitive. But, said attorney Nora Ahmed of the ACLU of Louisiana, it functions like a punishment, and keeping people detained in miserable conditions is “very helpful to the administration’s massive deportation drive.”

Short of agreeing to be deported, the best chance to get out of detention is to try the habeas process, given the Trump administration’s commitment to keeping noncitizens locked up while their cases play out in immigration courts.

Immigration courts are administered by the executive branch, staffed by Justice Department employees. Habeas petitions allow detainees to turn to the judicial branch for a chance at release. The immigration case and the habeas case proceed on separate tracks. If someone wins their release from detention via a habeas petition, that doesn’t resolve their immigration case — it just means they get to fight it from home.

In 2022, dismayed by the barriers to legal access, legal aid groups launched an effort to help Louisiana immigration detainees file habeas petitions without an attorney. They distributed detailed guides in multiple languages; some of their petition templates still appear to be in use.

With the Trump administration’s mass-detention push, the demand for such petitions has skyrocketed.

Word of mouth spreads quickly behind bars, said attorney Jessica Gutierrez of Louisiana-based legal aid group Immigration Services & Legal Advocacy, and pro se noncitizens frequently file without knowing whether they have a solid legal claim for release. Some pro se petitions emphasize the bad conditions behind bars, which some judges found aren’t an appropriate argument in habeas claims. Others appear to have miscalculated or misunderstood the legal standard for when their detention qualifies as “prolonged.”

“All you’re hearing is other detainees being like, ‘Oh, I filed a habeas. Someone told me you could do this and you get out, so you should try it too,’” Gutierrez said. “And that’s what we’re seeing.”

This year, the Western District of Louisiana has the ninth highest rate of pro se noncitizen habeas claims, according to a Bloomberg Law analysis of courts where 10 or more such claims were filed.

One was filed by a Venezuelan man who said ICE falsely suspected him of gang membership because of a tattoo; in detention, he said, he was given spoiled food and forced to use medication he was allergic to. His pro se petition was rejected for not being in an approved format. When he didn’t correct it within 30 days, his case was dismissed altogether.

The few successful pro se petitioners generally won release on the same grounds: they’d been locked up too long. Under a 2001 Supreme Court decision, if the government can’t show someone’s deportation is reasonably foreseeable six months after a final order authorizing their removal from the US, a detainee should be released.

The successful petitioners include a Georgian woman whose filing detailed, in neat, loopy handwriting, her worsening medical conditions after more than a year in custody and a Vietnamese citizen ordered released in July who, at that point, had been detained about a year after her removal order became final.

But the wave of more recent detainees, like Mancillas, wouldn’t qualify for release under the six-month rule. That clock starts running only after an immigration judge’s order of removal becomes final.

Too Hard to Win

On the January day Mancillas was picked up, his longtime partner Marta Orozco got a call as she drove from their elder daughter’s school. Mancillas had been detained, his boss told her through a Spanish speaker. She hit the brakes right away.

“And I started crying,” she told Bloomberg Law in Spanish. “Because it was the last thing I thought could happen.” Mancillas had no criminal history, he said. He came to the US as a minor; he also applied for a visa intended for victims of crime and their families, based on the fact that his father had been attacked. He was the breadwinner; Orozco looked after their two daughters, then aged 2 and 6.

A pro bono attorney who had helped Mancillas with his immigration case said she could review the habeas paperwork, but that she’d never filed one before. Another lawyer told her he didn’t usually take Louisiana cases — they’re too hard to win.

So Orozco ended up working with a man she learned about on TikTok who offered help with immigration services. She paid him $800 to write a habeas corpus petition that she filed in Louisiana court pro se on Mancillas’ behalf, under her name.

The petition argued that Mancillas had the constitutional right to a bond hearing in immigration court at which he could argue for his release. But the day after it was filed, the court said it had been submitted on an improper form and gave 30 days to get something on the docket in an approved format.

Orozco contacted the form preparer, who told her what to fix and instructed her to submit it again. Records show a “duplicate deficient petition” was filed Feb. 18.

While the Fifth Circuit has found that immigration detention statutes don’t entitle petitioners like Mancillas to a bond hearing, some attorneys successfully argued that the constitutional principles of due process grant them the right to argue for their release in immigration court.

An attorney might have been able to win Mancillas’ release on that kind of claim. But when Mancillas didn’t re-submit a petition in the proper format within 30 days, his case was stricken altogether.

With Mancillas gone, Orozco had to make ends meet; she started babysitting and selling food she cooked outside their mobile home.

In April, about four months after Mancillas was locked up, a fire started in an air conditioning unit in the kitchen window, Orozco said. When it reached the gas tanks she used for cooking, she said, it exploded, destroying the trailer and their cars. Orozco and the girls were briefly left homeless. The family dog was killed.

Not long afterward, Mancillas was taken to Guatemala.

He recalls an immigration judge telling him his best option was to take voluntary departure, just as he’d heard from the immigration officer who arrested him.

All summer, he’s had to adjust to life away from his partner and their girls. He lives with his parents and has found some work, though for much less pay.

He talks to Orozco every day. He can’t sleep, remembering the way the guards would burst into the room in the detention center in the middle of the night. He hopes his visa will come through.

The situation for noncitizens is “continuing bad” in the US, he said. “It’s so bad.”

‘Give Everybody Their Fair Shake’

It might be tough to win a habeas petition in the Western District of Louisiana, but that’s not political, said Doughty, the chief judge.

“We want to follow the law and give everybody their fair shake in court,” he said. “I’m very conservative, but I’ve had many of them I’ve ruled on, I’ve let them out, they won, and all the other judges have too. It just depends on the facts.”

The court has made active efforts to meet the surge of noncitizen habeas petitions, Doughty said. They’ve divided the petitions evenly between judges instead of assigning them by geographical area, which would have left the judges who sit in areas with detention centers dealing with the bulk of petitions. A retired magistrate judge from Kansas has recently agreed to come work in the district, and will handle only habeas petitions.

And, Doughty said, the number of law clerks assigned only to pro se cases is set to more than double. Those clerks review pro se filings to help determine if they have a valid legal claim; lately, they’ve been “bombarded,” Doughty said. The court is expecting an allocation by the Administrative Office of the US Courts of at least 10, and Doughty said he’s asked for expedited funding to get them on the job sooner.

Perhaps most consequentially, Doughty signed an order in April that’s intended to create a pipeline directing pro se petitioners to the Federal Public Defender’s office. Attorneys with that office can screen certain cases, see if there’s a valid claim, and represent the petitioner going forward.

That was the federal defenders’ idea, Doughty said, and he welcomed it.

“We’ve got everybody involved in it, we’re really trying to do what we can,” he said. “When it started exploding, we saw immediately we needed to do something.”

The Federal Public Defender’s office didn’t respond to repeated interview requests. But Doughty praised its efforts and said it’s taken a significant number of cases.

As of this spring, public defenders are representing an Afghan man who’d been in immigration detention since January 2025. Going back to Afghanistan would put him in severe danger, he’d written — his prior work for a US government contractor would put a target on his back.

A judge rejected his petition, saying he wouldn’t have a valid legal claim until six months after his removal order became final. The man filed a new petition in May, after the federal defender order took effect — and this time, he was appointed a lawyer.

While the order is an “amazing start,” said legal aid attorney Gutierrez of ISLA, it hasn’t been a cure-all.

“Federal public defenders themselves are already at capacity with their own workload, and they’re learning something new,” she said. “So it’s not as easy as just being able to take on all of these cases.”

Earlier this year, ISLA and the National Immigration Project of the National Lawyers Guild launched a Habeas Project, which connects detained noncitizens with free legal representation.

The demand has been overwhelming, Gutierrez said.

“Unfortunately, we still have so many people on the wait list just waiting to be placed because there’s a limited number of volunteers,” she said. “But there’s so many cases.”

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement plans to create "mobile detention facilities" for immigrant detainees in Pennsylvania, according to publicly available government documents. It's part of a massive detention expansion that began last year when the agency turned into the highest-funded U.S. law enforcement agency, with a $75 billion supplement from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

This shift in strategy comes after ICE started buying large warehouses nationwide to turn into mega detention centers.

Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons described wanting squads of trucks rounding up immigrants and having the deportation process run like "[Amazon] Prime, but with human beings."

The plans faced widespread pushback from communities near the warehouses and from immigration activists.

"I don't understand. What do we need this for?" Linda Powell, a resident of Williamsport, Md., told NPR in March.

ICE had recently purchased a warehouse near her home, and she was worried about the impact on the town's infrastructure. She also had humanitarian concerns about conditions in the facility: "We don't need it here."

This was the sentiment in various towns that staged protests. Several states, including Maryland, sued. ICE has since backed off the plans and, according to data gathered by watchdog group Project Salt Box, is selling most of those warehouses, indicating that the project has largely failed.

But the Trump administration is also detaining immigrants at record numbers — roughly 100,000 people arrested in the last two months.

While the warehouse project has flopped, records show that in the last few months ICE has quietly expanded its detention system in other ways.

In an August earnings call for the private prison company GEO Group — one of ICE's main contractors — an investor asked CEO George Zoley whether ICE was still aiming to reach 100,000 operational beds.

"I think so, for the most part," Zoley responded, saying ICE presently has 68,000 beds. "So they have another 30,000 or so more beds to go."

Fast-forward to this week: On Sunday, the Department of Homeland Security (which oversees ICE) signed construction contracts worth over $7 billion to expand immigration detention in New York, Texas, Arizona, Florida and California. It also announced that it will expand in Colorado, Washington and Pennsylvania.

Buried in the paperwork first obtained by Project Salt Box is a document regarding expansion in Pennsylvania. ICE says it's looking for "mobile detention facilities," which it describes as being run by GTI (the transportation subsidiary of GEO Group).

"What they describe is a network of vans that would follow officers into the field as they make these arrests," says Michael Wriston, a co-founder of Project Salt Box. "Very conspicuously missing from this description was: What are the standards? You know, how long a person can be kept in a van. How are people using the bathroom? How are they feeding them?"

The only details about the mobile units provided in the document are that they will be used "until full" or until the operation is done and that women can't be held in them for over 10 hours.

Neither ICE nor the GEO Group responded to NPR's request for comment about the vans.

Wriston, a former military intelligence analyst, thinks the focus on Pennsylvania is because it's such a large state where many police departments are not allowed to work with ICE. That means detained immigrants can't be held at local jails.

Of the tens of thousands of people currently in ICE detention, around 70% have no criminal record. Wriston says the need for mobile detention centers gives a sense of how these crackdowns aren't necessarily going after hardened criminals, as President Trump has said in the past.

"If this were targeted immigration enforcement, if this were truly 'worst of the worst'-type enforcement, it stands to reason that ICE would have a list of a couple of names, and then an officer or a team of officers would go out and make an arrest. This describes sweeps, immigration sweeps."

The mobile detention facilities, he says, are more than just a blip in the paperwork. They show the scope of the mass deportations.

text:
Immigrant advocates went to federal court Tuesday seeking an immediate order blocking the Tennessee Highway Patrol from conducting traffic stops in tandem with federal immigration agents.

In its federal lawsuit, the Tennessee Immigrant & Refugee Rights Coalition and seven Tennessee taxpayers alleged the THP is violating state law and the U.S. Constitution by making traffic stops of motorists suspected of being noncitizens solely based on their ethnic or racial appearance and then allowing Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents — riding along or stationed nearby — to demand immigration papers and detain drivers.

“The THP is using its traffic stop powers to help ICE do something that the Supreme Court has forbidden: to conduct ‘roving patrol[s]’ in which officers stop motorists on roads in the interior of the United States to check immigration status absent any substantial reason to think they lack status,” read their motion for a preliminary injunction blocking the joint traffic stops.

State attorneys defending the Tennessee Highway Patrol and the Tennessee Department of Homeland Security argued in court filings that state troopers have only engaged in legal traffic stops, based on probable cause of a traffic or criminal violation, and defended the cooperative effort between state troopers and ICE agents.

“Interagency law enforcement collaboration is not taboo,” they wrote in legal filings. State attorneys urged the court to reject the “extraordinary demand” that THP cease cooperative efforts with ICE . “THP’s collaboration with federal counterparts makes Tennessee safer,” they wrote.

Immigrant rights group sues Tennessee Highway Patrol over motorist stops

The state attorneys also raised procedural objections, arguing the plaintiffs lack legal standing to file the lawsuit, the federal court lacks jurisdiction to hear the lawsuit and the state has sovereign immunity against the legal claims.

In court on Tuesday, Assistant Attorney General Samantha Morris argued that ICE agents riding along with state troopers was not a constitutional violation, noting that interagency collaborations are common. Morris compared the practice to bringing drug-sniffing K-9 dogs on patrol to deploy when troopers conducting stops then have reasonable suspicion of potential drug violations.

Michael Holly, who represents the plaintiffs, said the comparison was apt “in a way.” Except, he said, a “drug dog doesn’t have a salary or an agenda.”

U.S. District Judge Aleta Trauger told attorneys Tuesday she hoped to “issue a fairly quick decision.”

The lawsuit was filed May 18, about a year after the THP and ICE conducted a week-long operation they dubbed “Operation Flood the Zone” focused on one Nashville neighborhood with a large immigrant population.

Dashcam and bodyworn camera videos obtained by a consortium of investigative news outlets later revealed troopers made pejorative remarks about their targets, described the Nashville operation as “hunting’ time,” competed among designated teams of ICE officers and troopers to make the most arrests and marked detainees’ arms with sharpies to indicate which team could take credit for the arrests.

Questioned months later by state lawmakers about alleged misconduct during the operation, THP Colonel Matt Perry said the agency has since rejected overtures from ICE to conduct future joint operations.

The Tennessee Highway Patrol, however, continues to work in tandem with ICE and other federal agencies as part of the Memphis Safe Task Force, convened last September via an executive order from President Donald Trump. In that role, the THP has conducted tens of thousands of traffic stops in Memphis. Neither the task force nor the THP has released data on how many of those traffic stops led to immigration arrests.

The injunction sought by the immigrant advocates and taxpayers, if granted, would prevent the THP from conducting traffic stops in tandem with ICE in its role as a member of the Memphis Safe Task Force.

text:
WEST HOLLYWOOD, Calif. (KABC) -- A Brazilian immigrant who has lived in West Hollywood for nearly a decade is facing potential deportation to a country he has no connection to. He spoke with Eyewitness News after more than a month in custody as his legal fight marches on.

Alex Pereira-Alves has spent six weeks at the Adelanto Detention Center after reporting for what was described as a spontaneous immigration check-in at an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in downtown Los Angeles.

During a video call last week, on his 34th day in detention, Pereira-Alves described feeling cut off from the outside world.

“I feel trapped,” he said.

Pereira-Alves, a legal Brazilian immigrant, reported to the ICE facility on Aug. 11. He said an official told him he could be deported under the current administration.

“One of them said, ‘Under this administration you are deportable.’ Then I said, ‘I can just buy my ticket and leave and go to Brazil, my country,’” Pereira-Alves said. “He said, ‘No, now we have to process you through the system.’ Then they handcuffed me, and the rest is history.”

The case became more complicated when Pereira-Alves faced the possibility of swift deportation to Equatorial Guinea. His immigration attorney, Jane Oak, immediately sought legal intervention.

SEE ALSO: Federal judge blocks deportation of West Hollywood man detained by ICE during immigration check-in

“I believe, with that injunction, that is what prevented him from getting removed to Equatorial Guinea,” Oak said.

Oak said Pereira-Alves has lived and worked legally in West Hollywood since 2018, when a judge granted a legal withholding on an order of removal from the country, as long as Pereira-Alves remained in good standing. Oak said Pereira-Alves has met that requirement.

The 2018 withholding that then allowed Pereira-Alves to stay and spared him from deportation back to Brazil is now trapping him in an immigration quagmire.

“He can’t get removed to Brazil, because the withholding of removal prevents that. He does not want to go to Equatorial Guinea, and he can’t designate a third country and he can’t be released from detention either,” Oak said.

Pereira-Alves’ phone calls and legal filings are costing his friends who support him thousands of dollars. His continued detention also comes at a cost to taxpayers, said his friend Jeff Markwardt.

“Everything costs money, and as taxpayers, we’re footing his bill,” Markwardt said.

Markwardt said Pereira-Alves is fortunate to have people helping him, while many others in detention do not have the same resources.

“Alex is lucky to have the support around him, but a lot of these folks are the most low-income, disadvantaged folks in our society,” he said. “Even if they do have someone on the outside, do those people have the funds to contribute?”

Pereira-Alves remains in detention in limbo while his attorney navigates a federal immigration and court process that she says is overloaded and appears to be changing daily.

“I don’t really feel safe,” Pereira-Alves said. “I will probably only feel safe when I arrive in my country.”

In a statement last month, confirming Pereira-Alves' detention and pending deportation, a spokesperson with the Department of Homeland Security said that detention is a choice and further encouraged people to self-deport. Pereira-Alves offered up that option, but says he was denied and forced into custody.

Eyewitness News reached out to DHS for an updated statement on his case but has yet to hear back.

title: Trump administration tells Congress it will admit 17,500 white South African refugees in 2027
authors: REBECCA SANTANA and SEUNG MIN KIM
description:
In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America.
The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.
Organizations that have historically worked to resettle refugees in new homes in America criticized the administration's decision to once again limit the program to white South Africans.
During his first administration, Trump slashed the number of refugees approved every year.
They are just one of South Africa's white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration plans to limit the number of refugees admitted to the country in 2027 to 17,500 mostly white South Africans, the administration told Congress Tuesday, as it continues to transform a program that at one point served as a pathway to safety for people fleeing war and strife from countries around the world.

In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America. The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.

The Trump administration has dramatically altered a refugee program that historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support as it welcomed tens of thousands of refugees from countries around the world to new lives in America, and instead the administration has transformed it into a vehicle to resettle white South Africans in America.

The administration told Congress in the announcement that it intended to spend about $500 million to resettle the new arrivals to the U.S.

Organizations that have historically worked to resettle refugees in new homes in America criticized the administration's decision to once again limit the program to white South Africans.

"For more than four decades, America's refugee program has provided a lifesaving pathway for people fleeing violence and persecution," said Naomi Steinberg, HIAS vice president for refugee and immigration policy and advocacy, in a statement. "But again, this administration is diminishing and distorting this legacy in service of its political whims. That is why we will never stop speaking out for a return to a program that welcomes refugees from around the world who have been persecuted because of who they are and what they believe."

Presidents set the cap on how many refugees the U.S. will approve through the program each year, and historically, they've allocated those numbers across various geographic regions while factoring in wars or conflicts that spark humanitarian needs around the globe. HIAS said an average of 92,000 people a year have been admitted to the U.S. since the program was launched in 1980.

Last year, the Trump administration initially set the cap at 7,500 — again predominantly Afrikaners — but later increased the total to 17,500 after it said that "unforeseen developments in South Africa created an emergency refugee situation."

During his first administration, Trump slashed the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration built the system back up, setting a goal of admitting 125,000 refugees in Biden's last year in office.

When Trump once again returned to the White House, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been slated to come to the U.S. Then the administration reopened the program, but limited it to white South Africans.

Afrikaners are the descendants of mainly Dutch and French colonial settlers who first arrived in South Africa in the 17th century. They are just one of South Africa's white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.

title: SF assemblymember's aide detained by ICE, faces deportation to Hong Kong - SF Standard
description: Catherine Stefani called for the release of Ho-Yin Mo, who was arrested last week during an enforcement operation at the Las Vegas airport.
text:
A Democratic staffer who has worked for several San Francisco elected officials was detained by federal immigration authorities Thursday in Las Vegas, the Department of Homeland Security confirmed.

Ho-Yin Mo, a field representative for Assemblymember Catherine Stefani, was arrested during an enforcement operation at Harry Reid International Airport and remained in custody Tuesday. A DHS spokesperson said Mo entered the U.S. in 2020 “on a temporary basis but illegally overstayed his welcome.”

Stefani on Tuesday called for Mo’s immediate release and insisted he is a legal employee of her office. The incident has shocked San Francisco’s political community, and friends have mounted an effort to support Mo’s legal defense as he fights deportation to Hong Kong.

“My message today is simple: I am respectfully calling for Ho Yin Mo’s release as soon as possible,” Stefani told The Standard. “Ho Yin is a selfless public servant and a valued, legal employee of the California state Legislature serving our San Francisco and Bay Area communities.”

The Trump administration has aggressively expanded the types of deportation cases pursued by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including by targeting those who have legally obtained work and have pending asylum claims. DHS implied, in its statement, that Mo was targeted despite his status landing in a legal gray area.

A DHS spokesperson said, “Work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States. DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this.”

Mo was previously an anchor and reporter at KTSF, a Chinese-language TV station based in the Bay Area. He also worked as a field representative for former Mayor London Breed’s 2024 reelection campaign.

Stefani praised Mo’s work on behalf of her office, saying he offers a unique form of outreach to Chinese American constituents who recognize him from his work as a TV reporter. text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is removing the names of its detainees who are facing final deportation orders from its public online database.

The move will disrupt detainees’ legal challenges to deportation and leave their whereabouts unknown to their lawyers and loved ones.

The agency quietly removed thousands of people from its online detainee locator on September 15, the Associated Press reports. Certain detention facilities will not be subject to the new order if judges have ruled that they are required to list detainees in their facilities.

The exact number of names removed is unclear, but judges have issued over 740,000 removal and voluntary departure orders this year, while reports have found that ICE arrested nearly 16,000 people in July who were subject to final removal orders. Experts and advocates have criticized the practice as digitally “disappearing” immigrants, saying that it’s yet another erosion of due process rights.

The agency has also issued a new policy barring immigration officials from sharing the locations of such detainees, two former Department of Homeland Security officials told The Washington Post.

This policy of hiding detainees’ locations will make it far harder or “nearly impossible” for many people to challenge their removals, legal experts said, as the agency rushes to make quotas for its mass deportation campaign.

American Civil Liberties Union Senior Staff Attorney My Khanh Ngo told AP that eight Somali men, her clients, detained at the U.S.’s Guantanamo Bay detention camp are among those whose names were removed. She said that such a move could make it “nearly impossible” to challenge many deportation cases.

“If you can’t find your client, don’t know what’s happening to your client, you can’t get that information to the court to stop their removal,” said Ngo.

“Families are freaking out because they think the person has been deported and they don’t know where the person might be,” said Greg Chen, senior director of government relations for the American Immigration Lawyers Association, per AP. “On the attorney side, this has serious implications for the ability to contact their client. It certainly has implications about how it will interfere with the attorney-client relationship.”

ICE has already faced scrutiny over its practices of quietly transferring detainees to different facilities without notification, often leaving families terrified when they find out that their loved one has been moved thousands of miles away.

Over the past year, the Trump administration has sent over 25,000 people to countries that they had no previous connection with, according to Refugees International. Under the direction of White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, the Trump administration transformed a former refugee bureau within the State Department into the “Office of Remigration,” which has authorized or pledged $410 million in agreements with 31 countries, mostly in Africa and Latin America.

title: Re-Rethinking Asian Exclusion and Color-Blind Immigration - Race, Racism and the Law
description:
However, for most of U.S. history, it was most accurate only with respect to white immigrants.
As late as 1960, the Asian population of the United States was around one-half of one percent.
Thanks to the Immigration and Nationality Act Amendments of 1965, U.S. immigration policy changed dramatically.
Polling at the time showed that the majority of the American people preferred white immigration, and felt little need to change existing race-based immigration policy.
In some substantial ways, we are experiencing an echo of the post-Civil War demand for Asian exclusion from the United States.
text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Gabriel J. Chin, Re-Rethinking Asian Exclusion and Color-Blind Immigration, 79 Southern Methodist University Law Review 35 (Winter 2026) (98 Footnotes) (Full Document)

AT least if the Supreme Court is a reliable reporter of American ideals, the United States has long deemed itself a nation of immigrants. In 1978, the Court stated: “As a [n]ation we exhibit extraordinary hospitality to those who come to our country, which is not surprising for we have often been described as 'a nation of immigrants.”’ In 1950, the Justices claimed: “The alien, to whom the United States has been traditionally hospitable, has been accorded a generous and ascending scale of rights as he increases his identity with our society.”

There is a large measure of truth to this judgment. However, for most of U.S. history, it was most accurate only with respect to white immigrants. In 1950, even as the Court claimed the nation had a tradition of hospitality, U.S. law racially restricted both naturalization and immigration. Indeed, for most of U.S. history, the law discouraged or prohibited non-white immigration, first through racially restrictive naturalization laws, and also through a series of specific bans aimed at persons of African ancestry in the Founding Era, and later, Asians. State and federal law restricted many benefits and opportunities by race and citizenship, as the United States encouraged white immigration to populate the nation’s expanding territory in the West, toward the Pacific Ocean.

In earlier decades, the Justices minced no words about the racial policy of U.S. law. Chief Justice Roger B. Taney, for example, explained why a “Malay” sailor from the Philippines could not be treated as white for purposes of the segregated evidence rules of the time: The colonists were all of the white race, and all professed the Christian religion; from the situation of the world at that time, no persons but white men professing the Christian religion could be expected to emigrate to Maryland; and if any person of a different color, or professing a different religion, had come into the colony, he would not, at that time, have been recognized as an equal by the colonists, or deemed worthy of participating with them in the privileges of this community. The only nations of the world which were then regarded, or perhaps entitled to be regarded, as civilized, were the white Christian nations of Europe; and certainly emigrants were not expected or desired from any other quarter.

The political community of the colony was composed entirely of white men professing the Christian religion; they possessed all the powers of government granted by the charter. Christian white men could not be reduced to slavery, or held as slaves in the colony; but they might, according to the laws of the colony, lawfully hold in slavery negroes or mulattoes, or Indians. The white race did not admit individuals of either of the other races to political or social equality; they were regarded and treated as inferiors, of whom it was lawful, under certain circumstances, to make slaves. Similarly, in The Passenger Cases, an antebellum decision limiting state authority to regulate immigration, the majority justified its decision on the ground that if the rule were otherwise, states could frustrate the federal policy of encouraging white migration. Justice Grier explained: “It is the cherished policy of the general government to encourage and invite Christian foreigners of our own race to seek an asylum within our borders, and to convert these waste lands into productive farms, and thus add to the wealth, population, and power of the nation.” Justice Catron noted: “We have invited to come to our country from other lands all free white persons, of every grade and of every religious belief ....”

Reconstruction, intended to be a systematic purge of race from U.S. law according to some, affected racial restriction in immigration almost not at all. Congress repeatedly considered and rejected proposals to make naturalization race-neutral, and included provisions in a number of civil rights laws and constitutional amendments consciously designed to allow racial discrimination against non-white noncitizens. As a generalization about the effects of Reconstruction, it might be said that a significant provision was made for African-Americans freed from slavery, but other forms of racial discrimination were allowed to continue, lest undesirable nonwhite immigration be permitted to occur. Into the twentieth century, the Justices self-consciously identified as white in their opinions.

An important discussion of immigration policy came in 1923 when the Court had to determine whether an Asian-Indian immigrant was white and therefore eligible to naturalize. The Court explained that those welcomed to the country were Europeans, and, therefore, an Asian-Indian was not among those invited to become citizens: The words of familiar speech, which were used by the original framers of the law, were intended to include only the type of man whom they knew as white. The immigration of that day was almost exclusively from the British Isles and Northwestern Europe, whence they and their forebears had come. When they extended the privilege of American citizenship to 'any alien being a free white person’ it was these immigrants--bone of their bone and flesh of their flesh-- and their kind whom they must have had affirmatively in mind. The succeeding years brought immigrants from Eastern, Southern and Middle Europe, among them the Slavs and the dark-eyed, swarthy people of Alpine and Mediterranean stock, and these were received as unquestionably akin to those already here and readily amalgamated with them. It was the descendants of these, and other immigrants of like origin, who constituted the white population of the country when section 2169, re-enacting the naturalization test of 1790, was adopted, and, there is no reason to doubt, with like intent and meaning. The policy of encouraging white migration and discouraging that of others was remarkably effective. As late as 1960, the Asian population of the United States was around one-half of one percent. Although many persons born in the United States traced their origin to Africa, few of them were immigrants or descendants of recent immigrants.

Thanks to the Immigration and Nationality Act Amendments of 1965, U.S. immigration policy changed dramatically. Before 1965, a supermajority of immigrants were white people from Europe. After, based on race-neutral selection criteria, a supermajority were non-white people from Asia, Africa, and Central and South America. I have argued that eliminating race was intentional, based on the civil rights ethic of the time (basically the same legislators supported and opposed the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 and the Immigration and Nationality Act Amendments of 1965) and contemporary evidence on the news media and in Congress recognizing that there was substantial unmet demand from nontraditional sources of immigration. Others disagree with what the results were expected to be. But no one questions that racial restrictions were in fact removed from the Immigration and Nationality Act, or that the demographics of the immigrant stream dramatically changed. Because of the race-neutral policy of the law, some forecast that the United States will become a majority-minority nation within a few decades.

Immigration reform in 1965 was an elite decision. Even if genuinely anti-racist on the part of many of the Senators and Representatives who passed it and the President who signed it, it was not a popular policy choice. Polling at the time showed that the majority of the American people preferred white immigration, and felt little need to change existing race-based immigration policy. However, in addition to domestic concerns, civil rights reforms were motivated by geopolitical considerations; the Cold War and the battle for the hearts and minds of those in the Third World were salient to Justices and elected officials even if less so to Joe and Jane Six-Pack.

Over time, the idea that race-neutral immigration benefited the United States grew. In 1965, according to Gallup, 7% of those surveyed thought immigration should be increased, while 33% thought it should be decreased. 39% supported the same level, while 20% had no opinion. By 2025, 64% of those polled thought immigration should be maintained or increased, and 30% supported a reduction. In a significant way, the decision of 1965 had been ratified by the people of the United States.

In 2025, the United States is experiencing something of the opposite of the 1965 reform--an elite reaction against immigration in the face of popular support for it. In some substantial ways, we are experiencing an echo of the post-Civil War demand for Asian exclusion from the United States. Many of the same issues are live again.

[ . . . ]

ANTI-ASIAN ALIEN LAND LAWS From the late 1880s until the 1950s, a number of states had laws specifically designed to restrict the rights of Asians to own real property. The purpose of these laws was to discourage immigration. To validate such laws, the Civil Rights Act of 1866 was amended in the drafting process to apply only to citizens. The Supreme Court upheld these laws in the 1920s. The laws generally did not classify by race but borrowed federal immigration classifications, for example, by allowing those racially eligible to naturalize to own land, or those who had filed valid declarations of intention to naturalize, and thus were necessarily racially eligible.

In the late 1940s and 1950s, such laws were invalidated by the Supreme Court in part, and by several state supreme courts under the Equal Protection Clause. Modern alienage jurisprudence would seem to invalidate such laws passed by states, either based on equal protection or federal preemption grounds.

A number of states have recently enacted new laws to prevent Chinese people and other undesirable foreign nationals from owning land. In particular, legal scholar Leo Yu has written about this phenomenon. Many of these laws are inapplicable to dual citizens or lawful permanent residents of the United States; some apply only to those domiciled in a specified foreign country. A U.S. district judge has enjoined an Arkansas statute; an appeal is pending in the Eighth Circuit. A Florida district court declined to enjoin a statute in that state; a panel of the Eleventh Circuit issued a temporary stay, but after full briefing and argument on the motion for a preliminary injunction, determined 2-1 that the statute was likely to be found constitutional.

There are strong arguments that the Eleventh Circuit’s decision is incorrect; the plaintiffs noted that the Court in Terrace did not apply strict scrutiny, but that cannot be dispositive in that the concept of strict scrutiny had not yet been developed when Terrace was decided.

They also did not account for the fact that Terrace applied ordinary equal protection review, but the substantive content of that review had changed. In Terrace, the Court said that states could freely borrow from federal classifications: “The state properly may assume that the considerations upon which Congress made such classification are substantial and reasonable. Generally speaking, the natives of European countries are eligible. Japanese, Chinese[,] and Malays are not.” But that legal principle was repudiated no later than 1948, when the Court rejected the idea that states could adopt federal immigration classifications for their own law: It does not follow ... that because the United States regulates immigration and naturalization in part on the basis of race and color classifications, a state can adopt one or more of the same classifications to prevent lawfully admitted aliens within its borders from earning a living in the same way that other state inhabitants earn their living. But perhaps the majority is right, and states are free to target at least some noncitizens based on their own vision of sound public policy. To draw from some of the political controversies of 2025, perhaps states have the power, if they choose, to ban land ownership by Palestinians or Ukrainians, while others will exclude Israelis or Russians. In addition to the foreign policy concerns that would be raised, individual nationals of these countries would no doubt feel aggrieved, as might U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents sharing those national origins. This is particularly so given that individuals do not necessarily share the political positions of the leaders of their country.

Whatever the outcome of the litigation surrounding the new alien land laws, their rise is another example of the rejection of the idea that the United States is a country that judges individuals as individuals, that people are welcome from anywhere so long as they share the values of the nation. Instead, it reflects the Amy Wax idea that we can tell a great deal about an individual based on their race or national origin.

In late November 2025, in response to a shooting of National Guard members by a lawfully admitted Afghani refugee, President Trump announced a “permanent pause” on immigration from developing countries to the United States. One commentator explained: The directive, which explicitly links the cessation of migration to the preservation of “Western Civilization” and the removal of “disruptive populations,” has precipitated a profound identity crisis for the American republic. It has resurrected political language and legal theories dormant since the 1920s, challenging the post-World War II understanding of the United States as a civic nation defined by adherence to constitutional ideals rather than ethno-cultural origins.

* * * The United States is in the middle of this history, so the outcome is uncertain. But whatever else it does, the resurgence of ethno-nationalism puts great pressure on the doctrines of the Supreme Court. It has embraced the idea that the Constitution is colorblind. Possessed of that idea, in one way or another, it has struck down a range of laws intended to protect the rights of people of color, including Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act and affirmative action in educational admissions. At the same time, it has embraced a presumption of good faith to uphold immigration and other actions, such as the Muslim Ban from the first Trump Administration, in spite of substantial evidence of animus.

The problem with this trust of government is that after cases like Yick Wo and Brown v. Board of Education prohibiting admitted racial discrimination and express racial classifications, would-be discriminators know they must use proxy categories. They may do so quite effectively, as the gerrymandering cases and voting rights cases, in the view of many, show. Immigration forms, fees, processes, and procedures can be used to effectively deprive people of rights. It could be argued that a range of recent decisions may be explained on the ground that the Supreme Court indulges a strong presumption that racial discrimination simply does not exist, rather than engaging in a vigorous, candid, effort to root it out. If this turns out to be the case, the United States could have colorblind law, but without ending intentional discrimination. It is difficult to imagine that resolution being either just or stable.

Edward L. Barrett Jr. Distinguished Professor of Law, UC Davis School of Law.

text:
Highlighting the growing list of people killed by federal immigration agents, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree and other Democratic members of Congress on Tuesday heard from family members of those killed about the Trump administration’s pattern of obstruction and lies about the shootings and victims themselves.

The shadow hearing, which was held in Washington, D.C., underscored that despite new leadership at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, little has changed.

U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who serves as ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, said that when Markwayne Mullin was tapped to replace Kristi Noem as DHS secretary, “There was hope that (ICE) would abandon the physical brutality and inhumanity of its tactics on the streets, there was hope that there would be accountability.”

That hope has been dashed, he said, most recently with the weekend shooting of a Venezuelan man in Austin, Texas.

California U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia, ranking member of the U.S. House Oversight Committee, said that as of September 2026, Democrats on the committee have documented over 1,000 “credible and verified instances and abuses” under President Donald Trump’s second administration. According to the lawmakers, 20 people have been shot by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, while 58 have died in ICE custody.

With a lack of subpoena power, Democrats do not have the ability to compel officials from the administration to testify. Instead, they’ve used this sort of forum, including one in Biddeford last month, to hear from willing witnesses.

‘Dual assassinations’

The members of Congress heard from family members and other representatives of Ruben Ray Martinez and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo of Texas, Renée Good and Alex Pretti of Minnesota, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero of Maine.

The witnesses all described how, in addition to a complete lack of information and oversight after the shootings, the federal government spread falsehoods about the people killed.

Sean Murphy, an attorney representing the Guerrero family, told the panel, “the dehumanization of the victims of these crimes is despicable.”

“The patterns of dual assassinations — one of the body and then of the character — is disgusting, and there’s a pattern that if you’re not seeing it, it’s because you have your eyes closed,” Murphy said.

Ronaldo Salgado and Lorenzo Salgado Jr., whose father was shot and killed in July while driving to work, said DHS provided little information about what led to the shooting but instead made repeated false claims that were later walked back, including that their father had been the target of the operation and had weaponized his vehicle.

“DHS also claimed there may have been drugs in the vehicle, which, if anyone who knew my father would tell you, is absurd, and which testing later proved to be false, as we all knew it would,” Lorenzo Salgado Jr. said.

Stella Carlson, a community activist who filmed the shooting of Pretti in Minneapolis, told the lawmakers that she felt like she “witnessed two assassinations, the first was the literal assasination of Alex and the second was the attempted assassination of his character.”

Pretti, an ICU nurse for the Department of Veterans Affairs who was observing ICE activities in his community, was described by the Trump administration as a “domestic terrorist.”

“We observed his murder with our own eyes, and the truth does not become less true because someone with great power tells a louder lie,” Carlson said. “When people are killed, and when the public is given false accounts of what happened, there must be accountability.”

ICE shot 23-year-old Ruben Ray Martinez in March 2025, making him the first U.S. citizen killed by ICE during the second Trump administration, though Blumenthal noted, “that fact was not disclosed to his family or to the public for nearly a year.”

His mother, Rachel Reyes, also told the panel about how video evidence and testimony from his lifelong best friend, who had been a passenger in the car at the time, contradicted the official account of the events that led to the shooting.

“Though the circumstances surrounding his death and these other victims are distinctly different, the pattern is the same: lives cut short by the same agency, agents without body cameras, no warnings, no attempt to de-escalate, excessive force followed by deflection and a lack of accountability after the fact,” Reyes said. “Other similarities are that these victims, despite being nonviolent community members with no criminal background, were disparaged and blamed to shift focus away from the officer’s misconduct.”

“What happened to my son is personal, but it should be a concern for us all,” she added.

Like the other accounts, a changing official narrative was also the case in Maine with Guerrero’s shooting.

At first, Mullin told independent U.S. Sen. Angus King that Guerrero “weaponized” his vehicle before being shot by an ICE agent. But ICE later said he attempted to flee and “fearing for public safety” an agent shot him.

‘Radio silence’ on Biddeford shooting

Murphy also said that he recently learned from the Maine Attorney General’s Office, which is currently investigating the deadly use of force in the shooting, that bullets fired by federal agents “struck and pierced” the carseat of Guerrero’s 3-year-old daughter, who was not in the car at the time, though initial reports said she was.

“The only justification given for Johan’s death was that it was in the interest of public safety. You know what actually keeps the public safe? Not shooting innocent and law-abiding fathers whose only dream is to build a better life for his family,” Murphy said.

Murphy added that there’s been “radio silence” from the federal government and that “DHS has still refused to even identify the name of the shooter” as well as any of the other federal agents present at the shooting.

Pingree said, “So many questions remain, and his family deserves to know how this happened. His family, his community, and the state of Maine need to know who will be held accountable.”

text:
NEW BEDFORD, Mass. —

Families and officials reacted with sadness and anger Tuesday after Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents carried out arrests in New Bedford, reportedly detaining up to a dozen people since Monday.

The windows of a pickup truck were shattered after ICE agents reportedly detained its driver outside a Dunkin' Donuts in New Bedford.

"He's a great father. He's a hard worker," said Leonarda Quino, the daughter of Camilo Quino, one of the detainees.

The family of Camilo Quino said he is 42, originally from Guatemala, and has lived in the United States for 23 years. He had just dropped off his teenage son at school before stopping at the coffee shop.

"On the way here, my mom showed me a video of my dad," said Felix Quino Tiniguar, Camilo's son.

Asked what he thought of the video, Felix said, "I was sad."

Immigrant advocates tracking the arrests said there were nine on Monday and several more on Tuesday. Some have advised immigrants to stay off the streets and remain at home until the operation ends.

"These kinds of operations involving people who are getting picked up who have families and jobs are enormously disruptive," said New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell. "Again, these are not hardened criminals. These are people just going about their life in our city."

ICE declined to comment on the arrests, stating only that it routinely conducts operations across New England.

The immigrant advocacy group LUCE held a press conference, calling for volunteers to help warn residents of ICE’s presence.

“We have had to decide whether to blow a whistle or scare the children. We shouldn't have to make that choice,” a representative from LUCE said.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey said an 8-year-old boy was left waiting at school because his father was detained before he could pick him up.

"To me, it's just another example of how cruel ICE has been, how wrong-headed this policy, and why it needs to stop. And Donald Trump needs to stop it," Healey said.

Standing on the steps of the federal courthouse that houses a district office of Sen. Rick Scott in Tallahassee, the Rev. R.B. Holmes Jr. challenged Florida's elected officials and candidates to publicly declare where they stand on deportation protections for Haitians, arguing that voters deserve answers before heading to the polls for the November election.

Joined by clergy members, civil rights advocates and elderly community activists on Sept. 22, Holmes held a "pray-in" to urge Scott and Sen. Ashley Moody to support legislation extending Temporary Protected Status, or TPS, for Haitians through April 2029.

The lead pastor at the historic Bethel Missionary Baptist Church, Holmes said he organized the pray-in at Scott's office after neither Scott nor Moody had responded to a July letter asking them to state their position on TPS. Requests for comments are pending with both Scott's and Moody's offices.

Pressing senators to respond

"Since they did not respond, we came here to have a little talk with Jesus," Holmes said as federal marshals observed the pray-in from a plaza overlooking the protest.

"We're here for several divine and theological and moral reasons," Holmes said. "This country is 250 years old. We cannot go back on our promise to be the land of freedom."

The demonstration focused on H.R. 1689, legislation approved by the U.S. House that would extend TPS protections for Haitians. Holmes said congressional action was urgent because conditions have worsened in Haiti, whose infrastructure and civil society were broken by a 2010 earthquake.

The fight over TPS is also emerging as a potential issue in the 2026 midterm elections. Holmes and other clergy members said they are pressing candidates for federal and state office to publicly state whether they support extending protections for Haitians.

"Tell us where you stand," Holmes said. "If you want to be our governor, if you want to be our senator, this is a defining moment. Where are you? You can't duck this. This is a moral layup. This is about compassion. This is about the American dream."

Holmes said neither Scott nor Moody responded to the July letter, but people "affiliated" with Moody had called to discuss scheduling a possible conversation with the senator about extending TPS protections.

Clergy frames debate as a moral issue

The pray-in drew support from clergy across denominations.

"I'm here because Haitians have been welcomed as refugees and this nation has a long history of welcoming people." said Rev. Richard Wilson, a retired pastor at Trinity United Methodist Church. "And I'm here because somebody's decided we will just kick everybody out who's not like us, and they haven't decided who is like us yet."

Nearly three dozen activists, mostly elderly carrying canes, in wheelchairs, blue jeans, and plaid shirts, recited prayers of compassion, commitment, courage and conviction during the 50-minute-long pray-in.

Congress created TPS in 1990 to provide temporary deportation relief and work authorization for people from countries affected by armed conflict and natural disasters.

Haiti first received TPS designation after the devastating 2010 earthquake. Immigration advocates estimate that roughly 158,000 Haitians in Florida have been affected by the decision to end TPS protections. Holmes said conditions in Haiti have deteriorated, making deportations particularly troubling.

Senate race highlights TPS divide

Scott has publicly expressed concern about conditions in Haiti but has not endorsed the House-passed extension and has argued Congress should pursue broader immigration reforms that allows immigrants who cannot safely return home to remain in the United States.

Moody was appointed to the Senate last year after Marco Rubio became secretary of state. She has not publicly endorsed the House-passed TPS extension but, according to WLRN, has discussed with Trump administration officials deciding TPS on a case-by-case basis.

Moody's positions contrasts sharply with her Democratic challenger Rep. Angie Nixon, D-Jacksonville.

Nixon has called for renewing and expanding TPS and creating a pathway to citizenship for immigrants covered by the program. Following an ICE sweep across Florida in September, Nixon accused federal officials of unfairly targeting Haitian Americans.

"Immigrant rights are human rights," Nixon said, criticizing Moody for supporting policies that could result in deportations.

At the Sept. 22 gathering, Holmes framed the debate in moral rather than partisan terms.

"This should not be about Republican or Democrat, conservative or liberal," said Holmes, a long-time registered Republican who switched to no-party-affiliation under the DeSantis administration. "This is about people. This is about families. These are our neighbors."

With the House-approved TPS extension stalled in the Senate, Holmes said the question facing elected officials is becoming increasingly direct: "Where do you stand on our Haitian neighbors?"
