name: Human Rights
title: ICE's culture of fear in Ohio is an un-American betrayal of our fundamental values
authors: Steven Volk, Marty Schladen, Megan Henry, Richard T. Herman
description:
A new report by the American Civil Liberties Union documents more than 1,200 incidents of abuse by ICE agents.
ICE agents have shot 16 people since January, with four fatalities.
Masked agents driving unmarked cars have been involved in aggressive vehicular pursuits causing a number of serious crashes.
In the United States, the Trump administration advertises its ability to inflict suffering on immigrants daily; all immigrants know the dangers they face.
Steven Volk is Professor of History Emeritus at Oberlin College, where he taught Latin American history for 30 years.
text:
On Aug. 27, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) released the details of a $16.7 million no-bid contract with Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, KY, for the purchase for their agents of 6,000 pairs of wearable gloves that are designed to deliver painful electric shocks.

The gloves, which the manufacturer, calls “Conductive Distraction and Deescalation Devices,” are, essentially, wearable tasers.

While the company advertises the gloves as a safe “use-of-force option,” as one critic observed, “Less than lethal doesn’t mean low risk.”

The company recommends that subjects not be shocked for more than 15 seconds, but ICE agents have a dismal record when it comes to any concern for the safety of their targets.

A new report by the American Civil Liberties Union documents more than 1,200 incidents of abuse by ICE agents.

The gloves are just one weapon in the agency’s arsenal of devices and policies designed to create a culture of fear among all immigrants residing in the United States, whether unauthorized or with full legal standing.

Tens of thousands of individuals have been kidnapped off the streets or pulled from their cars and hustled off to squalid detention camps where dozens have died.

ICE agents have shot 16 people since January, with four fatalities.

Masked agents driving unmarked cars have been involved in aggressive vehicular pursuits causing a number of serious crashes.

They have smashed their way into cars while small children cowered in the back seat. Detention center employees have force fed hunger-striking detainees.

We know that fear is the objective when the administration cheerfully publicizes its policy of deporting immigrants to destinations known to be politically unstable and extraordinarily dangerous.

To date, more than 23,000 immigrants have been deported to 26 countries where deportees have no ties, no history, and no knowledge of local languages.

These include the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, South Sudan, Equatorial Guinea, and Iran.

Recently, the administration has increased its deportation flights to Haiti, a country largely controlled by terror gangs. As the United Nations’ human rights expert for Haiti bluntly expressed, “This is insane.”

If fear is the intention, it is working. There is not one immigrant I know who hasn’t heard of “horrific” conditions in detention camps, of young children left on their own after masked agents spirited their parents away following a traffic stop, of immigrants shuffled from Ohio to Florida to Louisiana, just to keep them from their lawyers.

Even Puerto Rican friends, U.S. citizens by birth, ask me if they should always keep their passports with them.

With the beginning of a new school year, immigrant students once again fear bullying from white students who tell them to “Go back home.”

A survey of high school principles last year described the “climate of distress” faced by immigrant students who are “harassed” by peers demanding to “see their papers.” But distress doesn’t pay attention to citizenship.

Recent studies indicate that the fear cultivated by immigration enforcement raids has negatively impacted the test scores not just of foreign-born Spanish speakers, but of U.S.-born Spanish speakers as well, and that any child whose parent is taken away potentially faces depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Fear, to repeat, is not an unintended byproduct of the administration’s anti-immigrant policies. It is the desired outcome. And as such, the administration has placed the United States in the company of some of the most authoritarian regimes of the late 20th century: the military dictatorships of Argentina, Brazil, Uruguay, and Chile from the 1960s through the 1980s.

My own encounter with a regime that stoked the fires of fear was in Chile, where my wife and I were living when General Augusto Pinochet overthrew the government of Salvador Allende.

From the moment the military moved against the Chilean president on Sept. 11, 1973, those of us who had supported Allende — the country’s democratically elected head of state — felt fear surround us like a heavy blanket.

We were constantly aware that we could be stopped, detained, and even killed for who we were, not for anything we had done.

As the months and years went on, it became clear that any who fell afoul of the regime, whether common laborer or Army general, could be “disappeared” or blown up by a regime-dispatched agent.

These Southern Cone countries constructed systems of terror that combined a fear of the known with a fear of the unknown.

In the United States, the Trump administration advertises its ability to inflict suffering on immigrants daily; all immigrants know the dangers they face.

But the unknown, the uncertainty, the constantly changing set of rules and regulations, are equally disruptive.

Will I be detained if I file for a government benefit to which I am legally entitled?

As a U.S. citizen, can I be deported for incorrectly filling in a line on my naturalization papers?

Will my children come home to an empty house because I couldn’t convince the deputy sheriff that I have a green card?

It is challenging to fully enumerate all the ethical, moral, and political failures of a government that deliberately nurtures a culture of fear as a means of achieving its goals.

Such a policy is appallingly sadistic, undemocratic, at odds with every faith belief, and, one would hope to say, un-American.

Use fear to cleanse the country of immigrants, as Trump’s xenophobic adviser, Stephen Miller, desires, and we will become like the ancient image of the snake devouring its own tail, the ouroboros.

We will consume ourselves by fear.

Steven Volk is Professor of History Emeritus at Oberlin College, where he taught Latin American history for 30 years. In 2001, he was recognized by the government of Chile for his efforts in helping to restore democracy in that country.

text:
U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement agents detained a California state employee working as a field representative for Assemblymember Catherine Stefani, D-San Francisco, on Thursday as he traveled through Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas.

The field representative, Ho Yin Mo, was a young member of Stefani’s team who previously worked as a TV reporter in the Bay Area before entering politics.

Stefani called on the federal government to release Mo in a statement, calling him a “selfless public servant and a valued, legal employee of the California State Legislature serving our San Francisco and Bay Area communities.”

In their own statement, a representative of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security who did not give their name said Mo had overstayed a visa beginning in 2020 and was arrested “during a targeted enforcement operation” at the Nevada airport. The DHS statement said Mo “lawfully entered the U.S. on a temporary basis,” in January 2020, but “illegally overstayed his welcome by failing to depart by May 15, 2020.”

That year, Mo was a student at the University of California, Berkeley, according to his LinkedIn profile. He had been studying at California higher education institutions since 2016, according to his profile, which would seem to contradict DHS’s claim.

“Work authorization or a pending application do NOT confer legal status in the United States,” the statement read, adding that DHS was focused on people with expired visas or other issues with their legal status who try to pass through airports.

Federal immigration agents have increasingly targeted travelers in U.S. airports in recent months, pulling people aside as they go through security check points or board and disembark planes. Many of those arrests have focused on people with expired visas, including many in legal gray areas — like those who have visa extensions or asylum claims pending with the federal government, according to reporting by news outlets like The New York Times and the States Newsroom. Under past administrations, the federal government has not targeted people with pending applications for legal status unless they committed crimes, but that’s changed during the second Trump administration.

U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli, a conservative firebrand and former state lawmaker himself, seized on Mo’s case on the social media site X.

“No one is above the law, not even the California Legislature and its staff,” he wrote in a statement.

According to ICE’s detainee tracker, Mo is currently being held in the agency’s Nevada Southern Detention Center in Pahrump, a desert town in the state’s southernmost tip.

The increase in airport arrests have dovetailed with stepped up efforts by ICE agents to detain people this summer, including increasing numbers of people who have not committed crimes unrelated to their immigration status. The uptick in detentions coincides with reports Trump administration officials have told DHS staff they want up to 2,000 arrests a day.

July and August saw some of the highest numbers of ICE arrests of Trump’s presidency, with both months near around 50,000 arrests, according to national media reports. Alongside increased arrests have come reports of worsening conditions in detention centers around the country.

Stefani asked for Mo’s quick return in her statement, and called him a valued member of her staff in a San Francisco Assembly district marked by its diversity.

“When Ho Yin (Mo) and I meet our Chinese American constituents, he brings a unique sense of belonging to so many who watched him as a TV reporter,” she said. “And his work goes far beyond presence. Ho Yin helps people access affordable healthcare coverage, childcare and food support. Our whole community eagerly awaits Ho Yin’s return to his home and his job where he is loved and adored.”

text:
Lorenzo Salgado Araujo’s wife used to spend her evenings cooking a big meal for her husband and waiting for him to return home from his job as a home builder. Now, his son told members of Congress, Salgado Araujo’s wife spends those evenings visiting her husband’s grave at the cemetery.

In a packed Senate hearing room, a rapt audience of dozens listened to the sons of Salgado Araujo, the mothers of Ruben Ray Martinez and Renee Good, as well as the woman who video-recorded the death of Alex Pretti and the lawyer for the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero.

Salgado Araujo, Martinez, Good, Pretti and Durán Guerrero were shot and killed by federal agents since the start of the Trump administration’s crackdown on immigrants. Some were U.S. citizens; others were immigrants.

“We still have so many questions,” said Lorenzo Salgado, one of Salgado Araujo’s sons. “What are the names of the ICE agents who killed our dad? Why do they get to be protected behind anonymity, while my brother and I stand before cameras, showing our faces, proudly saying our first and last name?”

The forum on Tuesday was led by Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Long Beach) and Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). It was the fifth such event that the two lawmakers have hosted since December, forums aimed at shedding light on what the lawmakers call the “lawless and abusive tactics” by immigration agents.

The forums are not official hearings because they have been organized without Republican support. Nothing has changed since the first forum, the lawmakers said, accusing the Department of Homeland Security of failing to fully investigate the deaths and prevent further ones.

Blumenthal noted that two days prior in Austin, Texas, another man was shot by ICE agents. Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a Venezuelan who was making a DoorDash delivery when ICE agents sideswiped his car, was seriously injured and placed in ICE custody with a bullet still lodged in his back.

Garcia said that, as of this month, Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have verified more than 1,000 instances of abuse by immigration agents under this administration.

“Every community in America should be asking itself: How long will it be until ICE is in our city?” Blumenthal said. “How long will it be until we have a grieving family, until another loss of life?”

Rachel Reyes sobbed as she recounted the moments leading up to the death of her son, Martinez. She said his death came nearly a year before Good’s and Pretti’s “yet far fewer people know his name” because the family was denied access to investigative reports and video evidence showing he had been shot by an immigration officer.

“It’s deeply distressing to know that Ruben’s final moments were consumed by confusion, fear, pain and disregard for his life,” she said. “Though the circumstances surrounding his death and these other victims are distinctly different, the pattern is the same: lives cut short by the same agency, agents without body cameras, no warnings, no attempt to de-escalate, excessive force followed by deflection, and a lack of accountability after the fact.”

Donna Ganger, the mother of Good, said her daughter should still be alive. Ganger described herself as a Republican and a Christian. While Jesus teaches forgiveness, she said, she deserves accountability too.

“I voted for President Trump under the impression that these agents were here to protect the citizens of the United States,” she said.

“This is madness,” Ganger added.

Stella Carlson said that when she saw Pretti, she decided to become “his backup.” Instead, she watched him die and then watched the agents who shot him flee. Two masked agents returned “and began to manipulate his dead body, ripping open his clothes as if to provide aid, but instead moving him around like a rag doll.”

Later, Carlson said, she witnessed top government officials lie about Pretti, calling him a domestic terrorist who wanted to “massacre law enforcement.”

“I am just a regular person, but I care deeply about my community, my state and my country,” she said. “I believe there is power in ordinary people speaking the truth.”

Good and Pretti were killed within weeks of each other in January during a period of increased immigration enforcement in Minneapolis.

Sean Murphy, who represents the family of Durán Guerrero, said he and Durán Guerrero’s widow recently attended a meeting with representatives of the Maine attorney general’s office to retrieve some of his property that isn’t considered evidence.

One item that wasn’t returned was his 3-year-old daughter’s car seat, which had been pierced by a bullet.

Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) asked each speaker what they think justice would look like.

Reyes said an independent investigation. Brent Ganger said that true justice isn’t possible because his sister can’t come back, but that accountability is possible if federal agents are held to the same accountability standards as local law enforcement.

To Carlson, justice would mean getting ICE off the streets and letting detainees return home. Murphy called for prosecution for the agent who killed Durán Guerrero.

For Lorenzo Salgado, justice would take another form: getting to see his mom heal and finally getting a full eight hours of sleep.

The forum came as congressional Democrats are seeking to edge out Republicans in the Nov. 3 election, and at times the Democrats seized it as a way to criticize the other party.

Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) asked members of the audience to stand up if they’ve been affected detrimentally by ICE. Ronaldo Salgado looked around the room as about a dozen people stood.

“The reality is that there are so many more stories. There are so many more names that you will never hear,” she said. Later, referring to Republicans, she added, “It’s time to vote them out.”

Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) noted that Reyes voted for Trump and asked her to say anything she would want him to hear now. Reyes said that, like many Latinos, she deeply regrets her vote.

“I haven’t heard anything from any Republican whatsoever,” she said. “I’m very disappointed, and he lied.”

Good’s brother Brent Ganger said his family has waited long enough for accountability for the damage caused by ICE. As a moderate, he said, he hoped that all members of Congress — even those not in attendance — were listening.

“We will not be quiet, and we will not go away,” he said.

text:
Austin police released new video Monday that shows ICE agents with Wilber Garcés Pérez 10 to 15 minutes before a federal immigration agent shot him in North Austin near Research Blvd. and Anderson Square.

The video comes from the personal dash camera of an off-duty Austin police detective running an errand in the area. It does not show the shooting itself, but APD Chief Lisa Davis said it is helping investigators establish a timeline.

The footage shows ICE agents talking to Garcés Pérez through the driver's-side window of his blue Toyota sedan on Sunday afternoon. They were parked on a neighborhood street near a shopping center and about 200 yards from where the shooting occurred 10 to 15 minutes later. Police say a vehicle pursuit occurred between that initial encounter and the gunfire.

“So when the officer turns into the store from that first video, at that point, those cars left, and he was in that store about 10 to 15 minutes,” Davis said. “There is some video that we have, and again, we're processing that video of a pursuit that went through some of the neighborhoods there, and it ended there.”

RELATED| APD releases video surrounding North Austin ICE shooting of Venezuelan man

KEYE

APD said it is continuing to collect and process video, along with other evidence, to get a better understanding of the pursuit and determine what might have led to the shooting.

Chief Davis says cellphone video recorded by the same off-duty APD detective captured the sound of three gunshots.

Garcés Pérez’s immigration attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, says that he was not trying to flee. She said he told her he was trying to pull over in a safer location.

Meanwhile, Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez remains in pain while in ICE custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall.

She said she spoke with him Tuesday morning after he was taken to a hospital because he was in severe pain and having trouble moving his shoulder.

“A nurse decided that he really did need to go to the hospital because he had so much pain, he wasn't able to move, and so they took him to a hospital,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez received morphine at the hospital but did not have surgery.

“The bullet is still in his body. It went back through near his spine, and it came out and broke his clavicle. So his clavicle is broken,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

When asked by CBS Austin whether Garcés Pérez had been told why he had not had surgery, Lincoln-Goldfinch said: “No, he has not been told why they won't do surgery on him. So that's unclear.”

CBS Austin reached out to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security for an update on Garcés Pérez’s condition, his medical treatment, and the events leading up to the shooting. We had not received a response as of Tuesday evening.

name: Policy
title: Trump administration tells Congress it will admit 17500 white South African refugees in 2027
authors: REBECCA SANTANA and SEUNG MIN KIM, Associated Press, REBECCA SANTANA, SEUNG MIN KIM, Associated Press
description:
In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America.
The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.
The administration told Congress in the announcement that it intended to spend about $500 million to resettle the new arrivals to the U.S.
Organizations that have historically worked to resettle refugees in new homes in America criticized the administration’s decision to once again limit the program to white South Africans.
They are just one of South Africa’s white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration plans to limit the number of refugees admitted to the country in 2027 to 17,500 mostly white South Africans, the administration told Congress Tuesday, as it continues to transform a program that at one point served as a pathway to safety for people fleeing war and strife from countries around the world.

In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America. The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.

The Trump administration has dramatically altered a refugee program that historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support as it welcomed tens of thousands of refugees from countries around the world to new lives in America, and instead the administration has transformed it into a vehicle to resettle white South Africans in America.

The administration told Congress in the announcement that it intended to spend about $500 million to resettle the new arrivals to the U.S.

Organizations that have historically worked to resettle refugees in new homes in America criticized the administration’s decision to once again limit the program to white South Africans.

“For more than four decades, America’s refugee program has provided a lifesaving pathway for people fleeing violence and persecution,” said Naomi Steinberg, HIAS vice president for refugee and immigration policy and advocacy, in a statement. “But again, this administration is diminishing and distorting this legacy in service of its political whims. That is why we will never stop speaking out for a return to a program that welcomes refugees from around the world who have been persecuted because of who they are and what they believe.”

Presidents set the cap on how many refugees the U.S. will approve through the program each year, and historically, they’ve allocated those numbers across various geographic regions while factoring in wars or conflicts that spark humanitarian needs around the globe. HIAS said an average of 92,000 people a year have been admitted to the U.S. since the program was launched in 1980.

Last year, the Trump administration initially set the cap at 7,500 — again predominantly Afrikaners — but later increased the total to 17,500 after it said that “unforeseen developments in South Africa created an emergency refugee situation.”

During his first administration, Trump slashed the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration built the system back up, setting a goal of admitting 125,000 refugees in Biden’s last year in office.

When Trump once again returned to the White House, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been slated to come to the U.S. Then the administration reopened the program, but limited it to white South Africans.

Afrikaners are the descendants of mainly Dutch and French colonial settlers who first arrived in South Africa in the 17th century. They are just one of South Africa’s white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.

text:
Austin police and the Travis County District Attorney's Office say they are actively investigating the shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez by an ICE officer. But so far, it's not clear how much evidence they'll be able to access from the Department of Homeland Security, which is conducting a separate investigation of the incident.

During a news conference on Tuesday, APD Chief Lisa Davis said her detectives are speaking "daily" with DHS and she had no reason to believe the department would withhold information. She said she didn't know what her detectives had requested or when they expected to receive it.

"These are some of our most elite investigators," she said. "They are fantastic. I trust them. I trust this investigation and it is absolutely in good hands."

She also said APD is investigating the shooting alongside Texas Rangers and the Travis County District Attorney's Office.

District Attorney José Garza told KUT that his prosecutors have asked federal investigators for digital and physical evidence to get a "complete accounting" of the shooting. They've also asked to interview the ICE officer who shot Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan national.

"We're still awaiting word on whether or not our request will be granted," he said, adding that the investigation is at a "preliminary moment."

Garza also wrote a letter to the agency asking that Garces Perez remain in the country. A federal judge ruled Tuesday that he must be present for a court hearing in San Antonio on Sept. 30, but Garza said he will need to stay far longer than that while investigators look into the shooting.

"From our perspective, Mr. Garces Perez is a material witness to the incident that took place in Austin," he said. "The Travis County District Attorney's Office thinks that it is critical that he remain in the United States so that he can participate in the investigation and any proceeding that may follow."

The incident comes after a rash of similar shootings by federal immigration agents across the country. Local officials this week expressed concern about whether federal investigators would share all the evidence with APD and Garza's office, citing cases in Minnesota and Houston where federal investigators withheld evidence and slowed local prosecutions.

KUT reached out to DHS to ask if the agency plans to share information with local law enforcement, but the agency did not respond. The FBI, which is assisting in the federal investigation, directed questions about evidence-sharing to DHS.

text:
SAN JUAN, Puerto Rico (AP) — Human Rights Watch released a report on Monday detailing the hardships faced by hundreds of people deported by the United States to gang-ravaged Haiti.

The report is the first intimate look at the lives of deportees who have declined to speak at length with journalists because they fear for their safety. Gang violence is surging and hunger and poverty are deepening.

The U.S. has deported more than 470 people to Haiti since July, including people who lost Temporary Protected Status, which had allowed them to live and work legally in the U.S.

The main international airport in Port-au-Prince is considered too dangerous because of persistent gang violence, so deportation flights are landing in the northern city of Cap-Haitien. Mayor Michel Saint-Croix told Human Rights Watch that the city’s population has tripled to more than 1 million in the past two years as it receives deportees and Haitians fleeing violence elsewhere in the country.

The deportees’ arrival has strained already limited resources. Haitian migration officials said the U.S. government has told them it planned to send as many as two deportation flights a week, each carrying about 200 people, according to the report.

Deportees share details of their lives

Human Rights Watch said it interviewed 44 deportees, as well as Haitian and international officials.

Deportees said they went for hours without food or water and days without bathing or changing clothes while held at U.S. immigration detention facilities. The interviewees said their belongings, including official documents and money, were not returned to them when they arrived in Haiti.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement responded Tuesday to a request for comment, saying that claims about “subprime conditions” at ICE detention centers are false.

“All detainees are provided with 3 meals a day, clean water, clothing, bedding, showers, soap, and toiletries,” it said in a statement, also asserting that detainees have access to phones to talk with relatives and lawyers. “Certified dieticians evaluate meals. In fact, ICE has higher detention standards than most U.S. prisons that hold actual U.S. citizens.”

It noted that deportees have included Haitians charged in the U.S. with crimes ranging from drug possession to sexual offenses.

Human Rights Watch said it reviewed passenger manifests for two deportation flights in August. Neither contained information about the deportees’ immigration status or the grounds for their removal.

Most of the 44 deportees interviewed said they had fled Haiti’s worsening security and humanitarian crises and settled in U.S. states, including Florida, New York, Indiana and Ohio. They found work in sectors such as construction, healthcare and manufacturing.

Many said they were from Port-au-Prince or surrounding areas, where armed men control an estimated 70% of the capital. Others said they were from the Artibonite region, which is under assault by violent gangs.

The deportees lived in the U.S. for anywhere from two to 14 years before being sent back to Haiti. Among them was a 38-year-old unidentified man who said he had lived in Florida since December 2019 and worked at the same hotel for more than six years.

His wife and 5-year-old son, who is a U.S. citizen, remain in Florida, according to the report.

“I worked so that he could grow up without the fear, violence, and uncertainty that I had known in Haiti,” the man was quoted as saying.

He and several other deportees said they had Temporary Protected Status, although the rights group noted it could not independently verify those claims.

A 47-year-old woman said she had lived in Miami with her husband, a U.S. citizen, and was arrested when she attended an interview to apply for permanent residence.

“Once detained, most interviewees said authorities did not allow them to contact their lawyers or appear before an immigration judge, while many received little or no information about their pending asylum claims, the grounds for their detention, or how they could challenge their deportation,” Human Rights Watch said.

Another deportee was a 24-year-old nursing assistant student who said she applied for asylum after fleeing Haiti in 2023 after gangs attacked her community.

Violence, hunger and poverty persist

At least 19,380 people were reported killed across Haiti between January 2023 and June 2026, according to the United Nations.

Hunger and poverty also are deepening as Haitian police and a U.N.-backed mission struggle to contain gang violence. More than 253,000 children aged six months to 5 years are expected to suffer acute malnutrition in upcoming months, according to a new report by Haiti’s government and agencies including UNICEF.

“The United States is returning people, some with pending asylum claims, to a country that doesn’t have the capacity to protect them from violence, let alone help them find food and shelter,” said Nathalye Cotrino, senior Americas researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The U.S. government should immediately halt these removals.”

Deportees arriving in Haiti are given a simple meal, a drink and about $77 in cash.

“After registering, deportees were left to fend for themselves, and many did not know what to do or where to go next,” the report said.

Austin police are sharing more information and videos from their response to Sunday's ICE shooting in North Austin.

APD held a press conference Tuesday to explain why their department responded to the scene.

RELATED COVERAGE: Austin ICE shooting: Agent was not wearing bodycam, reports say

New video appears to show man involved in traffic stop

What they're saying:

The new video released by APD appears to show 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was involved in a traffic stop with federal agents before leading them on a pursuit, minutes before he was shot by a federal agent.

APD released video captured on an off-duty APD detective's personal dashcam and cellphone, as well as body camera footage from an on-duty officer.

The dashcam video appears to show a blue sedan pulled over by black SUVs which have their lights on. Federal officers can be seen interacting with the person inside.

The detective then turned into a shopping complex and continued on with personal errands. When he came back to his vehicle after about 10–15 minutes, he heard sirens and began recording with his cellphone.

He then heard three gunshots.

The detective called the police watch lieutenant to report what he had witnessed and to request officers respond to the scene.

APD also released body camera footage from an officer that responded to the scene.

Chief Davis says that the beginning of the video was muted "in order to protect the investigation" and the audio picks up when the officer interacts with the person inside the blue sedan, who APD says is Perez.

In the body cam video, Perez can be seen with a gunshot wound to his back and heard complaining about pain in his shoulder.

This initial traffic stop reportedly happened about 200 yards away from the scene of the shooting.

During the press conference, Chief Davis said that a pursuit took place and that APD is processing video from surrounding neighborhoods. Perez said through a translator during a press conference on Monday that he had been sideswiped by ICE agents while DoorDashing and was trying to find a place to park.

When asked about Perez's account, Chief Lisa Davis said Tuesday she would not speculate.

What you can do:

Chief Davis is asking for anyone who witnessed the incident or has video, photos or information that could help the investigation to come forward.

"Even information that may seem minor or insignificant can help investigators piece together a timeline and better understand what occurred. The responsibility of the Austin Police Department is to follow evidence wherever it leads and to conduct this investigation objectively and within the authority granted to us," Davis said.

What happened in the ICE shooting on Sept. 20 in Austin?

The backstory:

It's still not clear exactly what happened during the law enforcement operation before the ICE agent opened fire in North Austin.

Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Rob Luckritz said emergency crews were notified of a reported shooting at about 12:56 p.m. in the 8000 block of Anderson Square.

Paramedics arrived within about 3 1/2 minutes and found an adult man with a gunshot wound. The man was transported to a local trauma center in serious but stable condition.

APD Chief Lisa Davis said the shooting involved a federal agent and later confirmed she had been told the agent was with ICE. Austin police were not involved in the shooting.

RELATED COVERAGE: Austin ICE shooting: Agent was not wearing bodycam, reports say

The man shot has been identified as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a Venezuelan national, by immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who is representing Perez and his family.

Perez told Lincoln-Goldfinch that he was driving for DoorDash on Sunday when an unmarked car sideswiped him. He did not know it was ICE.

He told Lincoln-Goldfinch that he did a U-turn under the highway and was then sideswiped again. He then said the agents got out of the unmarked car and shot him in the back of the neck. They then pulled him from the car.

RELATED COVERAGE: Austin ICE shooting: New details released on man shot by ICE agents

Lincoln-Goldfinch said there was no foot chase. However, ICE said there was a foot chase.

DHS officials have confirmed that Perez is from Venezuela and say he entered the country illegally and had a final order of removal.

Perez was taken into federal custody to the South Texas ICE processing center in Pearsall, but has since been taken back to the hospital, according to Rep. Joaquin Castro.

text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A judge has ordered a Venezuelan man shot in Texas by a federal immigration officer to appear in court as his attorneys seek to stop his removal from the U.S. and criticize his medical care, saying he remains in pain from a bullet lodged in his back.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, was back in a federal detention center Tuesday after being treated and released at a hospital for a second time since he was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent on Sunday in Austin, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.

Austin police on Tuesday released body camera footage showing Garces Perez hunching over in the front seat of his car and grabbing his shoulder and rocking back and forth after the shooting. An officer later cut off Perez’s shirt, and a wound can be seen in his upper back.

Democratic U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro of Texas said he planned to visit Garces Perez on Wednesday to “check on his condition and demand his release.” The Department of Homeland Security defended Garces Perez’s treatment and its operations, saying ICE would not slow down or leave Austin.

Castro has joined other Democrats in sharply criticizing the shooting, which came amid a surge in enforcement during President Donald Trump’s second term. The encounter has sparked protests in Austin, including a gathering outside the Texas Capitol on Monday night.

Judge sets court hearing for Garces Perez

Garces Perez was making a DoorDash delivery Sunday afternoon when ICE officers in an unmarked truck sideswiped his car twice, Lincoln-Goldfinch has said. He was shot and taken to a hospital, then released into ICE custody with a bullet still in his back, she said.

U.S. District Judge Orlando Garcia ordered Garces Perez to appear in person at a hearing Sept. 30 in San Antonio in response to a lawsuit filed by his attorney, who is seeking to stop attempts to remove him from the country. In the order, Garcia wrote that “petitioner must be present at the hearing.”

In court filings, Garces Perez’s lawyers said he was forced to sleep on a cement floor at an ICE temporary processing center before being transferred to a detention center in the rural town of Pearsall. They also alleged that he was questioned without an attorney present.

Garces Perez entered the U.S. in 2024 using CBP One, a program begun under President Joe Biden that allowed migrants to make appointments with U.S. authorities to be considered for asylum, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. President Donald Trump ended the program on his first day in office.

Garces Perez was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch. She said a judge issued a deportation order after the man missed an immigration court hearing because the notice was sent to a former address.

Austin police release body camera footage

Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said Tuesday that an off-duty detective reported the incident after witnessing and recording black SUVs surrounding a dark blue Toyota Corolla. Ten to fifteen minutes later, Davis said, he takes a video where three gunshots and sirens can be heard.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to questions Tuesday about whether the federal officer who shot Garces Perez was wearing a body-worn camera. Davis said she did not know whether federal officers on the scene were wearing body cameras.

ICE has said its field officers nationwide will have body-worn cameras by the end of September.

Davis said there was a pursuit that went through some side neighborhoods that ended on a side street about 200 yards (meters) from where Perez was eventually shot. The body worn camera videos released by Austin police do not show what led up to the shooting. The body warn camera footage begins with an officer walking up to Garces Perez’s car after the shooting and interacting with federal officers on the scene.

The videos are partially muted, and Garces Perez is speaking Spanish to the officers. State troopers are also on the scene. An officer asks one of the federal officers if Garces Perez is under arrest and is told yes.

On Monday, Perez called into a news conference and told reporters he had received no pain medication and slept on the floor. DHS said in a statement Tuesday that Garces Perez was receiving medical care “around the clock, including pain medication” and had slept on a bed.

title: What Makes Someone a “Public Charge”? Understanding DHS's New Rule | JD Supra

text:
September 18, 2026 marks a shift in how USCIS evaluates the public-charge ground of inadmissibility for covered adjustment-of-status applications. DHS's rescission of the 2022 public-charge regulations takes effect that day, and USCIS's revised Policy Manual guidance applies to Forms I-485 subject to the public-charge grounds that are postmarked or electronically submitted on or after September 18, 2026. That said, the change affects how the ground is evaluated, not whether it applies: the statutory ground of inadmissibility under INA § 212(a)(4) remains in place.

Under the revised framework, USCIS officers must evaluate the statutory factors in INA § 212(a)(4), including age, health, family status, assets, resources, and financial status, and education and skills, along with other evidence relevant to whether the applicant is likely at any time to become a public charge. USCIS states that this assessment is individualized and based on the totality of the circumstances.

The change does not establish an automatic bar based on benefit receipt. Instead, for means-tested benefits received on or after September 18, USCIS may consider benefit history together with the applicant's financial circumstances, household circumstances, education and skills, health, and other evidence in the record. For employment-based and investor applicants, that makes the framework, its transition rules, and the scope of evidence USCIS may consider worth understanding in detail.

What Changed, and What USCIS Now Applies

Two related agency actions underpin this change. First, DHS rescinded the 2022 public-charge regulations in a final rule, Public Charge Ground of Inadmissibility, 91 Fed. Reg. 45,324 (July 20, 2026), effective September 18, 2026. USCIS subsequently issued Policy Manual guidance on August 18, 2026, explaining that officers will adjudicate public-charge inadmissibility under the post-rescission framework.

The underlying statute has not changed. INA § 212(a)(4) continues to require officers to consider, at a minimum, five factors: age; health; family status; assets, resources, and financial status; and education and skills.

What has changed is the framework surrounding those factors. USCIS may now consider additional case-specific evidence, including receipt of means-tested public benefits, as part of an individualized totality-of-the-circumstances determination. USCIS directs officers to make case-by-case determinations based on the totality of the circumstances rather than on any single factor.

In other words, the revised framework is not simply a question of whether an applicant has received a particular benefit. Benefits history may be considered alongside financial resources, employability, household circumstances, health, and the rest of the record. USCIS describes its guidance as controlling and intended to guide, rather than prescribe, how officers exercise discretion in individual cases. The guidance also supersedes prior related guidance, including the 1999 Interim Field Guidance.

Transition Rules for Filings and Benefits

The effective date creates two separate questions: which public-charge framework applies to the filing, and which benefits USCIS may consider.

For Forms I-485 subject to the public-charge grounds that are postmarked or electronically submitted on or after September 18, 2026, USCIS applies its revised guidance. The final rule separately addresses how USCIS considers means-tested benefits received before that date.

The timing of benefit receipt is evaluated on its own track. For means-tested benefits received before September 18, 2026, USCIS says it will consider only public cash assistance for income maintenance and long-term institutionalization at government expense. For means-tested benefits received on or after September 18, 2026, USCIS states that officers may consider any and all means-tested public benefits as part of the totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

That distinction matters. The date of the I-485 filing determines which framework governs the case, while the date a benefit was received determines the range of benefits USCIS says it may weigh. As a result, a filing made under the revised framework can involve benefit history from before the effective date, with that earlier history evaluated under the narrower transition rule.

Revised Form I-485 Takes Effect Without a Grace Period

A second change is procedural rather than substantive.

Beginning September 18, 2026, USCIS accepts only the 09/18/26 edition of Form I-485. There is no grace period for the previous 01/20/25 edition. USCIS states it will reject the prior edition if it is postmarked or electronically submitted on or after September 18, 2026.

Who Is Subject to the Public-Charge Ground?

Public charge is not limited to family-based immigration.

According to USCIS, all adjustment applicants are subject to the public-charge ground unless their immigration category is exempt. Among the USCIS-listed covered adjustment categories are employment-based priority workers; EB-2 professionals with advanced degrees or exceptional ability; EB-3 skilled workers, professionals, and other workers; investors; religious workers; immediate relatives and family-preference applicants; and diversity visa immigrants adjusting status.

USCIS also identifies numerous exempt groups, including refugees, asylees, Special Immigrant Juveniles, VAWA self-petitioners, T and U nonimmigrants, certain Cuban and Haitian entrants, Afghan and Iraqi interpreters and certain Afghan and Iraqi nationals employed by or on behalf of the U.S. government, and registry applicants, among others. Because the list contains category-specific exemptions, the applicable adjustment category determines whether the public-charge ground applies in a given case.

The Benefits Inquiry Under the Revised Framework

The benefits inquiry is a central feature of the revised framework.

USCIS's guidance allows officers to consider a broader range of means-tested benefits, meaning benefits granted based on a household's income level. USCIS identifies examples such as cash assistance for income maintenance, housing assistance, food stamps, financial aid for college, and similar benefits.

Still, receipt of a public benefit does not automatically make an applicant inadmissible as a public charge. Rather, it may be one factor within the broader individualized determination.

For that reason, the relevant question is not simply whether a benefit was received. Its timing and type, along with the applicant's household circumstances and broader financial picture, may form part of the record USCIS evaluates.

Employment-Based and Investor Cases Under the Revised Framework

For employment-based and investor adjustment applicants who are subject to the public-charge ground, the statutory factors may make financial and employment-related evidence particularly relevant. USCIS must consider the applicant's age, health, family status, assets, resources, financial status, education, and skills, and may consider other evidence relevant to the likelihood of becoming a public charge.

Depending on the facts of a case, the record may include information relating to current and prospective employment, income, assets and liabilities, business-related financial documentation, household resources, education, professional qualifications, and skills. These are not a separate set of regulatory requirements; rather, they are examples of evidence that may relate to the statutory totality-of-the-circumstances assessment.

The Role of Form I-864 in the Analysis

In many employment-based cases, no Form I-864, Affidavit of Support Under Section 213A of the INA, is required. USCIS identifies Form I-864 as a factor it may consider where applicable, while the public-charge inquiry remains individualized and fact-specific. Where Form I-864 is not part of the filing, USCIS may still assess the statutory financial and other factors based on the record before it.

Public-Charge Bonds Remain Available

The revised framework retains the possibility of a public-charge bond in certain circumstances.

If USCIS finds an adjustment applicant inadmissible only on public-charge grounds, an officer may invite the applicant to post a bond using Form I-945. An applicant cannot independently submit Form I-945 for this purpose; USCIS must first issue an invitation in a Notice of Intent to Deny.

When determining the bond amount, USCIS may consider the government assistance the applicant could be eligible for and potentially receive over the following five years. A cash bond or a Treasury-certified surety bond may be used.

Pending Litigation and Potential Developments

The revised framework is already the subject of legal challenges.

On September 14, 2026, New York and a multistate coalition filed a challenge to the DHS final rule in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York. The complaint is docketed as New York v. U.S. Department of Homeland Security, No. 26-cv-7978 (S.D.N.Y.). New York City, joined by local-government plaintiffs including Chicago, San Francisco, Santa Clara County, Seattle, and King County, filed a separate action in the same court. The plaintiffs' claims are allegations and have not been adjudicated.

As of September 18, 2026, this article has not identified an order staying implementation of the final rule. Because procedural developments can occur quickly, the status of the litigation should be checked against the relevant court dockets before publication or republication.

Several questions remain open. Courts could address whether preliminary relief is appropriate. USCIS adjudications and Requests for Evidence may provide more insight into how the guidance is applied in practice. The DHS rule and USCIS guidance discussed here principally concern DHS/USCIS adjudications; immigrant-visa applicants processing abroad should separately monitor Department of State guidance. And, as cases develop, fact patterns involving household benefits, derivative family members, and variable, newly established, or startup-based income may help clarify how the framework operates.

Practical Effects of the September 18 Change

For covered adjustment applications filed on or after September 18, 2026, the operative issues include the applicable Form I-485 edition, whether the adjustment category is exempt from the public-charge ground, and the timing and type of any means-tested benefits reflected in the record. USCIS will accept only the 09/18/26 edition of Form I-485 for forms postmarked or electronically submitted on or after that date; the prior 01/20/25 edition will be rejected if filed on or after September 18.

The revised framework does not replace the statutory requirement to consider the five INA § 212(a)(4) factors. It instead permits USCIS to consider a broader set of relevant evidence, including any means-tested public benefits received on or after the effective date, in a case-by-case totality-of-the-circumstances analysis.

text:
He watched immigration agents shepherd other detainees from Venezuela, Cuba, Haiti and Central America across the tarmac towards three sleek white buses on the Mexican side of the port of entry.

Betancourt had no intention of boarding those buses. “I’ll just refuse to go. It’s my right,” he remembers thinking.

By then, Betancourt was used to the vagaries of American immigration enforcement. Since the Venezuelan journalist was detained on July 14, 2025, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents had shuttled him between 12 different detention facilities and had already attempted to deport him twice.

The first time had been in late December 2025, when immigration agents bussed Betancourt to San Diego’s border with Tijuana. Betancourt told authorities that they couldn’t obligate him to cross — Mexico wasn’t his country, he was scared of what would happen if he were sent there without any legal status, and deporting him without due process was illegal. The agents relented and returned him to detention.

Then, a month later at Arizona’s Mesa Gateway airport, immigration agents tried to force Betancourt onto a plane to Venezuela. He told them that an immigration judge had granted him protection from deportation to Venezuela in a 2024 court order, a decade after he fled political persecution in Caracas. ICE agents ignored his objections until a U.S. Marshal intervened on his behalf.

In Nogales, though, things unfolded differently. Four armed immigration agents clambered into the van and closed in around Betancourt. “They’ll deport you with punches if it’s necessary,” Betancourt said.

During six months in detention, Betancourt regularly experienced what he described as inhumane and dehumanizing treatment, including periods of up to 25 hours in shackles, and days on end shut with other immigrants in holding rooms so cramped that the detainees had to take turns lying down to rest. But he was determined to continue fighting his case, and return to the life he’d built with his family over the last decade in Miami. And to do so, he would need to remain inside the United States.

Hoping to avoid a beating, Betancourt crossed the border intending to explain his case to Mexican migration authorities — maybe they would listen. “But they didn’t respond,” he said. “They literally pretended not to hear me.”

The American agents forced Betancourt onto the Mexican bus with around 40 other detained passengers. Moments later, they were rolling south through rural Sonora towards an unknown destination in an unfamiliar country.

title: Supreme Court Appeal Opens Door to Khan Suri's Redetention - The Hoya
description:
The district court that freed Khan Suri found the government likely violated the First Amendment by targeting Khan Suri for protected speech and familial associations.
Jackson Schnabel (SFS ’27), who is currently Khan Suri’s student, said the government’s purported interest in efficiency is baffling.
Khan Suri expects the Supreme Court to take the case, he said Monday, because they want to block noncitizens from using federal court to secure their freedom.
Florez said that if the Supreme Court takes Khan Suri or Khalil’s case, the impact will reverberate for years.
Schnabel, who has attended campus protests and Khan Suri’s legal hearings, said he is disappointed that the legal battle remains ongoing.
text:
The U.S. Supreme Court is considering the Trump administration’s Sept. 21 request to redetain Georgetown University postdoctoral researcher Badar Khan Suri after an appeals court ruling kept him out of immigration detention.

A federal district judge released Khan Suri in May 2025 and the U.S. 4th Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed the decision two months ago. Now, if the Supreme Court chooses to take the case — which experts say it appears likely to do — the justices will settle noncitizens’ ability to contest their detention in federal court.

The Supreme Court appeal comes 18 months after federal immigration agents detained Khan Suri for 58 days, drawing on a rarely-used statute to allege he threatened U.S. foreign policy.

Adnan Rashid (GRD ’24), one of Khan Suri’s closest friends who has supported him and his family through their legal proceedings, said he believes the federal government wants to silence the postdoctoral researcher’s speech.

“The government is trying to find a needle in a haystack but there is no needle — he is just a bookish person who sticks to reading and teaching,” Rashid told The Hoya. “They’re trying to find a crime where there is no crime.”

Noor Zafar, one of Khan Suri’s lawyers, said the lower federal courts were right to free Khan Suri from indefinite detention.

“Our client should never have been jailed for exercising his First Amendment rights in the first place and we will continue fighting to keep him free and with his family,” Zafar wrote to The Hoya.

The government’s lawyers have argued, however, that constitutional challenges to detention cannot be heard in federal courts — only in immigration courts, which are overseen by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). Khan Suri’s lawyers have long asserted that immigration courts are politically biased, a product of the Trump administration’s purge of immigration judges.

Khan Suri’s legal team has until Oct. 21 to file an opposing brief. Until then, the Supreme Court cannot formally decide if it will hear the case. No Supreme Court precedent explicitly governs federal judges’ jurisdiction over detention claims.

To justify Khan Suri’s detainment, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Khan Suri was spreading “Hamas propaganda” and antisemitism — citing online posts about him and his connection to his father-in-law, a former Hamas official. He denies these allegations, and the government has published limited evidence to support its claims.

The district court that freed Khan Suri found the government likely violated the First Amendment by targeting Khan Suri for protected speech and familial associations.

In its Supreme Court appeal, the DOJ does not argue that it acted constitutionally — merely that federal courts cannot decide if it did. Their claim centers on three sections of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) they say are meant to “eliminate” district courts from overseeing noncitizens’ detention.

Instead, Trump administration lawyers assert that federal law channels all immigration cases solely into immigration court so noncitizens get “just one bite at the apple — not zero or two.” Under the government’s proposed scheme, Khan Suri would remain detained throughout his lengthy immigration proceedings.

But Khan Suri’s lawyers — and the 4th Circuit — said those INA provisions only apply to deportation proceedings, and detention remains a separate legal issue. In the 4th Circuit’s decision, Judge DeAndrea Benjamin wrote that “no provision within the immigration code deprived” federal courts of jurisdiction over immigration detention.

Jackson Schnabel (SFS ’27), who is currently Khan Suri’s student, said the government’s purported interest in efficiency is baffling.

“It does no good if you have to challenge the illegality of your detention if you have to wait for all of these removal proceedings to go through,” Schnabel told The Hoya. “That just allows the illegal detention to continue — it allows it to exist even when it’s blatantly illegal.”

“If they don’t want there to be a drain on federal resources, they shouldn’t detain people for their speech,” Schnabel added.

In a Monday speech to Georgetown students after the appeal, Khan Suri said constitutional challenges are what “keeps a democracy a democracy.”

Yassine Florez (GRD ’26), a student organizer and close friend of Khan Suri’s family, said he was surprised the appeal came so quickly, but believes the Supreme Court will agree with the 4th Circuit.

“I am confident because we do have the precedent of winning,” Florez told The Hoya.

“He was able to win in the circuit court when no one else could,” Florez added.

The 4th Circuit is one of three federal appeals panels that have recently considered constitutional challenges to immigration detention — and the only one that has sided with noncitizens. Former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil is currently preparing a Supreme Court challenge to a 3rd Circuit decision in January that confined his case to immigration court.

The federal government cited this divide as a reason the Supreme Court should hear the case, positioning Khan Suri as an “ideal vehicle” to clarify case law that will apply to the entire country. In general, circuit splits make the Supreme Court more likely to rule on a legal issue.

Khan Suri expects the Supreme Court to take the case, he said Monday, because they want to block noncitizens from using federal court to secure their freedom.

Florez said that if the Supreme Court takes Khan Suri or Khalil’s case, the impact will reverberate for years.

“The whole goal of this appeal to the Supreme Court is to cement a law that the government can imprison anyone for as long as they want before deciding if they’re guilty or innocent,” Florez said.

“Whether or not they’re pro-justice, this will set a precedent for every case in the future,” Florez added.

Nader Hashemi, Khan Suri’s supervisor at Georgetown, said the case could become “one of those classic Supreme Court cases” that define the current political moment.

“It will speak volumes about what direction politically this country is headed in — in an authoritarian direction, or whether the Supreme Court will establish a guardrail,” Hashemi told The Hoya.

Khan Suri’s case has become a touchpoint for the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown and a rallying cry across the Georgetown community. Student protesters have said the case is emblematic of federal crackdowns on academic freedom.

Schnabel, who has attended campus protests and Khan Suri’s legal hearings, said he is disappointed that the legal battle remains ongoing.

“We had the win when the ruling actually came out, but now we need to continue in this part of the fight,” Schnabel said. “But I am still optimistic that the rule of law, the rule of justice, will prevail in the long run — that as facts actually get considered, it will continue to be abundantly clear that what is going on is unconstitutional.”

At Khan Suri’s parallel immigration trial last week, over a dozen students attended the hearing in support as nine witnesses testified that he should remain in the United States.

Hashemi said that while political headwinds — including the Supreme Court’s current conservative majority — are against Khan Suri, he hopes the court looks solely at the facts and case law.

“You have to keep reminding people that his case is still pending, that the Trump administration is unrelenting in its attempt to deport him,” Hashemi said. “The challenge of Badar Khan Suri’s supporters is to keep his case in the public eye and keep reminding people of what’s coming next, what’s at stake here, why his cause matters.”

Darius Wagner (CAS ’27), president of Georgetown’s student government, said Khan Suri’s case is emblematic of the university’s commitment to studying authoritarianism and democracy.

“I think this will only continue to inspire students to keep pursuing those truths, and that is why I think it’s also really important that we all stand by Dr. Badar Khan Suri, because he’s a representation of our best values of our academic freedom and of our founding principles for freedom of speech,” Wagner told The Hoya.

Rashid said that even as Khan Suri faces a constant “onslaught” of litigation, he remains committed to his research and teaching.

“It’s fear, but he has hope,” Rashid said. “He believes in American democracy and freedom of speech and the Constitution. He believes in it, and that’s one of the reasons why he has hope.”

In an interview after his immigration hearing, Khan Suri said he hopes to live a “happy, cheerful life” as an academic.

“Someday, somewhere I’m sure I will get justice,” Khan Suri told The Hoya last Wednesday.

description:
In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America.
The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.
The administration told Congress in the announcement that it intended to spend about $500 million to resettle the new arrivals to the U.S.
Organizations that have historically worked to resettle refugees in new homes in America criticized the administration’s decision to once again limit the program to white South Africans.
They are just one of South Africa’s white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.
text:
By REBECCA SANTANA and SEUNG MIN KIM

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration plans to limit the number of refugees admitted to the country to 17,500 mostly white South Africans, the administration told Congress Tuesday, as it continues to transform a program that at one point served as a pathway to safety for people fleeing war and strife from countries around the world.

In a notice to Congress obtained by The Associated Press, the administration said the white South Africans faced seizures of their land and other forms of persecution and would be likely to assimilate when they come to America. The South African government has repeatedly rejected the idea that the white South Africans, who are Afrikaners, are a persecuted minority in the home country.

The Trump administration has dramatically altered a refugee program that historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support as it welcomed tens of thousands of refugees from countries around the world to new lives in America, and instead the administration has transformed it into a vehicle to resettle white South Africans in America.

The administration told Congress in the announcement that it intended to spend about $500 million to resettle the new arrivals to the U.S.

Organizations that have historically worked to resettle refugees in new homes in America criticized the administration’s decision to once again limit the program to white South Africans.

“For more than four decades, America’s refugee program has provided a lifesaving pathway for people fleeing violence and persecution,” said Naomi Steinberg, HIAS vice president for refugee and immigration policy and advocacy, in a statement. “But again, this administration is diminishing and distorting this legacy in service of its political whims. That is why we will never stop speaking out for a return to a program that welcomes refugees from around the world who have been persecuted because of who they are and what they believe.”

Presidents set the cap on how many refugees the U.S. will approve through the program each year, and historically, they’ve allocated those numbers across various geographic regions while factoring in wars or conflicts that spark humanitarian needs around the globe. HIAS said an average of 92,000 people a year have been admitted to the U.S. since the program was launched in 1980.

Last year, the Trump administration initially set the cap at 7,500 — again predominantly Afrikaners — but later increased the total to 17,500 after it said that “unforeseen developments in South Africa created an emergency refugee situation.”

During his first administration, Trump slashed the number of refugees approved every year. The Biden administration built the system back up, setting a goal of admitting 125,000 refugees in Biden’s last year in office.

When Trump once again returned to the White House, he immediately suspended the refugee program, stranding people around the world who had been slated to come to the U.S. Then the administration reopened the program, but limited it to white South Africans.

Afrikaners are the descendants of mainly Dutch and French colonial settlers who first arrived in South Africa in the 17th century. They are just one of South Africa’s white minorities, which also include South Africans of British descent.

title: After ICE shooting, Venezuelan man's quick release from Austin hospital raises questions
authors: Uriel J. García, Zach Leggio, Alex Nguyen, Gabby Birenbaum, Colleen DeGuzman, Matthew Watkins, Jessica Priest, Hien An Ngo, Alejandra Martinez, Alejandro Santos Cid
description:
The bullet fired by a federal immigration officer is still lodged to his back, according to Garces Perez and his immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.
His lawyer said that Garces Perez did have a work permit and a driver’s license but expired in December.
By Tuesday afternoon, Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela was back at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall.

The off-duty detective’s footage first showed Garces Perez pulled over and two ICE officers speaking with him.
text:
About four hours after Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was admitted to an Austin hospital with a gunshot wound, the Venezuelan man was discharged Sunday and taken 135 miles south to an immigration detention center where some detainees have complained about inadequate medical care.

The bullet fired by a federal immigration officer is still lodged to his back, according to Garces Perez and his immigration lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. After he began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” Garces Perez was taken to another hospital for treatment, the lawyer said.

His lawyers, Democratic leaders and immigrant advocates have questioned whether Garces Perez received proper medical treatment and whether he was taken into custody before he could fully heal.

Garces Perez was working as a DoorDash delivery driver when he was shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during a traffic stop in North Austin. His lawyer said that Garces Perez did have a work permit and a driver’s license but expired in December. After he was taken to the hospital, Lincoln-Goldfinch said she and Garces Perez’s wife were not allowed to visit him.

On Monday evening, after he called into a news conference to say that he has not received any medication, he was transported to a second hospital after he complained of losing feeling on the left side of his body, his lawyer said.

“Wilber tells me that after he spoke publicly, guards at the Pearsall detention center forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

By Tuesday afternoon, Garces Perez, 28, of Venezuela was back at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall.

Doctors who have treated immigrants injured by ICE say that while Garces Perez’s treatment may seem harsh, it appears that medical staff and ICE officers treated him like any other person in this situation.

DHS released a statement Tuesday saying Garces Perez is receiving “medical care around the clock, including pain medication.” The statement also said ICE officers do not control the medical treatment for the bullet lodged in his back.

“ICE does not and would not advise, nor be the authority on, a medical procedure for an illegal alien at a hospital,” the statement said.

Marc F. Stern, a doctor and an assistant professor at the University of Washington, said he doesn’t like to see any patient recovering in a detention center, but unless ICE forced the medical staff to release Garces Perez prematurely it is common for patients with a lodged bullet to be discharged. He added that in many cases attempting to remove a bullet does more harm than good.

“We’d all like to believe the system works but under the current administration the rule of law has suffered a lot,” Stern said. “So do we have the confidence that all of this is happening correctly? I would hope so.”

Brian Elmore, a doctor who has treated injured immigrants in Mexico and is a current Global Emergency Medical fellow at the University of Virginia, said he recently discharged a Maryland man who also had a bullet lodged in his back. He said it is important to have a post-discharge treatment plan.

“In somebody that isn’t detained, these patients would have close follow-up with their trauma surgery team and be discharged with pain medication,” he said. “The problem with these patients is that they are often discharged in conditions where they receive inappropriate or absent medical care.”

Naureen Shah, director of immigration policy with the American Civil Liberties Union, recently wrote a report titled “Agents of Chaos and Cruelty,” which she said documents ICE’s pattern of excessive force and civil rights violations under the Trump administration.

Shah said that even if a doctor discharged him, the detention center Garces Perez is in is not ideal.

“It’s probably one of the worst places to take a person who has a bullet lodged to his back,” she said.

The ACLU recently filed a $10 million claim against the ICE facility in Pearsall, saying a client experienced medical neglect and mistreatment in detention.

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Austin, said Tuesday that ICE should immediately release Garces Perez, who has a pending removal order and has applied for political asylum, so that he can “receive medical treatment.”

“Mr. Garces Perez is not receiving the care he needs in detention,” Casar wrote in a letter signed by over 100 Democratic members of Congress. “While he remains in the United States, he should be allowed to receive medical care and pursue all legal options available to him. Finally, Mr. Garces Perez and the ICE agent responsible must remain in Texas until a thorough, independent investigation into the shooting is complete.”

Gov. Greg Abbott, who has ordered state police to work with ICE officers operating in Texas, has not directly discussed the shooting. Asked about the shooting at an unrelated Tuesday news conference, the governor said details remain “sketchy.”

“There’s not full information yet available about exactly what happened and what the status is right now,” he added. “But we’ll work to stay on top of it.”

Tuesday afternoon, Austin Mayor Kirk Watson and the city’s police chief, Lisa Davis, addressed questions about Garces Perez’s medical treatment.

Speaking at a news conference, Davis said it is hospital policy to not allow family members to visit patients who are detained while receiving medical attention, but she could not speak to why Garces Perez was released when he was.

“If APD were to bring someone in that was under arrest and detained … if families showed up, no, they would not be allowed to come back and talk with that person,” Davis said. “That is what the protocol is.”

Watson said that when he arrived at Dell Seton Medical Center, he was concerned to hear that Garces Perez’s wife was not given any update on his condition and was seeking clarity on rumors that Garces Perez had died.

“By the time I got down to the hospital, he had obviously already been taken away from the hospital by the ICE officers, and nobody had been told that — I may have been the first one that was told,” Watson said. “That wasn’t part of the hospital operation, it was because of my pursuit of trying to get to the truth about what was going on.”

During the news conference, Davis also showed new footage from an off-duty APD detective’s dashcam and cell phone camera, as well as the bodycam footage from APD officers who arrived on the scene.

The off-duty detective’s footage first showed Garces Perez pulled over and two ICE officers speaking with him. Davis said there was a brief vehicle pursuit, which APD is still investigating, that finished under an overpass where the shots were fired.

Davis confirmed that there is no evidence of a foot chase.

The bodycam footage was muted as APD officers first interact with the ICE officers, but the audio began as APD officers removed Garces Perez from his vehicle and provided medical help. The ICE officers had not provided medical assistance prior to APD’s arrival. The footage was muted to preserve APD’s investigation, Davis said.

APD officers then called 911, and emergency medical services arrived three minutes later.

Elmore questioned why ICE officers didn’t immediately provide aid.

“Any law enforcement officer should have basic first aid skills and been capable of assessing Wilber for life-threatening injuries and administering aid,” he said.

title: Federal judge questions ICE credibility in hearing on Oregon arrests - Minnesota Lawyer
description:
Preliminary injunction bars ICE warrantless arrests without evasion risk.
Four immigrants testify about ICE arrest encounters in Oregon.
The Ashland arrest was among four arrests described in testimony and declarations that lawyers said showed that federal agents have continued making arrests that violate the injunction.
“We’re confident that the judge is going to make a good decision that restores the validity of the force of his injunction, preventing warrantless arrests in Oregon,” Cunnings said.
